Our Story

Founded by a clinician who lived the lonely bit too

Louis Maxwell is a First Contact Practitioner in UK primary care (HCPC PH128483). When he was diagnosed with lumbar spine degeneration at just 28, he expected clear guidance. Instead, his GP handed him a sheet of home exercises — nothing else.

No treatment plan. No follow-up. No support for managing a lifelong condition. Living with that kind of pain is exhausting.

You are not alone in that gap. It became the mission ofLiving With Arthritis. We exist to give people what Louis did not get: clinically honest, emotionally kind guidance — and a human reply when you need one.

We are a young charity (registered 15 June 2026, no. 1218461), serving people across the UK and independent of Arthritis UK. We will not invent a large clinical board. Louis reviews our content. Motion is lotion — and we are building this with you.

Every resource is free, because no one should choose between affordability and care.

/about/uk-arthritis-search-insights:
Honest data caveats

  • A live Google Trends (GB) geo pull for arthritis returned HTTP 429 Too Many Requests at research time (9 September 2026). We do not claim a live regional RSV league table.
  • Semrush MCP keyword research could not run because the account had insufficient API units. Public Semrush website overview pages were usable and are cited. Top-up: semrush.com/mcp-access.
  • Where search geography is incomplete we use labelled proxies (related joint-query volume; clinical prevalence by region).

1. Where in the UK do people search most?

Absolute related search demand for knee and hip replacement terms is highest in Greater London. Elanic Medical’s Google Keyword Planner analysis (Dec 2024–Nov 2025) put UK averages at about 370,440 searches/month for knee/hip replacement terms (~255,770 knee; ~114,670 hip), with Greater London leading (~47,310/month knee; ~25,080/month hip). Source: Guardian Series / Elanic.

Raw search volume is not the same as per-capita need. London’s self-reported long-term MSK prevalence was 13.4% in 2023 versus England 18.4% (OHID Fingertips / GP Patient Survey).

Highest regional prevalence (a proxy for local info need) is the North East at 23.1% in 2023. South West (~19.0%) and North West (~19.1%) sit above or near the England average. Deprived areas also concentrate MSK burden (OHID; Arthritis UK State of MSK Health 2025).

Priority lensWhere to leanWhy (sourced)
Absolute related search volumeGreater London + large metrosElanic Keyword Planner knee/hip
Prevalence / unmet needNorth East, then northern/deprived localitiesFingertips GPPS; deprivation gradients
Content localisation“Find NHS MSK / physio near you” by ICB / nationNHS community MSK self-referral pathway

2. What related topics do people search alongside arthritis?

Pain is the dominant accompanying theme for inflammatory arthritis in UK Google Trends research (2011–2022): mean RSV for “pain” with RA 58, PsA 34, AS 39 — far above stiffness, fatigue, mood or work (typically 2–7 where available). Source: Rheumatology keae163.087.

Public Semrush organic keywords for Arthritis UK (UK database, Jul 2026) show medicine and supplement adjacency — for example arthritis (position 2, volume 74,000), naproxen (position 4, volume 165,000), and glucosamine (position 1, volume 27,100). Source: Semrush arthritis-uk.org overview.

NHS pathway language people are steered toward includes physiotherapy, occupational therapy, community MSK self-referral, medicines, TENS, aids and surgery when severe. Flare / pacing education is a strong long-tail theme in NHS trust leaflets.

3. What other sites appear for “managing arthritis pain”?

Without Semrush SERP API units we could not dump a live ranked top-10 for the exact phrase on google.co.uk. Below is the verified competitive set that consistently surfaces for this intent in UK search and NHS/NICE pathways.

  • Arthritis UKStrong UK charity authority — managing arthritis pain / symptoms hubs.
  • NHS.ukCondition and treatment hubs; community MSK self-referral pathways.
  • NRASRheumatoid arthritis pain management (non-drug and drug pathways).
  • Patient.infoUK consumer clinical encyclopaedia for OA and arthritis.
  • NICEOA quality standards and chronic pain guideline NG193 inform NHS authority.
  • US / international publishersHealthline, Mayo Clinic, WebMD and Arthritis Foundation still compete in UK SERPs.

Expect NHS + Arthritis UK to own YMYL trust signals. Living With Arthritis differentiates with lived-experience, UK practical daily living, peer support, and clear “what to do next on the NHS” guidance — without claiming medical authority over NHS or NICE.

/accessibility:
Living With Arthritis is committed to ensuring digital accessibility for all users, including people with visual, hearing, motor and cognitive impairments. We continuously work to improve the user experience for everyone and apply the relevant accessibility standards.

This website aims to conform to Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA. These guidelines explain how to make web content more accessible to people with a wide range of disabilities.

Accessibility Features

High Contrast & Colour

All text and interactive elements meet WCAG 2.1 AA contrast ratios (minimum 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text). Our colour palette is tested for the three most common types of colour-blindness.

Full Keyboard Navigation

Every feature — menus, modals, forms, tabs and help chat — is fully operable using keyboard alone. Visible focus indicators appear on all interactive elements with a minimum 2px outline.

Screen Reader Compatible

Semantic HTML5 landmarks, ARIA labels, roles and live regions ensure complete compatibility with JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack screen readers.

Responsive & Adaptive

The site adapts from 320px mobile to ultra-wide desktop. Touch targets are a minimum 44×44px. Text reflows correctly up to 400% zoom without horizontal scrolling.

Language & Localisation

Content is written in plain English (en-GB) at an average reading age of 12–14 years, following UK health content design principles for health literacy.

Alternative Formats

All images include descriptive alt text. Our help chat provides text-based assistance as an alternative to visual navigation. PDF resources are tagged for accessibility.

Conformance Status

We aim to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA across all pages. Where we have identified areas that do not yet fully meet this standard, we are actively working to resolve them. Our site is regularly tested using automated tools (axe, Lighthouse) and manual keyboard/screen reader testing.

Known Limitations

  • Some third-party pages we link to, including the GoFundMe campaign, may have accessibility limitations outside our direct control.
  • Older blog images may have generic alt text — we are progressively improving these.
  • Complex interactive charts may not be fully accessible to all screen readers — text alternatives are provided.

Feedback & Contact

We welcome your feedback on the accessibility of this website. If you encounter any barriers or have suggestions for improvement, please contact us:

Email: info@livingwitharthritis.org.ukPhone: 07760 512 084

We aim to respond to accessibility feedback within 5 working days.

Enforcement Procedure

If you are not satisfied with our response, you can contact the Equality Advisory Support Service (EASS) for further assistance.

/arthritis-flare-ups:
Pillar Guide · 12 min read

Evidence-based strategies to recognise, relieve, and prevent arthritis flare-ups — written for UK patients and aligned with national clinical and NICE guidance.

What should I do during an arthritis flare-up?

Pace activity, use heat or cold as appropriate, take only medicines advised by your GP or pharmacist, and track triggers. Seek urgent care for a single hot joint with fever or sudden inability to weight-bear. This is educational guidance, not personal medical advice.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Frequently asked questions

An arthritis flare-up is a spell of worse pain, stiffness or swelling than your usual day. Rest the sore joint, use ice or heat as it feels comfortable, and contact a GP or NHS 111 if it is not settling — this page is general UK information, not personal medical advice.

Need a short checklist right now?

Download or print our one-page flare action plan — pace, heat/cold, medicines you already have, and when to seek help.

Open the flare action plan Free symptom and flare tracker (PDF)

How do you stop an arthritis flare-up fast?

Rest the joint for 24–48 hours, apply an ice pack for 15–20 minutes every few hours for hot, swollen joints (or heat for stiffness), take a short course of an NSAID like ibuprofen with food, and keep gently moving within a comfortable range. UK guidance recommends contacting your GP or rheumatology team if a flare lasts more than a week, you have a new fever, or symptoms keep worsening despite self-care.

If you live with osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or psoriatic arthritis, you'll know that symptoms don't stay constant. Periods of increased pain, swelling, and stiffness — known as flare-ups — can disrupt daily life without warning. In the UK alone, over 10 million people live with arthritis, and flare management is one of the most searched topics among patients.

This comprehensive guide brings together the latest evidence on what triggers flare-ups, how to find relief quickly, and practical strategies to reduce their frequency. Whether you've been recently diagnosed or have managed arthritis for years, this page is designed to be your go-to resource.

What Is an Arthritis Flare-Up?

A flare-up is a temporary period when your arthritis symptoms — pain, stiffness, swelling, and fatigue — become noticeably worse than your usual baseline. Flares can last anywhere from a few hours to several weeks, depending on the type of arthritis and the trigger.

In osteoarthritis (OA), flares are often triggered by overuse of a joint or changes in weather. In rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA), flares are driven by immune system activity and can be more unpredictable. Understanding the difference matters because the management approach varies.

Key point: Flare-ups are a normal part of living with arthritis. Having a plan in place can significantly reduce their impact on your quality of life and help you feel more in control.

Common Flare-Up Triggers

Identifying your personal triggers is one of the most powerful steps you can take. While triggers vary between individuals, research and patient surveys consistently highlight these common culprits:

Cold & Damp Weather

UK winters are a well-known trigger. Low barometric pressure may increase joint fluid pressure, while cold reduces blood flow to extremities.

Overexertion

Doing too much on a 'good day' is a classic pattern. Pacing activities is crucial to avoid the boom-and-bust cycle.

Poor Sleep

Sleep deprivation increases inflammatory cytokines and lowers pain thresholds. Prioritising sleep hygiene is essential.

Stress & Anxiety

Psychological stress triggers cortisol dysregulation and heightened inflammation, directly worsening arthritis symptoms.

Pro-Inflammatory Diet

Excess sugar, processed foods, saturated fats, and alcohol promote systemic inflammation that fuels flare-ups.

Missed Medications

Skipping or inconsistently taking prescribed DMARDs or biologics (in RA/PsA) can trigger rebound flares.

Recognising Flare-Up Symptoms Early

Catching a flare early allows you to intervene before it peaks. Watch for these warning signs — many patients report subtle changes 24–48 hours before a full flare:

  • Increased joint stiffness, especially morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes
  • Swelling, warmth, or redness around one or more joints
  • Unusual fatigue or a general feeling of being unwell
  • Pain that disrupts sleep or wakes you at night
  • Reduced grip strength or difficulty with fine motor tasks
  • Mood changes — irritability, low mood, or brain fog
  • Skin flares (in psoriatic arthritis)
  • Increased reliance on pain medication

Keeping a symptom diary helps you spot patterns and identify your unique early warning signs. Our Self Help Tool makes finding the right exercises effortless.

Immediate Relief During a Flare-Up

When a flare hits, your priority is to reduce inflammation, manage pain, and protect the affected joint. Here's a practical action plan aligned with national clinical guidance:

1

Apply Ice or Heat

Use an ice pack wrapped in a towel for 15–20 minutes on swollen joints to reduce inflammation. For stiffness without significant swelling, a warm compress or hot water bottle may be more effective. Alternate as needed.

2

Rest the Affected Joint

Reduce load on the flaring joint but avoid complete immobility, which can increase stiffness. Gentle range-of-motion movements every few hours maintain flexibility.

3

Use Over-the-Counter Pain Relief

Topical NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen gel) applied directly to the joint are a first-line option with fewer systemic side effects. Oral paracetamol or ibuprofen may also help — follow dosage guidance and consult your pharmacist.

4

Elevate and Support

Elevate swollen joints above heart level where possible. Use supports, splints, or compression garments recommended by your physiotherapist to reduce strain.

5

Pace Your Activities

Break tasks into smaller chunks with rest periods. Use assistive devices — jar openers, long-handled reachers, ergonomic tools — to reduce joint stress.

Get Personalised Exercise Support

Our Help Chat can recommend exercises, diet tips, and coping strategies tailored to your arthritis type.

Start a chat

Diet & Nutrition During Flare-Ups

What you eat directly affects inflammation levels. During a flare, doubling down on an anti-inflammatory diet can accelerate recovery. The Mediterranean diet is the most studied and recommended pattern for arthritis patients.

Eat More

  • • Fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) — aim for 2 portions/week
  • • Berries, cherries, and dark leafy greens
  • • Extra virgin olive oil as your primary cooking fat
  • • Nuts and seeds (walnuts, flaxseeds, chia)
  • • Whole grains, legumes, and pulses
  • • Turmeric with black pepper, ginger, garlic

Eat Less

  • • Processed and red meats
  • • Refined sugars and sugary drinks
  • • Fried foods and trans fats
  • • Excessive alcohol (especially during flares)
  • • White bread, pastries, and refined carbohydrates
  • • High-sodium processed foods

Turmeric deserves special mention: a 2016 systematic review found that curcumin at around 1000 mg/day significantly reduced arthritis pain and inflammation, sometimes comparable to NSAIDs. Take it with piperine (black pepper extract) for better absorption. Always check with your GP if you're on blood thinners.

For detailed meal plans and anti-inflammatory recipes, visit our Diet & Nutrition Hub.

Exercise During Flare-Ups

It might seem counterintuitive, but complete rest during a flare can make things worse. Gentle movement prevents stiffness, maintains muscle strength around the joint, and supports blood flow to promote healing.

Flare-Friendly Exercise Guide

Gentle Range-of-Motion

  • • Ankle circles
  • • Wrist rotations
  • • Shoulder rolls
  • • Knee bends
5–10 min, 2×/day

Low-Impact Cardio

  • • Short walks (10–15 min)
  • • Stationary cycling (low resistance)
  • • Pool walking or aqua therapy
15–20 min, most days

Restorative Stretching

  • • Chair yoga
  • • Gentle hamstring stretches
  • • Cat-cow spinal movement
  • • Deep breathing exercises
10–15 min, daily

The golden rule: if exercise increases your pain significantly for more than 2 hours afterwards, you've done too much. Scale back and try again more gently. Between flares, build up with our structured programmes on the Exercise Hub.

Hydrotherapy (exercising in warm water) is particularly effective during flares — the buoyancy reduces joint load by up to 90% while the warmth soothes stiffness. Ask your GP or physiotherapist about public hydrotherapy referrals.

Mental Health & Emotional Wellbeing

The psychological impact of flare-ups is often underestimated. Living with unpredictable pain affects mood, relationships, work, and self-esteem. Research shows that people with arthritis are 2–3 times more likely to experience anxiety or depression than the general population.

  • Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR): Clinical trials show 8-week MBSR programmes reduce pain perception and improve coping in arthritis patients. Free resources are available through the official UK health apps library.
  • Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT): NICE recommends CBT for chronic pain. It helps reframe catastrophic thinking patterns that amplify the pain experience. Ask your GP for an GP referral.
  • Peer Support: Connecting with others who understand is powerful. Join our Community Hub for moderated discussions and shared experiences.
  • Pacing & Acceptance: Learning to pace activities and accept limitations on bad days (without guilt) is a clinically recognised strategy that reduces the boom-bust cycle.

If you're struggling emotionally during a flare, the national mental health helpline is available 24/7 on 111 (option 2), and the Samaritans can be reached on 116 123.

Medications & Supplements

Your medication strategy during a flare depends on your type of arthritis and what your rheumatologist or GP has prescribed. Here's a general overview aligned with NICE guidance:

OptionWhen to UseNotes
Topical NSAIDsFirst-line for localised OA flaresIbuprofen gel — fewer side effects than oral
Oral NSAIDsModerate-severe OA/RA flaresUse lowest effective dose, short duration; gastroprotection may be needed
CorticosteroidsSevere RA/PsA flaresShort courses or joint injections — prescribed by rheumatology
DMARDs / BiologicsOngoing RA/PsA managementDo not stop during flares — contact your team for dose review
ParacetamolMild pain, or alongside other treatmentsLimited anti-inflammatory effect; safer long-term profile

Evidence-Based Supplements

Curcumin (Turmeric)

500–1000 mg/day

Strong evidence

Take with piperine; anti-inflammatory comparable to NSAIDs in some trials

Omega-3 Fish Oil

2–3 g EPA+DHA/day

Moderate-Strong evidence

Reduces morning stiffness and joint tenderness in RA

Glucosamine + Chondroitin

1500 mg + 1200 mg/day

Mixed evidence

Some patients report benefit; may take 2–3 months to notice effects

When to See Your GP

Seek medical advice if:

  • A flare lasts more than two weeks despite self-management
  • You develop a hot, red, significantly swollen joint — this could indicate infection (septic arthritis), which is a medical emergency
  • You experience new symptoms such as fever, unexplained weight loss, or rash alongside joint pain
  • Your current medications are no longer controlling symptoms effectively
  • Flare-ups are becoming more frequent or severe over time
  • You're experiencing significant mood changes, anxiety, or depression related to your condition

Prevention Strategies

While you can't eliminate flare-ups entirely, you can significantly reduce their frequency and severity with consistent, proactive habits:

Follow a Mediterranean Diet

Anti-inflammatory eating reduces baseline inflammation levels, making flares less likely and less severe.

Maintain a Healthy Weight

Every pound lost removes approximately 4 pounds of pressure from your knees. Even modest weight loss (5–10%) improves symptoms.

Exercise Regularly Between Flares

Build strength, flexibility, and cardiovascular fitness when you're feeling well. Stronger muscles better protect joints.

Prioritise Sleep

Aim for 7–9 hours. Use sleep hygiene practices: consistent bedtime, cool room, no screens 1 hour before bed.

Manage Stress Proactively

Build mindfulness, breathing exercises, or journaling into your daily routine — don't wait until you're overwhelmed.

Take Medications Consistently

For RA/PsA, consistent DMARD or biologic use is the single most important factor in preventing flares.

Pace Your Activities

Use the 'activity-rest-activity' pattern. Plan demanding tasks for your best times of day and alternate with rest.

Track Your Patterns

Use a symptom diary to identify personal triggers — weather, food, activity, stress — and adjust proactively.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does an arthritis flare-up last?

Most flare-ups last between a few days and two weeks. If symptoms persist beyond two weeks or worsen rapidly, contact your GP or rheumatology team for advice.

Can weather trigger arthritis flare-ups?

Many people in the UK report increased joint pain and stiffness during cold, damp weather. While research is mixed, barometric pressure changes may affect joint fluid pressure. Keeping warm and staying active indoors can help.

Should I rest or exercise during a flare-up?

A combination is best. Rest the most affected joints but keep moving gently. Low-impact activities like swimming, walking, or chair-based stretches help maintain mobility without aggravating inflammation.

What foods make arthritis flare-ups worse?

Pro-inflammatory foods such as processed meats, refined sugar, fried foods, excess alcohol, and foods high in saturated fat can worsen inflammation. An anti-inflammatory Mediterranean-style diet is widely recommended.

Is turmeric effective for arthritis flare-ups?

Research supports curcumin (the active compound in turmeric) at around 500–1000 mg/day with piperine for improved absorption. Studies show it can reduce pain and inflammation, sometimes comparable to NSAIDs. Always consult your GP before starting supplements.

Evidence-based management of arthritis and chronic musculoskeletal pain

Chronic pain is one of the most common reasons people in the UK seek medical help, and arthritis and fibromyalgia are two of the leading drivers. Search behaviour reflects this — huge volumes of people look up knee arthritis, fibromyalgia and back pain relief every month. Managing these conditions well requires a combined approach: appropriate medical input, physiotherapy and steady lifestyle change, rather than reliance on any single intervention.

Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease driven by gradual cartilage loss. When it affects weight-bearing joints such as the knee or hip, simple things — walking, climbing stairs, standing up from a chair — can become painful. First-line management is conservative: weight management to reduce load on the joints, and progressive strengthening of the surrounding muscles so they can act as shock absorbers. When conservative care is not enough, additional options include Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS), a non-invasive method that uses low-voltage currents to interrupt pain signals and stimulate endorphin release. TENS is not a cure, but it is a useful adjunct for many people who want to reduce reliance on stronger painkillers.

Fibromyalgia is a different problem. It is characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain alongside fatigue, disrupted sleep and brain-fog. Rather than a structural joint disease, fibromyalgia is increasingly understood as a disorder of pain processing in the central nervous system: sensory signals are amplified, so ordinary stimuli register as painful. Management focuses on calming that overactive signalling — graded aerobic exercise, sleep hygiene, pacing, cognitive approaches, and sometimes medications such as duloxetine or pregabalin under specialist guidance.

Back pain follows similar principles. Acute back pain usually settles with gentle movement and time; chronic back pain responds best to a structured plan that strengthens the deep core muscles and corrects long-standing posture habits. Injections, short courses of steroids or nerve blocks can give meaningful temporary relief, but they rarely fix the underlying cause. The most durable results come from consistent stretching, strengthening and gradual return to normal activity guided by a physiotherapist.

This is general information, not medical advice. Speak to a GP, rheumatologist or physiotherapist before starting any new treatment or stopping existing medication.

/arthritis-mental-health:
Living with arthritis is not just a physical experience. Persistent pain, fatigue and uncertainty take a real toll on mood, sleep and identity. This evidence-based guide covers what to look out for, what helps, and where to get support — for you and the people around you.

Mental health impact of arthritis

Arthritis is a whole-life condition. Alongside swollen joints and morning stiffness come broken sleep, cancelled plans, uncertainty about the future and, for many people, a slow renegotiation of who they are at work and at home. Those losses are real, and they show up in mood, motivation and concentration long before anyone calls it a mental health problem.

The strain tends to build in three ways. Pain itself is processed in brain regions that also handle emotion, so persistent pain lowers mood and lowers the threshold at which the next pain feels unbearable. Fatigue shrinks the activities that normally restore you. And unpredictability — not knowing whether tomorrow is a good day or a flare — makes planning, socialising and working feel risky, so people withdraw.

Naming this early matters. Distress that is recognised and treated responds well; distress that is dismissed as "just part of arthritis" tends to deepen and can make pain, disability and treatment adherence measurably worse.

Depression in arthritis

Depression is more common in people with inflammatory and degenerative arthritis than in the general population, and it is frequently missed because low mood, tiredness and poor sleep are all assumed to be joint symptoms. The distinguishing features are persistence and pervasiveness: low mood or loss of pleasure on most days for two weeks or more, along with hopelessness, guilt, loss of appetite, difficulty concentrating, or thoughts that life is not worth living.

Treatment works. UK Talking Therapies services accept self-referral in England — you do not need to go through your GP — and offer cognitive behavioural therapy adapted for long-term conditions. Antidepressants can help, and some, such as duloxetine or low-dose amitriptyline, are used in chronic pain in their own right; your GP can discuss whether one is suitable alongside your arthritis medication.

Tell your rheumatology team as well as your GP. Uncontrolled inflammation drives mood symptoms, so a flare that is treated properly often lifts mood as a side effect, and knowing you are struggling may change how the team plans your care.

Anxiety & pain

Anxiety in arthritis usually attaches to something specific: fear of a flare, fear of falling, fear of a joint replacement, fear of losing a job or a benefit. That vigilance is understandable, but it has a cost — muscles stay braced, breathing gets shallow, sleep becomes light, and the nervous system reads ordinary sensations as danger. Pain feels sharper as a result.

The most common downstream problem is avoidance. Stopping the walk, the swim or the social event reduces anxiety in the moment and increases disability over months, because deconditioning makes the next attempt harder. Graded, paced return to activity — small, boring, repeatable amounts — breaks that cycle more reliably than waiting until you feel confident.

Practical anchors help: slow breathing with a longer out-breath, a written flare plan so a bad day has a script rather than a panic, and pacing that budgets activity across the week instead of overdoing good days and paying for it afterwards.

Coping strategies

Pacing is the foundation. Break tasks into shorter blocks with planned rests, alternate heavier and lighter jobs, and stop before the pain forces you to. The aim is a steady, sustainable level rather than the boom-and-bust pattern most people fall into.

Keep the parts of life that carry meaning. Adapt rather than abandon: a shorter walk, a seated version of a hobby, an online rather than in-person meet-up. Activity that matters to you protects mood far better than rest does.

Sleep and movement are treatments, not extras. A consistent wake time, a cool dark bedroom, timing pain relief so it covers the first part of the night, and daily low-impact movement all improve pain and mood together. Alcohol is a poor sleep aid and worsens both.

Finally, be specific when you ask for help. "I need someone to do the weekly shop on Thursdays" is easier for family to act on than "I am struggling", and it protects you from the exhaustion of explaining an invisible condition over and over.

Mindfulness & meditation

Mindfulness does not switch pain off. What trials in chronic pain consistently show is a change in the relationship with pain: less pain-related distress, less interference with daily life, and lower anxiety scores. For many people that is the difference between a day lost and a day managed.

Start small and unglamorous. Ten minutes of guided body scan or breath-focused practice most days, at a time you can protect, beats an ambitious plan you abandon. Free NHS-endorsed apps and audio guides are widely available, and gentle mind-body movement such as tai chi or chair yoga combines the same attentional practice with the joint-friendly exercise arthritis needs anyway.

If your mind wanders constantly, nothing has gone wrong — noticing and returning is the practice. If sitting still increases distress, which sometimes happens with trauma or severe anxiety, use a movement-based version and mention it to your GP or therapist.

Support resources

Your GP is the usual first stop and can refer, prescribe and sign-post. In England you can also self-refer to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing your GP first; equivalent services exist across Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Rheumatology teams often include specialist nurses with a telephone advice line — use it during a flare rather than waiting for the next appointment. Occupational therapy can reduce the daily friction that grinds mood down, and physiotherapy can rebuild confidence in movement after a long avoidant period.

Peer support matters more than people expect, because it removes the work of explaining. Our own community pages and moderated groups are one route; local hospital and council-run pain management programmes are another.

If pain is dominating life, ask about a pain management programme — these are group, multidisciplinary and specifically designed to improve function and mood rather than to eliminate pain.

When to seek help

Book a routine GP appointment if low mood, anxiety or sleep problems have lasted more than two weeks, if you have stopped doing things you used to enjoy, if you are drinking more, or if you are taking more pain relief than prescribed to cope with how you feel.

Seek help the same day if you feel unable to keep yourself safe, if you have thoughts of harming yourself, or if you are so distressed you cannot function. Call 111 for urgent advice, Samaritans free on 116 123 at any hour, or text SHOUT to 85258.

Call 999 if you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has taken an overdose. Asking for help early is not an overreaction — it is the same principle as treating a flare before it becomes a hospital admission.

Daily tips for joint health

Small, everyday habits that ease stiffness, support mobility, and help you live well with arthritis.

Morning Stretches

Start each day with 5 minutes of gentle stretching to ease morning stiffness.

Stay Hydrated

Aim for 6-8 glasses of water daily — dehydration can worsen joint stiffness.

Anti-inflammatory Snacks

Keep walnuts, berries, and dark leafy greens handy for quick, joint-friendly snacking.

Walk 20 Minutes

A steady 20-minute walk can ease stiffness, lift mood and support joint health — start gently.

Prioritise Sleep

Quality sleep reduces inflammation — aim for 7-9 hours with a consistent schedule.

Pace Yourself

Balance activity with rest. Break tasks into smaller chunks to protect your joints.

/conditions/arthritis:
Last reviewed 11 July 2026

What is arthritis and how is it treated?

Arthritis describes over 100 conditions that affect the joints — causing pain, stiffness, swelling and reduced movement. Osteoarthritis (wear-related) and rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory) are the most common forms in the UK. Effective management combines targeted exercise, weight optimisation, an anti-inflammatory diet, medical treatment for pain and inflammation, and — when needed — specialist rheumatology care, injections or joint replacement surgery. Early diagnosis and a structured care plan dramatically improve long-term outcomes.

Medically reviewed by Maxwell

First Contact Practitioner • HCPC PH128483 • Last updated June 2026

Reviewer details and the site's clinical review process are documented in our editorial standards.

What is arthritis?

Arthritis is not a single disease — it is a broad term covering more than 100 joint conditions. The two most common are osteoarthritis, where joint cartilage gradually wears down, and rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks the joint lining.

More than 10 million people in the UK live with arthritis. It is the leading cause of pain and disability and affects people of every age — including children with juvenile arthritis.

What are the symptoms of arthritis?

  • Joint pain that worsens with activity or after rest
  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Swelling, warmth or redness around a joint
  • Reduced range of movement
  • Grating, popping or clicking sounds (crepitus)
  • Fatigue and low-grade fever (inflammatory types)

How is arthritis diagnosed?

A GP or first-contact practitioner will take a detailed history, examine your joints and check for swelling or restricted movement. Blood tests (CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, uric acid) and imaging (X-ray, ultrasound, MRI) help identify the type and severity of arthritis and rule out other causes.

What do arthritis patients commonly look for?

People newly diagnosed — and those managing arthritis long-term — typically search for help in four areas:

  • Pain relief options: topical and oral anti-inflammatories, heat and cold therapy, compression supports, splints and pain-relief gels.
  • Diagnostics: faster access to imaging and rheumatology assessment, sometimes via private clinics.
  • Specialist care: physiotherapy, rheumatology, podiatry and occupational therapy.
  • Supplements & nutrition: glucosamine, chondroitin, collagen, omega-3, turmeric and an anti-inflammatory eating pattern.

This is educational information only — we don't endorse specific brands or products. Always speak to a clinician before starting a new treatment, supplement or device.

What are the evidence-based treatment options for arthritis?

  • Exercise: progressive strength, mobility and aerobic training reduce pain and improve function — see our exercise guide.
  • Weight management: a 5–10% reduction in body weight significantly reduces knee and hip load.
  • Anti-inflammatory diet: Mediterranean-style eating — see our diet guide and foods to avoid.
  • Medication: paracetamol, topical and oral NSAIDs, DMARDs and biologics for inflammatory arthritis.
  • Injections & surgery: corticosteroid or hyaluronic acid injections, and joint replacement when conservative care has been exhausted.
  • Mental health support: chronic pain affects mood — see our mental health guide.

Frequently asked questions

What is arthritis?

Arthritis is an umbrella term for over 100 conditions that cause joint pain, stiffness and swelling. The most common forms in the UK are osteoarthritis (wear-related) and rheumatoid arthritis (inflammatory).

What are the early warning signs of arthritis?

Persistent joint pain, morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, swelling around a joint, reduced range of motion and warmth or redness over a joint. Symptoms lasting more than two weeks warrant a GP review.

How is arthritis diagnosed?

A clinician reviews your symptoms, examines affected joints, and may request blood tests (CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP) and imaging (X-ray, ultrasound or MRI) to confirm the type of arthritis.

Can arthritis be cured?

Most forms of arthritis cannot be cured, but symptoms can be effectively managed with exercise, weight management, an anti-inflammatory diet, medication, and in some cases joint replacement surgery.

What treatments help most?

Evidence consistently supports a combination of progressive exercise, weight optimisation, topical or oral anti-inflammatories, physiotherapy and joint protection strategies. Inflammatory arthritis often needs DMARDs or biologics.

When should I see a specialist?

Ask your GP for a rheumatology referral if you have suspected inflammatory arthritis, persistent unexplained joint swelling, or symptoms that are not responding to first-line care.

Can arthritis come and go?

For some types, yes. Inflammatory arthritis (like rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis) commonly flares and eases in cycles — periods of active symptoms followed by remission. Gout is defined by sudden attacks with symptom-free periods between them. Osteoarthritis behaves differently: it’s typically a gradual, progressive condition, though day-to-day pain can still vary with activity, weather, or overuse. If symptoms are genuinely disappearing and returning, that pattern itself is a useful thing to describe to a GP or rheumatologist, since it helps narrow down which type of arthritis is involved.

/conditions/calcific-periarthritis:
What is Calcific Periarthritis?

Calcific periarthritis is a sudden, intensely painful inflammation of the soft tissue around a joint, caused by deposits of calcium hydroxyapatite crystals forming inside a tendon or its surrounding tissue. The shoulder is by far the most common site — usually the supraspinatus tendon of the rotator cuff — but it can also affect the hip, wrist, finger, knee or foot.

Unlike osteoarthritis, the joint surface itself is usually healthy. The pain comes from the body's inflammatory reaction as the deposit forms and then breaks down. Attacks typically peak over 1–2 weeks and settle over 6–12 weeks, and in most people the calcium deposit eventually resorbs on its own. It is most common between the ages of 30 and 60 and slightly more common in women.

Symptoms

  • Sudden, severe pain around the shoulder or another joint, often waking you at night
  • Pain that comes on over hours to a couple of days with no injury
  • Marked loss of movement — lifting the arm above shoulder height may be almost impossible
  • Local warmth, swelling and tenderness over the tendon rather than the joint line
  • Pain lying on the affected side
  • In milder cases, a nagging ache and catching sensation with overhead activity
  • Occasionally a mild fever and raised inflammatory markers, which can mimic infection

When to see a GP

If you have persistent joint pain, swelling or stiffness, book a GP appointment. Early diagnosis means earlier access to the right care and better long-term outcomes.

Causes & Risk Factors

  • Calcium hydroxyapatite crystal deposition within a tendon, then an inflammatory flare as it resorbs
  • Repetitive overhead loading of the rotator cuff — sport, manual work, decorating
  • Reduced local blood supply and age-related tendon change (most common at 30–60)
  • Diabetes and thyroid disorders — both raise the risk noticeably
  • Kidney disease and disorders of calcium or phosphate handling
  • Female sex and a previous episode on the other side

Treatment & Management

  • NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) with stomach protection — first-line for the acute flare
  • Relative rest and ice for the first few days, avoiding overhead loading
  • Ultrasound-guided steroid injection for pain that does not settle with tablets
  • Barbotage (needle lavage) — an ultrasound-guided procedure that breaks up and washes out the deposit
  • Extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) for persistent deposits
  • Physiotherapy once the acute pain eases, to restore range and rotator-cuff strength
  • Surgery (arthroscopic removal) is rarely needed and reserved for long-standing, disabling cases

Best Diet

No diet dissolves a calcium deposit, and cutting calcium out of your diet does not help — it weakens bone without changing the tendon. What diet can do is dampen the inflammatory response and support the conditions linked to recurrence.

Eat more

  • Oily fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel) twice a week for omega-3
  • Fruit, vegetables, wholegrains, olive oil, nuts and pulses
  • Adequate protein to support tendon repair and muscle around the joint

Limit

  • Ultra-processed food, refined sugar and sugary drinks
  • Alcohol, particularly while taking NSAIDs

If you have diabetes or a thyroid condition, keeping it well controlled is one of the few things shown to reduce the chance of a further episode.

Exercise & Movement

During the acute attack, stop overhead loading — pushing through it prolongs the flare. As pain eases, graded movement prevents the shoulder stiffening into a frozen state.

  • Pendulum swings and passive range-of-movement work in the first two weeks
  • Assisted elevation with a stick or the other arm as pain allows
  • Isometric rotator-cuff holds before progressing to resistance bands
  • Scapular setting and postural work to offload the cuff
  • Gradual return to overhead lifting only once full pain-free range has returned

/conditions/fibromyalgia:
What is fibromyalgia?

Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition causing widespread pain, fatigue, sleep problems and 'fibro fog'. It's a disorder of pain processing rather than joint damage. NICE recommends graded exercise, CBT and paced activity as first-line management.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Frequently asked questions

What is Fibromyalgia?

Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that causes pain all over the body, often alongside extreme tiredness, poor sleep and difficulty concentrating ("fibro fog"). It is thought to be caused by changes in the way the central nervous system processes pain signals.

Around 1 in 20 people in the UK are affected, with women more commonly diagnosed than men. While there is no cure, a combination of pacing, gentle exercise, sleep hygiene and medication can dramatically improve quality of life.

Symptoms

  • Widespread pain on both sides of the body, above and below the waist, lasting more than 3 months
  • Profound fatigue not relieved by rest
  • Sleep problems — non-restorative sleep, restless legs
  • Cognitive difficulties ('fibro fog') — memory and concentration issues
  • Headaches and migraine
  • Irritable bowel symptoms
  • Heightened sensitivity to light, sound, smells or touch
  • Anxiety or low mood

When to see a GP

If you have persistent joint pain, swelling or stiffness, book a GP appointment. Early diagnosis means earlier access to the right care and better long-term outcomes.

Causes & Risk Factors

  • Central sensitisation — the nervous system amplifies pain signals
  • Triggering events — physical injury, infection, surgery, emotional stress
  • Genetic vulnerability — fibromyalgia often runs in families
  • More common alongside rheumatoid arthritis, lupus or osteoarthritis
  • Sleep disorders and unrefreshing sleep

Treatment & Management

  • Pacing — balancing activity and rest to avoid boom-and-bust cycles
  • Graded exercise built up slowly, especially aerobic and aquatic work
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for pain coping and sleep
  • Antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine) — used at low doses for pain and sleep
  • Pregabalin or gabapentin for nerve-related pain
  • Sleep hygiene — consistent bedtime, cool dark room, no screens late
  • Mindfulness, yoga and tai chi

Best Diet

No single diet treats fibromyalgia, but a balanced anti-inflammatory pattern can ease fatigue and support a healthy weight.

  • Mediterranean diet rich in vegetables, fish, olive oil and whole grains
  • Limit caffeine, alcohol and ultra-processed foods that disrupt sleep
  • Stay well hydrated
  • Check vitamin D and B12 levels — deficiencies are common in fibromyalgia
  • If certain foods seem to trigger symptoms, keep a brief food and symptom diary

Exercise & Movement

Movement is one of the most effective treatments for fibromyalgia, even though pain and fatigue can make it feel counter-intuitive. Start tiny and build slowly.

  • Walking — start with 5 minutes a day and add a minute each week
  • Aquatic exercise in a warm pool — particularly well-evidenced
  • Tai chi and yoga for gentle strength, balance and breathing
  • Pilates for core strength without high impact
  • Strength work 2 days a week — light weights or resistance bands

A "good" session should leave you no more sore than usual the following day. If it does, drop back and rebuild.

/conditions/foot-and-ankle-arthritis:
Common types of foot and ankle arthritis

  • Big toe arthritis (hallux rigidus) — the most common foot osteoarthritis. The big toe stiffens and hurts when you push off; a bony bump often appears on top of the joint.
  • Midfoot arthritis — deep ache across the top of the foot, worse on uneven ground or after previous injury.
  • Ankle osteoarthritis — less common than knee or hip OA but often disabling; many cases follow an old fracture, dislocation or repeated severe sprain.
  • Rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis in the feet — small toe joints, ball-of-foot pain, swelling and deformity; footwear and early rheumatology care matter.

Gout also loves the big toe — see our gout guide if flares are sudden, hot and intensely painful.

What are the symptoms?

  • Pain with every step — or a deep ache that builds after walking
  • Morning stiffness — brief in osteoarthritis, often longer in inflammatory arthritis
  • Swelling — around the ankle, midfoot or big toe joint
  • Reduced push-off — especially with hallux rigidus
  • Instability or fear of falling — stiff, painful ankles alter balance (see our falls prevention guide)
  • Shoe struggle — standard footwear presses on bony bumps or swollen toes

What causes it?

  • Previous injury — ankle fractures and severe sprains are the leading risk for ankle OA
  • Age and cumulative load — cartilage wear in the big toe and midfoot after 50
  • Inflammatory disease — rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis frequently involve the feet
  • Biomechanics and footwear — high heels, narrow toe boxes and uncorrected flat or high-arch patterns
  • Family history — especially for hallux rigidus and Heberden-like patterns in the toes

Daily tasks most affected

Walking on uneven ground84% Standing for long periods78% Finding comfortable shoes72% Climbing stairs61% Getting going after sitting55%

What are the best exercises?

Keep the ankle and toes moving within a comfortable range. Warm the foot in a basin of warm water for 10 minutes first. Full routine: foot and ankle arthritis exercises.

Range of motion

  • Ankle circles — 10 each way, both feet
  • Alphabet tracing — write letters in the air with your big toe
  • Toe spreads and towel scrunches — strengthen intrinsic foot muscles

Strength and balance

  • Heel raises — hold a counter, rise onto toes, lower slowly. Build to 2 sets of 10–15
  • Band dorsiflexion — pull toes toward you against a light band
  • Single-leg stance — near a wall; progress toward 30 seconds each side

Avoid: high-impact jumping, barefoot walking on hard floors during flares, and forcing a painful big toe into deep bend.

Footwear, orthotics and lifestyle

  • Wide, deep toe box and adjustable fastenings for day-to-day swelling
  • Rocker or stiff sole for big toe arthritis to reduce joint bend at push-off
  • Removable insoles so NHS or private orthotics can fit
  • Low heel — under about 2.5 cm reduces forefoot pressure
  • Pair footwear changes with the same anti-inflammatory pattern in our Diet Hub

Daily foot-care checklist

Footwear

Wide toe box, grip sole, low heel.

Mobility

Ankle circles and toe work daily.

Balance

Brief single-leg practice near a counter.

Warm-up

Warm soak before the first walk.

How is it treated in the UK?

Self-management

  • Supportive shoes and activity pacing
  • Daily mobility and balance routine
  • Topical NSAID gel around the painful joint if suitable for you
  • Heat before activity; short ice packs after a flare

NHS pathway

  • GP — assessment, X-rays or blood tests when inflammatory disease is possible
  • Podiatry — biomechanics, orthotics, footwear advice
  • Physiotherapy — graded loading and balance (self-referral in many areas)
  • Orthopaedics — injections, fusion or replacement when conservative care is not enough
  • Rheumatology — if RA, PsA or other inflammatory disease is suspected

If referrals are delayed, our waiting-list help guide covers what you can do meanwhile.

When should you see your GP?

  • Foot or ankle pain lasting more than a few weeks
  • Warm, red or markedly swollen joint
  • New deformity, ulcers, or numbness in people with diabetes
  • Falls or near-falls linked to unstable ankles
  • Known inflammatory arthritis with a new foot flare

What are the first signs of foot or ankle arthritis? Early signs include morning stiffness in the ankle or big toe, a deep ache with the first steps of the day, swelling around the joint after walking, and shoes that suddenly feel tight over a bony bump on top of the big toe joint. What is the best footwear for foot arthritis? Look for a wide, deep toe box, a firm heel counter, cushioned sole, low heel (under 2.5 cm) and adjustable fastenings. For big toe arthritis, a stiff or rocker sole reduces bending at the painful joint. Removable insoles leave room for orthotics. What exercises help ankle arthritis? Daily ankle circles, alphabet tracing with the big toe, towel scrunches, gentle calf raises and single-leg balance near a counter maintain mobility and stability. Stop short of sharp pain and warm the foot first. See our ankle arthritis exercises guide for a full routine. Can NHS podiatry help with foot arthritis? Yes. Ask your GP for a podiatry referral, or self-refer where your area allows it. Podiatrists assess biomechanics, advise on footwear and can prescribe custom orthotics that redistribute pressure away from painful joints. When should I see a GP about foot or ankle pain? Book an appointment if pain lasts more than a few weeks, limits walking, comes with warm swelling or deformity, or follows an old fracture. /conditions/knee-arthritis:
What is knee arthritis?

Knee arthritis is the gradual wearing down of the cartilage that lines the knee joint. The knee has three compartments — medial (inside), lateral (outside) and patellofemoral (under the kneecap) — and arthritis can affect any combination of them.

As cartilage thins, the bones underneath thicken, small bony spurs (osteophytes) form, and the lining of the joint can become inflamed. This produces the familiar mix of pain, stiffness and swelling.

How common is it in the UK?

Around 4.11 million people in the UK live with knee osteoarthritis, making it the single most common cause of mobility loss in older adults.

What are the symptoms of knee arthritis?

  • Pain on stairs — particularly going downstairs, when load on the patellofemoral joint peaks
  • Morning stiffness — usually under 30 minutes; longer suggests inflammatory arthritis
  • Swelling — a "boggy" feeling around the kneecap, often worse after activity
  • Crepitus — grinding or clicking when bending the knee
  • Giving way — the knee buckles momentarily, usually because the quadriceps have weakened
  • Reduced range — difficulty fully straightening or bending the knee

What causes knee arthritis?

  • Age — most cases develop after 45
  • Body weight — every extra pound transmits ~4 lb of force through the knee
  • Previous injury — meniscus tears, ACL ruptures and fractures multiply risk 3–6×
  • Occupation — repeated kneeling, squatting or heavy lifting (carpet fitters, tilers, farmers)
  • Sex — women are roughly 1.5× more likely to develop knee OA after menopause
  • Alignment — bow-legs (varus) load the medial compartment; knock-knees (valgus) load the lateral

Symptom impact (typical patient survey)

Pain on stairs88% Morning stiffness76% Swelling after activity64% Sleep disturbance52% Giving way38%

What are the best exercises for knee arthritis?

NICE lists exercise as a core treatment for everyone with knee OA — not optional. The most effective programmes combine quadriceps strengthening with low-impact aerobic work.

Strengthening

  • Straight-leg raises — the safest way to load the quadriceps without bending the knee. 3 sets of 10, daily.
  • Wall sits — start at 10 seconds, build to 60. Stop above 90° of knee bend if painful.
  • Step-ups — onto a low step, controlling the lowering phase. 2 sets of 10 each leg.
  • Glute bridges — strong glutes reduce knee load by improving hip mechanics.

Low-impact cardio

  • Stationary cycling — set the saddle high enough that the knee is almost straight at the bottom
  • Swimming or aqua-aerobics — buoyancy removes 70–90% of body weight from the joint
  • Walking — start with 10-minute blocks, build to 30; cushioned shoes only

What diet helps knee arthritis?

Weight loss is the single most powerful non-surgical treatment for knee arthritis. A 5% reduction in body weight typically delivers a 20–30% drop in knee pain. Pair calorie control with the Mediterranean pattern covered in our Diet Hub:

  • Oily fish twice a week (salmon, mackerel, sardines)
  • Plenty of vegetables, berries, nuts, olive oil and whole grains
  • Limit ultra-processed food, sugary drinks and excess alcohol

Daily knee-care checklist

Strength

Straight-leg raises and wall sits — start small, build slowly.

Cycle

Cycling is easier on the knee than running or jumping.

Weight

Losing 5% of body weight often eases knee load a lot.

Ice

Ten minutes after activity if the knee is warm or swollen.

How is knee arthritis treated?

Self-management

  • Daily strengthening programme
  • Weight management
  • Heat before activity, ice after
  • Walking pole on the opposite side to offload the painful knee

Medical treatments

  • Topical NSAIDs (ibuprofen or diclofenac gel) — first-line per NICE for knee OA
  • Oral NSAIDs / paracetamol — short courses where topical isn't enough
  • Corticosteroid injection — short-term flare relief, typically lasting 4–12 weeks
  • Physiotherapy — supervised exercise plus manual therapy

Surgery

Total or partial knee replacement is considered when pain disturbs sleep, severely limits daily activity, and at least 3–6 months of conservative treatment has not worked. Around 100,000 knee replacements are performed in the UK each year, with 90%+ still functioning well at 15 years.

What Is Osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease where the protective cartilage that cushions the ends of your bones gradually wears down over time. As cartilage deteriorates, bones begin to rub against each other, causing pain, swelling, stiffness, and reduced mobility.

Unlike inflammatory types of arthritis, OA is primarily a mechanical condition — though inflammation does play a role, particularly during flare-ups. It most commonly affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine, but can occur in any joint.

How Common Is Osteoarthritis in the UK?

Around 8.75 million people aged 45 and over in the UK have sought treatment for osteoarthritis (Arthritis Research UK, now Arthritis UK, 2013; cited by NICE CKS). It is the single most common cause of disability among older adults in England and Wales, and its prevalence is rising due to an ageing population and increasing obesity rates.

What are the symptoms of osteoarthritis?

Symptoms typically develop slowly and worsen over time. They may include:

  • Joint pain — especially during or after activity, often described as a deep ache
  • Stiffness — particularly after rest or first thing in the morning (usually lasting less than 30 minutes)
  • Swelling — caused by inflammation of soft tissues around the joint
  • Tenderness — the joint may feel tender when light pressure is applied
  • Loss of flexibility — difficulty moving the joint through its full range
  • Grating sensation (crepitus) — a feeling or sound of bone rubbing on bone
  • Bone spurs — extra lumps of bone that form around the affected joint

When to See a GP

If you experience persistent joint pain or stiffness that doesn't improve, book an appointment with your GP. Early diagnosis can help you access the right support and slow progression.

What causes osteoarthritis?

Osteoarthritis develops when the cartilage protecting bone surfaces breaks down faster than it can repair itself. Several factors increase your risk:

  • Age — most common after age 50, though younger people can develop it after injury
  • Sex — women are more commonly affected, particularly after menopause
  • Obesity — excess weight places additional stress on weight-bearing joints; losing even 5% of body weight can significantly reduce knee pain
  • Previous joint injury — trauma from sports, accidents, or occupational overuse
  • Genetics — a family history increases risk
  • Repetitive stress — occupations involving repeated movements (kneeling, heavy lifting)
  • Other conditions — diabetes, metabolic disorders, and congenital joint issues

What are the best exercises for osteoarthritis?

Regular exercise is one of the most effective treatments for OA. It strengthens muscles around joints, improves flexibility, reduces pain, and helps manage weight. Always start gradually and consult a physiotherapist if unsure.

Aerobic / Low-Impact

  • Walking — aim for 30 minutes most days; use supportive footwear
  • Swimming & water aerobics — buoyancy reduces joint stress while providing excellent exercise
  • Cycling — stationary or outdoor; gentle on knees and hips

Strengthening

  • Straight-leg raises — strengthen quadriceps without stressing the knee
  • Wall sits — build leg strength gradually
  • Bridges — target glutes and core stability
  • Resistance bands — gentle, progressive strengthening

Flexibility & Balance

  • Yoga — improves range of motion and mental well-being
  • Tai chi — evidence-based benefits for balance and pain reduction
  • Daily stretching — 5-10 minutes morning and evening

What is the best diet for osteoarthritis?

An anti-inflammatory diet, particularly the Mediterranean diet, is the most evidence-supported dietary approach for OA management. It can help reduce inflammation, manage weight, and improve overall joint health.

Foods to Eat

  • Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines (omega-3 fatty acids, at least twice weekly)
  • Colourful vegetables — broccoli, spinach, kale, peppers (antioxidants)
  • Berries — blueberries, strawberries, cherries (anthocyanins)
  • Olive oil — extra virgin (oleocanthal has anti-inflammatory properties)
  • Nuts & seeds — walnuts, almonds, flaxseeds
  • Whole grains — oats, brown rice, quinoa
  • Turmeric & ginger — natural anti-inflammatory compounds

Foods to Limit

  • Processed and ultra-processed foods
  • Added sugars and sugary drinks
  • Red and processed meats
  • Refined carbohydrates
  • Excessive alcohol

Daily Self-Care Checklist

Stay Active

Regular low-impact exercise like walking, swimming, or cycling strengthens muscles and reduces joint pain.

Healthy Weight

Losing just 5% of body weight can significantly reduce pain in knees, hips, and other weight-bearing joints.

Eat Well

An anti-inflammatory Mediterranean diet rich in fish, vegetables, and olive oil helps manage symptoms.

Sleep Well

Good sleep supports healing and pain management. Use pillows to support affected joints at night.

How is osteoarthritis treated?

While there is no cure for osteoarthritis, a combination of approaches can significantly improve quality of life:

Self-Management

  • Stay active with regular low-impact exercise
  • Maintain a healthy weight
  • Pace activities to avoid overloading joints
  • Use heat or cold packs for symptom relief
  • Try supportive aids (walking sticks, splints, shoe insoles)

Medical Treatments

  • Paracetamol & NSAIDs — for pain and inflammation (topical NSAIDs preferred for knees/hands)
  • Physiotherapy — tailored exercise programmes and manual therapy
  • Steroid injections — for short-term relief during severe flare-ups
  • Joint replacement surgery — for severe cases when other treatments have not worked

Supplements

Glucosamine, chondroitin, and collagen supplements have some evidence for modest symptom relief, though results are mixed. Turmeric/curcumin (500-1000 mg/day) shows more consistent anti-inflammatory benefits. Always consult your GP before starting supplements.

The Osteoarthritis Journey: From Diagnosis to Management

Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis — a degenerative, wear-related condition that develops slowly over years. Most people first notice deep joint ache after activity, morning stiffness that eases within 30 minutes, and a gradual loss of range of movement. Diagnosis is usually clinical, supported by X-ray when needed.

Management is a journey, not a single decision. Conservative care — exercise, weight optimisation, an anti-inflammatory diet, pacing and supportive aids — is the foundation for everyone. If symptoms progress, escalation can include topical or oral anti-inflammatories, physiotherapy-led rehabilitation, injections, and, when conservative care has been exhausted, joint replacement surgery. Decisions are shared between you, your GP, physiotherapist and (if needed) an orthopaedic surgeon.

Common OA Interventions

  • Unloader knee braces — offload the affected compartment in medial knee OA
  • Imaging — X-ray, MRI or ultrasound when red flags or surgical planning warrant it
  • Viscosupplementation — hyaluronic acid (gel) injections, often for knee OA
  • Corticosteroid injections — short-term flare control
  • Joint replacement surgery — knee, hip or thumb replacement for end-stage OA
  • Regenerative medicine — platelet-rich plasma (PRP) and stem-cell options, where evidence is still developing

For exercise programmes see our exercise hub or the joint-specific hip osteoarthritis exercise routine. For nutrition strategy see our diet guide and foods to avoid with arthritis.

/conditions/psoriatic-arthritis:
What is psoriatic arthritis?

Psoriatic arthritis is a chronic inflammatory condition that combines the joint inflammation of arthritis with the skin disease psoriasis. The immune system attacks both the joints and skin, causing pain, swelling, stiffness, and characteristic scaly skin patches.

PsA can affect any joint and varies considerably between individuals. It was once considered a mild form of arthritis, but we now know it can be progressive and destructive if left untreated.

Five Patterns of Psoriatic Arthritis

  • Asymmetric oligoarthritis — fewer than 5 joints, different on each side (most common pattern)
  • Symmetric polyarthritis — resembles rheumatoid arthritis, affecting joints on both sides
  • Distal interphalangeal (DIP) — affects the small joints nearest the fingernails
  • Spondylitis — inflammation of the spine and sacroiliac joints
  • Arthritis mutilans — severe, destructive form (rare)

What are the symptoms of psoriatic arthritis?

PsA symptoms can develop gradually or suddenly, and may alternate between flares and periods of remission:

Joint Symptoms

  • Joint pain, swelling, and warmth — can affect any joint
  • Dactylitis ("sausage digits") — entire finger or toe swells, a hallmark of PsA
  • Enthesitis — pain where tendons and ligaments attach to bone (Achilles heel, elbow, sole of foot)
  • Morning stiffness — lasting over 30 minutes
  • Lower back pain — from spinal involvement (spondylitis)

Skin & Nail Symptoms

  • Psoriasis plaques — red, scaly patches on elbows, knees, scalp, or other areas
  • Nail changes — pitting, ridging, crumbling, separation from the nail bed (onycholysis)
  • Scalp psoriasis — thick, crusted plaques

Other Symptoms

  • Fatigue — significant and pervasive
  • Eye inflammation (uveitis) — red, painful eyes requiring urgent treatment

What causes psoriatic arthritis?

PsA is an autoimmune condition with both genetic and environmental triggers:

  • Psoriasis — the strongest risk factor; 70-80% develop skin symptoms before joint symptoms
  • Genetics — HLA-B27 gene (especially with spinal involvement); family history of psoriasis or PsA
  • Age — most commonly develops between ages 30 and 50
  • Obesity — increases risk and reduces treatment effectiveness
  • Nail psoriasis — nail involvement is a strong predictor of developing PsA
  • Infections or physical trauma — may trigger onset in genetically susceptible individuals
  • Smoking — increases risk, though less strongly than in RA

How is psoriatic arthritis treated?

Treatment aims to control both joint inflammation and skin disease, prevent joint damage, and maintain quality of life:

Mild Disease

  • NSAIDs — ibuprofen, naproxen for pain and inflammation
  • Topical treatments — for skin psoriasis (corticosteroid creams, vitamin D analogues)
  • Local steroid injections — for individual swollen joints

Moderate to Severe Disease

  • Methotrexate — first-line DMARD, treats both joints and skin
  • Leflunomide — alternative DMARD
  • Azathioprine — immunosuppressant DMARD used when other options aren't suitable
  • Apremilast — PDE4 inhibitor, oral option for joints and skin

Biologic Therapies

  • Anti-TNF — adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, certolizumab, golimumab
  • IL-17 inhibitors — secukinumab, ixekizumab (excellent for skin and joints)
  • IL-23 inhibitors — guselkumab, risankizumab
  • JAK inhibitors — tofacitinib, upadacitinib (oral alternatives to biologics)

What exercises help psoriatic arthritis?

Regular exercise is vital for managing PsA — it maintains joint function, supports weight management, improves mood, and may help reduce skin symptoms through stress reduction.

  • Swimming — excellent for joints; chlorinated water may irritate skin psoriasis (use emollients before and after)
  • Walking & cycling — low impact, effective for cardiovascular fitness
  • Pilates & yoga — improve flexibility, core strength, and stress management
  • Strength training — protects joints by strengthening surrounding muscles
  • Hand exercises — important if fingers are affected

Skin Care During Exercise

Wear moisture-wicking, loose-fitting clothes. Apply emollients before swimming. Shower promptly after exercise and moisturise to prevent skin flares.

What foods help psoriatic arthritis?

Diet plays a role in managing both the skin and joint components of PsA:

  • Mediterranean diet — anti-inflammatory pattern that benefits both joints and skin
  • Omega-3 fatty acids — from oily fish, may reduce joint and skin inflammation
  • Maintain healthy weight — obesity worsens PsA and reduces treatment effectiveness; weight loss improves outcomes
  • Limit alcohol — can trigger psoriasis flares and interact with medications
  • Vitamin D — many people with psoriasis are deficient; discuss supplementation with your GP
  • Turmeric — curcumin has anti-inflammatory properties that may benefit both skin and joints

Some individuals report food triggers for skin flares (gluten, nightshades, dairy). Keeping a food diary may help identify personal triggers, though evidence for elimination diets is limited.

What is rheumatoid arthritis?

Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system mistakenly attacks the synovium — the lining of the membranes that surround your joints. This causes inflammation that can eventually destroy cartilage and bone within the joint.

RA typically affects joints symmetrically — if one wrist is affected, the other usually is too. It most commonly begins in the small joints of the hands, wrists, and feet, but can affect larger joints and even other body systems including the skin, eyes, lungs, heart, and blood vessels.

RA vs Osteoarthritis: Key Differences

  • Cause: RA is autoimmune; OA is degenerative wear-and-tear
  • Pattern: RA is symmetrical; OA often affects one side more
  • Morning stiffness: RA lasts over 30 minutes; OA usually under 30 minutes
  • Age of onset: RA can start at any age (commonly 30-60); OA typically after 50
  • Systemic effects: RA can affect organs; OA is localised to joints
Rheumatoid Arthritis VS Osteoarthritis

Autoimmune attack on joints

Cause

Wear-and-tear cartilage loss

Symmetrical (both sides)

Pattern

Often one side or localised

30+ minutes, often hours

Stiffness

Usually under 30 minutes

Any age (commonly 30–60)

Onset

Typically after age 50

What are the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis?

RA symptoms can vary in severity and may come and go in periods called flares. Common symptoms include:

  • Joint pain and swelling — warm, tender joints, especially in hands, wrists, and feet
  • Prolonged morning stiffness — lasting more than 30 minutes, often hours
  • Fatigue — persistent tiredness and lack of energy
  • Symmetrical joint involvement — both sides of the body affected equally
  • Rheumatoid nodules — firm lumps under the skin near affected joints
  • General malaise — feeling unwell, flu-like symptoms during flares
  • Weight loss — unexplained weight loss in early stages

Early Warning Signs

See your GP urgently if you experience persistent joint swelling, morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, or fatigue with joint symptoms. Early treatment within the first 12 weeks of symptoms ("window of opportunity") dramatically improves long-term outcomes.

What causes rheumatoid arthritis?

The exact cause of RA is unknown, but it involves a combination of genetic and environmental factors:

  • Genetics — the HLA-DR4 gene increases susceptibility; family history raises risk
  • Sex — women are 2-3 times more likely to develop RA than men
  • Smoking — the single most significant modifiable risk factor; smokers have higher risk and more severe disease
  • Age — can occur at any age but most commonly starts between 30 and 60
  • Obesity — increases risk and can reduce treatment effectiveness
  • Hormonal factors — changes in hormone levels (pregnancy, menopause) can influence RA

How is rheumatoid arthritis diagnosed?

There is no single test for RA — diagnosis combines symptoms, blood tests and imaging. If you have persistent joint swelling or morning stiffness lasting over 30 minutes, your GP will usually refer you to a rheumatologist.

Blood tests

  • Rheumatoid factor (RF) — an antibody present in around 70-80% of people with RA, though it can also be positive in other conditions or absent in early disease
  • Anti-CCP antibodies — more specific to RA than RF and can appear years before symptoms start
  • ESR and CRP — inflammatory markers that rise during active disease and help track flares

Imaging

X-rays can show joint space narrowing and bone erosion, though early RA often looks normal on X-ray. Ultrasound and MRI are more sensitive and can detect synovitis (joint lining inflammation) before permanent damage occurs — useful for catching RA early, within the "window of opportunity."

A rheumatologist confirms diagnosis using a combination of these results alongside the pattern and duration of your symptoms, since no single blood test or scan is diagnostic on its own.

How is rheumatoid arthritis treated?

Modern treatment aims to achieve remission — a state where the disease is controlled and no active inflammation is present. The UK follows a "treat to target" approach.

DMARDs (Disease-Modifying Anti-Rheumatic Drugs)

Methotrexate is usually the first-line treatment, often combined with other DMARDs like sulfasalazine or hydroxychloroquine. If first-line DMARDs are not tolerated or effective, azathioprine may be used as an alternative immunosuppressant DMARD. DMARDs slow disease progression and prevent joint damage — they are the cornerstone of RA treatment.

Biologic Therapies

If DMARDs alone are insufficient, biologic therapies (anti-TNF drugs, rituximab, tocilizumab, abatacept) or JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib) may be prescribed. These target specific parts of the immune system driving inflammation.

Symptom Relief

  • NSAIDs — reduce pain and inflammation
  • Corticosteroids — short-term use during flares (oral or injection)
  • Physiotherapy — maintain joint function and strength
  • Occupational therapy — adapt daily activities to protect joints

What exercises help rheumatoid arthritis?

Exercise is safe and beneficial for RA — it reduces fatigue, improves mood, and maintains joint function. The key is choosing appropriate activities and adapting intensity during flares.

  • Hydrotherapy / swimming — warm water eases stiffness; buoyancy protects joints
  • Walking — start with short distances and gradually increase
  • Gentle yoga — focus on modified poses; avoid extreme positions during flares
  • Hand exercises — maintain grip strength and dexterity
  • Strength training — light weights, higher repetitions, avoiding inflamed joints
  • Range of motion exercises — daily gentle stretches to preserve flexibility

During flares: reduce intensity but try to maintain some gentle movement. Complete rest can worsen stiffness. Listen to your body and work with your physiotherapist.

What foods help rheumatoid arthritis?

While no diet can cure RA, anti-inflammatory eating patterns can complement medical treatment and help manage symptoms:

Recommended

  • Oily fish — salmon, mackerel, sardines (omega-3s reduce inflammation)
  • Fruits & vegetables — wide variety for antioxidants
  • Olive oil — extra virgin, rich in anti-inflammatory oleocanthal
  • Turmeric — curcumin has evidence-based anti-inflammatory effects
  • Green tea — polyphenols may help modulate immune response

Foods to Limit

  • Processed foods and refined sugars (promote inflammation)
  • Excessive red meat
  • Alcohol (can interact with RA medications, particularly methotrexate)
  • Trans fats and fried foods

Important: If you are on methotrexate, discuss alcohol intake and folic acid supplementation with your rheumatologist.

Frequently asked questions

What is rheumatoid arthritis? Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease where the immune system mistakenly attacks the lining of the joints (synovium), causing inflammation, pain, swelling, and eventually joint damage. How is rheumatoid arthritis different from osteoarthritis? Unlike osteoarthritis which is a wear-and-tear condition, RA is an autoimmune disease. RA typically affects joints symmetrically, causes prolonged morning stiffness (over 30 minutes), and can affect other organs. OA is localised and caused by cartilage breakdown. What is the best treatment for rheumatoid arthritis? Early treatment with DMARDs (disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs) such as methotrexate is the gold standard. Biologic therapies may be added if DMARDs alone aren't sufficient. Exercise, diet, and stress management also play important roles. Can rheumatoid arthritis be cured? There is currently no cure, but early aggressive treatment can achieve remission in many patients. Modern therapies have dramatically improved outcomes, allowing many people with RA to lead active, fulfilling lives. Does diet affect rheumatoid arthritis? Yes. An anti-inflammatory Mediterranean diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids, fruits, vegetables, and whole grains can help reduce inflammation and complement medical treatment. Some patients also find benefit from eliminating specific trigger foods. Blog & Stories

Cookies are small text files placed on your device when you visit a website. Cookies may be set by the website you are visiting ("first-party cookies") or by third parties whose services appear on the page ("third-party cookies").

Living With Arthritis uses cookies for the following purposes:

Essential Cookies

These cookies are strictly necessary for the website to function. They enable core features such as security, form submissions, user authentication and accessibility. You cannot opt out of these cookies as the website would not work properly without them.

  • Session management and authentication tokens
  • Security and fraud prevention

Functional Cookies
