/guides/arthritis-pain-relief:
1. Move — gently, often

Movement is the single most evidence-supported treatment for arthritis pain. Joints are nourished by motion; rest stiffens them within hours. Aim for little and often, not heroic sessions.

  • Walking — start at 10 minutes twice a day, build to 30 minutes
  • Cycling or swimming — minimal joint load, big cardio benefit
  • Tai chi — reduces pain and improves balance; see our tai chi guide
  • Range-of-motion work — bend and straighten each painful joint through its full pain-free range, twice a day

For joint-specific routines, browse the exercise hub. Many people with hip or knee OA start with swimming / pool drills or our walking with arthritis guide. See also the osteoarthritis hub.

2. Use heat and cold — match it to the joint

  • Heat (10–20 min) — for stiff, aching joints, especially first thing. A warm shower, microwaveable wheat bag or warm bath all work.
  • Cold (10–15 min, wrapped) — for hot, swollen, flaring joints. A bag of frozen peas in a tea-towel is the cheapest cold pack you'll find.
  • Alternate — some people find swapping heat and cold every few minutes settles a persistent ache.

3. Get the right medicines

For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE guidance recommends trying a topical NSAID gel first. Paracetamol is not routinely offered as first-line treatment and may be considered only infrequently when other options are unsuitable.

  • Topical NSAID gel first — ibuprofen or diclofenac, applied 3× a day to the painful joint. Fewer side effects than tablets.
  • Oral NSAIDs — short courses with food, at the lowest effective dose. Always check with your pharmacist if you take blood thinners, have asthma, or have stomach problems.
  • Paracetamol — useful as an add-on, less effective on its own than once thought.
  • Capsaicin cream — derived from chilli; NICE evidence supports a possible benefit for knee osteoarthritis, but it can sting at first and is not a routine first-line option.
  • Corticosteroid injections — your GP can refer for these for a single severely painful joint.

If you take regular painkillers more than 2–3 times a week, book a GP review.

4. Eat to lower inflammation

A Mediterranean-style diet is the most consistently effective dietary pattern for arthritis pain. The core idea is simple: more plants, more oily fish, more olive oil; less ultra-processed food, less sugar, less alcohol.

  • Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) twice a week for omega-3s
  • A handful of nuts most days
  • Olive oil as the main cooking fat
  • Plenty of beans, lentils and whole grains
  • Less than 14 units of alcohol a week; ideally less

Losing even 5% of body weight measurably reduces knee and hip pain.

5. Protect your sleep

Poor or disrupted sleep can increase pain sensitivity. Pain disturbs sleep, and broken sleep can magnify pain — breaking the loop matters.

  • Same bed-time and wake-time, 7 days a week
  • Bedroom cool, dark, screen-free for the last 30 minutes
  • Pillow between knees if hip or back pain disturbs you
  • If pain wakes you most nights, ask your GP about a short course of slow-release pain relief

6. Manage flares

Flare-ups are part of life with arthritis. See our flare-up guide for the full playbook. The short version:

  • Don't stop moving — drop intensity, not movement itself
  • Cold pack for hot, swollen joints; heat for stiff ones
  • Pace the day — alternate 20 minutes of activity with 5 minutes of rest
  • Topical NSAID gel 3× a day
  • Sleep, hydration, simple food — the basics matter most when you feel worst

When to see your GP

Book an appointment if:

  • Pain has lasted more than six weeks
  • A joint is hot, red or swollen
  • Morning stiffness regularly lasts over an hour
  • Pain wakes you at night
  • You're taking regular painkillers more than 2–3 times a week
  • You're losing weight, feeling feverish or generally unwell alongside joint pain

If you're already on a waiting list, our waiting-list help guide covers what you can do in the meantime.

Build your own plan

Use our self-help tool to put these ideas into a simple weekly routine.

/guides/azathioprine-for-arthritis:
Medication Guide

A plain-English UK guide to azathioprine — how it works, TPMT testing, dosing, side effects, blood monitoring and the conditions it's prescribed for.

Azathioprine is one of the oldest and most widely used disease-modifying drugs in UK rheumatology, prescribed for lupus, vasculitis, severe rheumatoid arthritis and several other autoimmune conditions. This guide explains exactly how it works, why TPMT testing matters before your first dose, what blood monitoring you'll need, and the side effects and interactions to be aware of — written in plain English and reviewed against UK BNF and British Society for Rheumatology standards.

Azathioprine for arthritis: an overview

Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) that has been used in UK rheumatology for more than 50 years. It works by quietening an overactive immune system — the underlying problem in lupus, vasculitis, rheumatoid arthritis and several other inflammatory conditions — rather than just masking pain.

It is rarely the first DMARD tried in rheumatoid arthritis (methotrexate is), but it is a mainstay treatment for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), vasculitis, autoimmune hepatitis-associated arthritis, and as a steroid-sparing option when long-term prednisolone is causing problems. It is also widely used in inflammatory bowel disease, where joint involvement is common.

Azathioprine works slowly — most people notice improvement at 8–12 weeks and full benefit by 3–6 months — so it is usually started alongside a short course of oral steroid that controls symptoms while the DMARD builds up.

How azathioprine works

Azathioprine is a "prodrug": once swallowed, the body converts it to 6-mercaptopurine, which interferes with the building blocks (purines) that immune cells need to multiply. By slowing the production of the most active lymphocytes, it dampens down the autoimmune attack on joints, kidneys, blood vessels and other tissues.

Because it suppresses immune cell turnover rather than blocking a single inflammatory signal, azathioprine is broadly active across many autoimmune conditions — but the same mechanism is why blood monitoring is essential.

Conditions azathioprine is used for

  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) — first- or second-line steroid-sparing agent, particularly for joint, skin and mild kidney involvement
  • Vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, polyarteritis nodosa) — used for maintenance after remission is induced
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — when methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide are unsuitable
  • Inflammatory bowel disease with arthritis — treats both gut and joint disease
  • Autoimmune hepatitis with joint symptoms
  • Polymyositis and dermatomyositis — as a steroid-sparing agent
  • BehÃ§et's disease with arthritis or uveitis

Before you start: TPMT testing and baseline checks

UK rheumatology shared-care guidance requires several checks before the first dose:

  • TPMT enzyme test — a single blood test that identifies the small number of people who break azathioprine down too slowly and are at high risk of toxicity
  • Full blood count (FBC) — baseline white cells, haemoglobin and platelets
  • Liver function tests (LFTs) — baseline ALT, AST and bilirubin
  • Urea and electrolytes (U&Es) — kidney function
  • Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV screen — to avoid reactivating hidden infections
  • Varicella (chickenpox) immunity check — vaccination may be needed before starting
  • Up-to-date pneumococcal and annual flu vaccines — give before starting where possible

If your TPMT activity is low, your specialist will start at a much lower dose or choose a different DMARD. If it is absent, azathioprine should not be used.

How azathioprine is taken

Azathioprine is taken as tablets (common tablet strengths include 25 mg and 50 mg). Rheumatology teams individualise the dose using body weight, TPMT status, blood results and the condition being treated — often referring to BNF / BSR shared-care ranges. Your rheumatology team will set your dose; never change it without specialist advice, and do not calculate a dose from this page.

Practical tips:

  • Take with or just after food to reduce nausea
  • Ask your team whether splitting the daily dose helps if a single dose causes stomach upset
  • Take it at the same time each day so it's easy to remember
  • Don't crush or break the tablets — wash your hands after handling
  • Store at room temperature, away from children

Blood-test monitoring on azathioprine

Regular monitoring is what makes long-term azathioprine safe. A typical UK shared-care schedule looks like this:

  • Weeks 0–6: FBC and LFTs every 1–2 weeks while the dose is being increased
  • Months 2–3: every 4 weeks
  • Long term (stable dose): every 12 weeks indefinitely
  • After any dose change: back to fortnightly bloods for 6 weeks

Your GP will usually do the bloods under a shared-care agreement with your rheumatology team. Don't skip them, even when you feel well — they pick up bone-marrow or liver problems before you would notice symptoms.

Side effects of azathioprine

Common and usually mild

  • Nausea, loss of appetite or mild stomach upset (especially in the first few weeks)
  • Mild hair thinning
  • A flu-like feeling — aches, mild fever, headache — in the first 1–2 weeks. If this is severe or persistent, contact your team; it can occasionally be a hypersensitivity reaction that means azathioprine must be stopped
  • Mouth ulcers

Less common but important

  • Bone-marrow suppression — low white cells (raised infection risk), anaemia or low platelets (easy bruising, bleeding)
  • Liver inflammation — usually picked up on routine bloods before symptoms appear
  • Pancreatitis — severe upper-abdominal pain radiating to the back; needs urgent assessment
  • Increased risk of infections — including shingles and chest infections
  • Long-term skin-cancer risk — sun protection (SPF 50, hats, covered clothing) is important; check your skin regularly
  • Small long-term increase in lymphoma risk — particularly with very long use; the absolute risk remains low and is usually outweighed by disease benefit

Contact your rheumatology team urgently if you develop fever, sore throat, unusual bruising or bleeding, severe stomach pain, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or a new rash.

Drug interactions to know

  • Allopurinol (for gout) — the most dangerous interaction. It blocks the breakdown of azathioprine; the azathioprine dose must be reduced to about a quarter, or a different DMARD chosen. Tell every prescriber if you take both.
  • Febuxostat — same problem as allopurinol; avoid the combination.
  • Trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole — raise the risk of low blood counts.
  • Warfarin — INR can change; more frequent monitoring is needed.
  • ACE inhibitors (ramipril, lisinopril) — occasionally cause anaemia when combined.
  • Live vaccines (MMR, yellow fever, nasal flu, BCG, shingles Zostavax) — avoid while on azathioprine. The non-live shingles vaccine (Shingrix), inactivated flu and pneumococcal vaccines are recommended.

Azathioprine, pregnancy and breastfeeding

Azathioprine is one of the few immunosuppressants that can usually be continued safely during pregnancy and breastfeeding when the underlying condition requires ongoing treatment. Long-term registry data from women with lupus and inflammatory bowel disease show no consistent increase in major birth defects. Untreated flares of lupus or vasculitis carry significant risks to both mother and baby, so stopping azathioprine in pregnancy is usually not recommended.

Plan any pregnancy with your rheumatology team. Men taking azathioprine can father children safely; older advice to stop the drug before conception has been superseded.

Living well on azathioprine

  • Sun protection — daily SPF 50 on exposed skin, covered clothing, hat. Have any new or changing moles checked promptly.
  • Vaccinations — annual inactivated flu, pneumococcal, COVID-19 boosters and the non-live shingles vaccine (Shingrix). Avoid live vaccines.
  • Infections — contact your GP early for sore throats, chesty coughs, urinary symptoms or shingles-type rashes. Don't wait it out.
  • Alcohol — stay within 14 units per week; avoid binges. Stop completely if your liver tests rise.
  • Diet and exercise — the usual anti-inflammatory pattern (see our Diet Guide and Exercise Guide) supports general health and helps offset steroid side effects if you are also on prednisolone.
  • Travel — get pre-travel advice 6–8 weeks ahead; some destinations need vaccines that must be planned around your immunosuppression.

How azathioprine is prescribed in the UK

Azathioprine for arthritis is a specialist-initiated drug. The typical pathway is:

  • Diagnosis and decision to treat by a rheumatologist (or other relevant specialist)
  • Baseline checks, TPMT test and counselling at the rheumatology clinic
  • First few weeks of prescribing and monitoring by the specialist team
  • Once the dose is stable, prescribing handed to the GP under a shared-care agreement, with the rheumatology team still reviewing you 6–12 monthly

Shared-care arrangements mean your GP can issue repeats, do your monitoring bloods and act on results — but anything unusual (low counts, raised liver enzymes, infections, planning pregnancy) should be flagged to your specialist team.

Questions to ask your rheumatology team

  • Why is azathioprine the right DMARD for me, rather than methotrexate or another option?
  • What was my TPMT result, and how does it affect my dose?
  • What target dose are we working towards, and over how many weeks?
  • Who arranges my monitoring bloods — and what do I do if I'm called for one I can't attend?
  • Which symptoms should make me contact you urgently?
  • Which vaccines should I have, and which should I avoid?
  • What's the plan for pregnancy / fatherhood if relevant?
  • If azathioprine doesn't work or I can't tolerate it, what's the next option?

Key takeaways

  • Azathioprine is a steroid-sparing DMARD widely used in lupus, vasculitis and some forms of inflammatory arthritis.
  • It works slowly — expect 8–12 weeks for benefit, 3–6 months for full effect.
  • A TPMT blood test before starting is essential to avoid severe toxicity.
  • Regular FBC and liver-function monitoring is what makes long-term use safe.
  • The dangerous interaction to remember is allopurinol; tell every prescriber.
  • It is usually safe to continue in pregnancy and breastfeeding under specialist supervision.
  • Pair with sun protection, vaccinations, early infection care, and exercise / diet support for the best long-term outcome.

This guide is educational and does not replace advice from your rheumatology team or GP. Always follow the dose and monitoring plan your specialist has set for you. Reference standards: BNF (British National Formulary) and British Society for Rheumatology (BSR) DMARD safety guidelines.

How do I improve bone density?

Weight-bearing exercise (walking, jogging, dancing), resistance training, calcium 700 mg/day and vitamin D 10 mcg/day support bone density. If your FRAX score is high, your GP may prescribe bisphosphonates.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Can you have osteoarthritis and osteoporosis at the same time?

Yes — they are different conditions but often coexist, especially in post-menopausal women. Osteoarthritis affects joint cartilage; osteoporosis weakens bones. Dual management focuses on calcium (700–1,200 mg/day), vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, strength training and DEXA screening when appropriate.

Medically reviewed by Maxwell

First Contact Practitioner • HCPC PH128483 • Last updated June 2026

Reviewer details and the site's clinical review process are documented in our editorial standards.

1. Osteoporosis vs osteoarthritis: what is the difference?

Osteoarthritis is a joint disease: cartilage thins, bones rub, pain and stiffness follow. Osteoporosis is a bone disease: bones lose density and become fragile, raising fracture risk — often silently until a fall.

2. Symptoms and risk factors

Osteoporosis is often called a "silent" condition because there are usually no symptoms until a fracture happens — most commonly in the wrist, hip or spine. Gradual loss of height, a stooped or curved upper back, and unexplained back pain from a spinal compression fracture can be later warning signs.

Key risk factors include being female and post-menopausal, a family history of hip fracture, low body weight, smoking, high alcohol intake, long-term oral steroid use, early menopause, and reduced mobility from another condition. Some inflammatory arthritis conditions also raise risk independently of steroid use.

3. Why arthritis and weak bones often occur together

Pain reduces activity, and inactivity weakens bones. Steroid medications used in inflammatory arthritis directly reduce bone density. Post-menopausal oestrogen loss accelerates both conditions. Sarcopenia and low body weight magnify the risk.

4. Calcium, vitamin D, magnesium: the mineral strategy

  • Calcium: 700–1,200 mg/day from dairy, fortified milks, sardines, leafy greens.
  • Vitamin D: 10 µg/day October–March (NHS), or 25 µg/day if deficient.
  • Magnesium: 300 mg/day (men), 270 mg/day (women) from nuts, seeds, wholegrains.
  • Vitamin K2: emerging evidence; sources include fermented dairy, eggs.

5. Load-bearing exercise for bone and joint health

Bones respond to load. Walking, dancing, tai chi, stair climbing and progressive resistance training all stimulate bone formation. Aim for 30 minutes of weight-bearing activity most days plus 2 strength sessions weekly. Avoid high-impact loading on inflamed or already-damaged joints.

6. Screening, testing and when medication is needed

A DEXA scan measures bone mineral density. NICE recommends scanning post-menopausal women with risk factors, anyone on long-term steroids, and those with a fragility fracture. Treatment (bisphosphonates, denosumab, HRT) is considered when T-score is below -2.5 or after a fragility fracture.

7. Can bone density loss be reversed?

Bone loss can be slowed, partially rebuilt and fracture risk substantially reduced through the right combination of nutrition, weight-bearing exercise and, where clinically indicated, medication. Full reversal to youthful bone density isn't generally realistic, which is why earlier action — ideally before or around menopause — gives the best long-term outcome.

8. Bone health, falls and frailty: the bigger picture

Osteoporosis rarely causes a fall by itself — its real danger is turning a minor stumble into a serious fracture. That's why bone density is best managed alongside muscle strength and falls prevention, not in isolation.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between osteoporosis and osteoarthritis?

Osteoporosis weakens bones, raising fracture risk. Osteoarthritis wears the cartilage in joints, causing pain and stiffness. Both can co-exist but have different causes and treatments.

Can I have both at the same time?

Yes — and many post-menopausal women do. Hormonal change, reduced activity from joint pain, and shared risk factors mean dual diagnosis is common.

How much calcium do I need?

UK adults need 700 mg/day, rising to 1,200 mg/day for post-menopausal women and adults with osteoporosis. Sources include dairy, fortified plant milks, sardines, leafy greens and beans.

Is weight-bearing exercise safe with arthritis?

Yes, when prescribed correctly. Walking, dancing, stair climbing and graded resistance training stimulate bone without damaging joints. Avoid high-impact loading on already-painful joints.

When should I get a bone density scan?

NICE recommends DEXA scans for post-menopausal women under 65 with risk factors (low BMI, family history, fragility fracture, long-term steroids), and all women over 65.

Do I need bone medication?

Bisphosphonates and other treatments are recommended when DEXA T-score is below -2.5, or with a prior fragility fracture. Your GP or specialist will assess fracture risk using FRAX.

What are the symptoms of osteoporosis?

Osteoporosis is often called a "silent" condition because it typically has no symptoms until a fracture occurs — most commonly in the wrist, hip or spine. Loss of height over time, a stooped posture, or back pain from a spinal compression fracture can be later warning signs.

What are the main risk factors for osteoporosis?

Being female and post-menopausal, family history of fracture, low body weight, smoking, high alcohol intake, long-term steroid use, and conditions that reduce mobility all raise risk. Early menopause and some inflammatory arthritis conditions also increase risk independently.

How does osteoporosis connect to falls and frailty?

Osteoporosis itself does not cause falls, but it turns a minor fall into a serious fracture. That is why bone density, muscle strength and falls prevention are usually managed together in older adults — see our falls prevention and frailty guides below.

Can osteoporosis be reversed?

Bone density loss can be slowed, partially rebuilt, and fracture risk substantially reduced with the right combination of nutrition, weight-bearing exercise and, where indicated, medication — but full reversal to youthful bone density is not generally realistic. Early action gives the best results.

/guides/can-exercise-make-osteoarthritis:
Clinical Guide

The short answer is no. NICE puts exercise ahead of medication for osteoarthritis. Here's how to move with confidence — and how to tell productive soreness from a flare.

Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse?

No — done correctly, exercise reduces OA pain and slows progression. Some soreness during and up to 2 hours after exercise is normal. Sharp, sudden or persistent pain lasting more than 24 hours means you've done too much; scale back but don't stop.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Exercise does not wear osteoarthritis joints out. UK NICE guidance (NG226) places structured movement ahead of medication as the first-line treatment. Problems come from doing too much too soon — not from movement itself. Start small, progress slowly, and learn to read your joints.

The short answer

No — for almost everyone with osteoarthritis, exercise does not make the condition worse. The opposite is true. UK NICE guidance (NG226) places structured exercise ahead of medication as the first-line treatment for osteoarthritis of the knee, hip and hand. The Chartered Society of Physiotherapy describes movement as "the single most important thing you can do" for arthritic joints.

The fear that exercise grinds joints down comes from the older "wear and tear" model of osteoarthritis. Modern research has overturned this: cartilage is living tissue that responds to gentle, repeated load by becoming better nourished and more resilient. Inactivity, not movement, is what allows joints to stiffen and surrounding muscles to weaken.

Why the "exercise wears joints out" myth persists

The myth survives for three reasons:

  • Mechanical intuition. Joints look like hinges, and hinges wear out with use. But cartilage is not a mechanical surface — it is metabolically active tissue that depends on loading for its nutrient supply.
  • Pain feels like damage. When a joint hurts during movement it is natural to assume harm is being done. In osteoarthritis, however, pain levels correlate poorly with the amount of joint change visible on an X-ray. Many people with severe X-ray changes have little pain; others with mild changes have significant pain. Pain is a protection signal, not a damage meter.
  • Bad early experiences. Doing too much too soon — long walks, heavy gardening, a sudden gym programme — provokes a flare, which then reinforces the fear of moving at all.

A 2022 Cochrane review of land-based exercise for knee osteoarthritis pooled 60 randomised trials and over 8,000 participants. It concluded that exercise reduces pain and improves function, with no evidence of joint harm.

Productive soreness vs flare pain

Learning to read your joints is the most useful skill for managing osteoarthritis. Use this simple framework:

  • Productive soreness (safe to continue). A mild ache up to about 4/10 during or after exercise. Eases as you warm up. Settles within 24 hours. Often felt in the muscles around the joint rather than deep inside it.
  • Flare pain (back off). Sharp, catching or locking sensations. Hot, swollen joints. Pain that stays above 4/10 for more than 24–48 hours or wakes you at night. Reduced range of motion.

Productive soreness is part of normal adaptation and can be exercised through. Flare pain is a signal to reduce load — not to stop moving altogether.

A practical framework for balancing rest with movement

The goal is steady, sustainable activity — not heroic effort followed by long recovery. Use this five-step framework:

  1. Start lower than feels necessary. If you can comfortably walk 30 minutes, start with 10. If a strength exercise feels easy at 3 sets of 10, stay there for two weeks before progressing. Small starting doses prevent the boom-and-bust cycle that breeds fear.
  2. Progress by no more than 10% per week. Add minutes, reps or resistance gradually. Most flares come from sudden jumps in volume, not from exercise itself.
  3. Use the 24-hour rule. If joint pain has settled to baseline within 24 hours, the previous session was appropriate. If not, scale the next session back by about 25%.
  4. Modify, don't stop, during flares. Switch to gentle range-of-motion work, water-based exercise, or seated movement for 24–48 hours. Returning to gentle activity quickly prevents deconditioning.
  5. Build a weekly mix. Aim for 150 minutes of low-impact aerobic work (walking, swimming, cycling), two short strength sessions for the muscles around your affected joints, and a flexibility practice such as tai chi or yoga.

When to seek professional advice

See a GP or physiotherapist if you experience any of the following:

  • Joint pain that has not settled after a week of reduced activity
  • Sudden swelling, redness or warmth in a joint
  • Locking, giving way or sharp catching sensations
  • Pain that wakes you at night or is unrelieved by rest
  • A new symptom you cannot explain

A physiotherapist can tailor a programme to your joints, stage of disease and goals. In the UK you can refer yourself directly to UK healthcare musculoskeletal physiotherapy in most areas, without going via your GP.

Bottom line

Exercise does not wear osteoarthritis joints out. Avoiding movement does far more harm than careful, progressive activity ever will. Start small, progress slowly, distinguish productive soreness from flare pain, and treat exercise as treatment — because that is what the evidence says it is.

Sources & disclaimer

Based on NICE guideline NG226 (Osteoarthritis in over 16s, 2022), Cochrane systematic reviews of land-based and aquatic exercise for knee and hip osteoarthritis, UK Chief Medical Officer Physical Activity Guidelines (2019), and guidance from the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy. For educational use only. Speak to a physiotherapist or GP before starting a new exercise programme, particularly with severe or unstable joint disease.

How do Hydrolysed collagen and Glucosamine (sulfate) compare?

Collagen and glucosamine are the two supplements people ask about most when they want to try something over the counter for arthritis. Both claim to support cartilage and reduce joint pain, both are sold in every UK pharmacy and health shop, and both have a mixed evidence base that's easy to misread. This guide compares them honestly — what each one is, what the trials actually show, sensible UK doses, safety, cost, and who each one tends to suit.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Collagen and glucosamine are the two supplements people ask about most when they want to try something over the counter for arthritis. Both claim to support cartilage and reduce joint pain, both are sold in every UK pharmacy and health shop, and both have a mixed evidence base that's easy to misread. This guide compares them honestly — what each one is, what the trials actually show, sensible UK doses, safety, cost, and who each one tends to suit.

Hydrolysed collagen

  • How it works: Collagen peptides are absorbed as small amino-acid fragments. Some reach cartilage and connective tissue, where they may stimulate the body's own collagen production and reduce inflammatory signalling.
  • Best for: Mild to moderate osteoarthritis with aching joints, people who also want skin, hair and tendon benefits, and those who cannot tolerate shellfish-derived glucosamine.
  • Common side-effects: Generally very well tolerated. Occasional mild bloating or an unpleasant aftertaste. Not suitable for vegetarians or vegans (usually bovine or marine).
  • UK healthcare availability: Not prescribed on the UK healthcare system for arthritis. NICE does not recommend it, but it is not discouraged either — considered a personal choice.
  • Typical UK cost: £10–£25 per month for a 10 g/day hydrolysed collagen powder or peptide capsules.

Glucosamine (sulfate)

  • How it works: A building block of cartilage. Taken orally, glucosamine sulfate may modestly slow cartilage breakdown and reduce pain signalling in the joint over several weeks.
  • Best for: Mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis, particularly in people willing to trial a supplement for at least 8–12 weeks before judging effect.
  • Common side-effects: Mild stomach upset, heartburn, occasional headaches. Caution in shellfish allergy, warfarin users (may raise INR), and poorly controlled diabetes.
  • UK healthcare availability: Not prescribed on the UK healthcare system. NICE 2022 osteoarthritis guidance specifically recommends against routine use, citing inconsistent evidence.
  • Typical UK cost: £8–£20 per month for 1,500 mg/day glucosamine sulfate; combined glucosamine + chondroitin products cost more (£15–£30).

What each one actually is

Collagen is the main structural protein in cartilage, tendon, skin and bone. Supplements are almost always 'hydrolysed collagen' or 'collagen peptides' — long chains broken down into short fragments the gut can absorb. Sources are usually bovine (cow hide), marine (fish skin) or, less commonly, chicken (type II collagen).

Glucosamine is a natural amino sugar the body uses to build the sticky, cushioning parts of cartilage (glycosaminoglycans). Supplements are extracted mainly from shellfish shells, though shellfish-free versions from fermented corn are now available. The sulfate form is the one used in most positive trials — the hydrochloride form has weaker evidence.

What the evidence actually shows

For glucosamine, the picture is genuinely mixed. Early European trials of pharmaceutical-grade glucosamine sulfate (usually 1,500 mg once daily) reported modest but real improvements in knee osteoarthritis pain and function over 6 months. Larger, more rigorous US trials (notably GAIT, 2006) found no meaningful difference over placebo. The most likely explanation is that a subset of people — often those with moderate knee OA — respond, while others don't. That's why NICE 2022 no longer recommends it routinely, but many patients still find it useful.

For collagen, the evidence is younger but more consistently positive for symptoms. Randomised trials of 10 g/day hydrolysed collagen or 40 mg/day undenatured type II collagen have shown reductions in knee OA pain and stiffness after 3–6 months, with effect sizes broadly comparable to glucosamine in some head-to-head studies. A 2019 meta-analysis in the International Journal of Rheumatic Diseases concluded collagen hydrolysate produced a significant reduction in joint pain versus placebo. Study sizes are still smaller than the glucosamine literature, so cautious optimism is the fair read.

Neither supplement has been shown to slow the underlying structural progression of osteoarthritis reliably. What they may do is reduce symptoms — pain, stiffness, morning discomfort — enough to keep you active, which is itself protective.

How quickly you'd notice a difference

Both supplements work slowly. Neither is a painkiller. A fair trial period is 8–12 weeks at a proper dose, taken daily. If you've had no benefit at all by three months, it's unlikely to start working later — stop and try something else.

Collagen often shows its earliest effects on non-joint tissues (skin firmness, nail strength, tendon comfort) within 4–6 weeks, with joint benefits appearing later. Glucosamine tends to be joint-specific — you either notice a reduction in that background knee ache after 6–10 weeks or you don't.

Sensible UK doses

Glucosamine: 1,500 mg glucosamine sulfate once daily, ideally with food. Splitting into 500 mg three times a day has no proven advantage. Combined glucosamine + chondroitin (1,500 mg + 1,200 mg) products are more expensive and the evidence for adding chondroitin is weaker than for glucosamine alone.

Collagen: 10 g/day of hydrolysed collagen peptides is the dose used in most positive trials, taken in water, coffee or a smoothie. Undenatured type II collagen (UC-II) uses a much smaller dose — 40 mg/day — and works by a different immune-modulating mechanism.

Safety, allergies and interactions

Both are among the safer supplements on the market, but not risk-free. Glucosamine can raise INR in people on warfarin — a genuine bleeding risk that's easy to miss. It may also nudge fasting glucose slightly higher, which matters if diabetes is poorly controlled. Anyone with a serious shellfish allergy should use a shellfish-free (fermented) glucosamine.

Collagen has very few interactions. Marine collagen shouldn't be used by anyone with a fish allergy, and bovine collagen is not suitable for vegetarians or those avoiding animal products for religious reasons (halal- and kosher-certified collagen exists, but you have to look for it).

So which should you try first?

If your main problem is knee osteoarthritis pain and you want the option with the longest evidence base — even if that evidence is mixed — start with 1,500 mg/day glucosamine sulfate for 12 weeks. It's the cheaper of the two, and if you're going to respond, you'll likely know by then.

If your joint pain is more generalised (hands, hips, back, tendons), if you also want potential skin and connective-tissue benefits, or if glucosamine has already failed for you, hydrolysed collagen at 10 g/day is the more sensible next step.

Some people take both. There's no known interaction and no reason not to — but it doubles the monthly cost, so it's worth trialling them one at a time first to see which (if either) is actually doing something for you.

At a glance

Hydrolysed collagenGlucosamine (sulfate)
Typical UK dose10 g/day hydrolysed peptides1,500 mg/day sulfate
Time to judge effect8–12 weeks8–12 weeks
Best evidence forKnee OA pain, tendon comfortKnee OA pain in responders
NICE 2022 guidanceNot recommended, not discouragedRecommend against routine use
Main safety flagFish/beef allergies; not veganWarfarin, shellfish allergy
Monthly cost£10–£25£8–£20
Slows joint damage?No proven structural effectNo proven structural effect

Key takeaways

  • Both are symptom supplements, not disease-modifiers.
  • Give either one a fair 12-week trial at a real dose before judging it.
  • Glucosamine sulfate 1,500 mg/day suits knee-only osteoarthritis best.
  • Hydrolysed collagen 10 g/day suits broader joint and tendon aches.
  • Check with a pharmacist if you take warfarin or have a shellfish allergy.
  • Neither replaces exercise, weight management or clinician-guided treatment.

/guides/diet:
Pillar Guide

Evidence-based anti-inflammatory and Mediterranean eating for arthritis in the UK — what helps, what to limit, omega-3s, supplements and a practical meal plan.

Best arthritis diet advice UK: an anti-inflammatory Mediterranean pattern — vegetables, oily fish, olive oil, wholegrains and pulses — is the best-evidenced approach. It may support joint comfort for some people but does not replace prescribed treatment.

What is the best anti-inflammatory diet for arthritis?

A Mediterranean-style pattern — vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, olive oil, oily fish, nuts and pulses, with less ultra-processed food — has the strongest evidence for supporting joint health. It does not replace prescribed treatment.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Frequently asked questions

What is the best diet for arthritis joint pain?

The best diet for arthritis is the Mediterranean diet — rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, olive oil, oily fish, nuts and pulses. NHS and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) guidance supports a Mediterranean-style pattern for general health and joint-friendly eating. For osteoarthritis, gradual weight loss where appropriate (often discussed as around 5–10% of body weight with a clinician) can ease load on weight-bearing joints — this is educational, not a personal target.

Why Diet Matters for Arthritis

The relationship between diet and arthritis is one of the most researched areas in rheumatology. While no single food can cure arthritis, mounting evidence demonstrates that what you eat can significantly influence inflammation levels, pain intensity, joint stiffness, disease activity and even the effectiveness of medications. Reviews of Mediterranean-style and anti-inflammatory dietary patterns (including work summarised for clinicians in journals such as Nutrients) suggest diet can support lower pain and inflammatory markers for some people — effects vary, and diet does not replace prescribed treatment.

For people with osteoarthritis, diet also plays a critical role in weight management. Excess weight is the single most modifiable risk factor for OA: every 1 kg of body weight lost reduces the load on each knee by approximately 4 kg with every step (Messier et al., 2013). For overweight individuals with knee OA, losing just 5–10% of body weight can produce clinically meaningful reductions in pain and improvements in function.

The Mediterranean Diet: The Gold Standard

The Mediterranean diet is the most extensively studied dietary pattern for arthritis and chronic inflammation. It consistently outperforms other diets in clinical trials for reducing inflammatory markers, joint pain and cardiovascular risk — which is elevated in people with inflammatory arthritis.

Want a plan to follow this week? See the focused 7-day Mediterranean eating plan for arthritis — UK shopping list, recipes and what to eat freely, weekly and rarely.

Core Principles

  • Abundant vegetables and fruits — aim for 7+ portions daily, focusing on colourful varieties rich in antioxidants (berries, leafy greens, tomatoes, peppers, beetroot)
  • Wholegrains — oats, brown rice, wholemeal bread, quinoa, bulgur wheat
  • Healthy fats — extra virgin olive oil as the primary fat source (rich in oleocanthal, which has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory properties)
  • Oily fish — at least 2 portions per week (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout) for omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA
  • Legumes and pulses — lentils, chickpeas, beans — excellent protein and fibre sources
  • Nuts and seeds — walnuts (highest plant omega-3), almonds, flaxseeds, chia seeds
  • Herbs and spices — turmeric, ginger, garlic, oregano, rosemary — many have documented anti-inflammatory properties
  • Moderate dairy — yoghurt and cheese in moderation; fermented dairy supports gut health
  • Limited red meat — no more than 1–2 portions per week; processed meats avoided
  • Limited sugar and refined carbohydrates — these promote inflammation

A landmark 2023 trial in Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases found that RA patients following a Mediterranean diet for 16 weeks experienced a significant reduction in DAS28 scores (a composite measure of disease activity) compared to controls, with improvements in fatigue and quality of life.

Key Anti-Inflammatory Foods

Omega-3 Fatty Acids

Omega-3s are the most well-evidenced dietary component for arthritis. EPA and DHA — found primarily in oily fish — are converted into anti-inflammatory compounds called resolvins and protectins that actively help resolve inflammation. A 2017 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology found that fish oil supplementation (2–4 g/day of combined EPA/DHA) significantly reduced joint pain, morning stiffness and NSAID use in RA patients.

Best food sources:

  • Salmon (wild-caught) — 2.2 g omega-3 per 100 g
  • Mackerel — 2.6 g per 100 g
  • Sardines — 1.5 g per 100 g
  • Trout — 1.0 g per 100 g
  • Walnuts — 2.5 g ALA (plant omega-3) per 30 g
  • Flaxseeds — 6.7 g ALA per 30 g (ground for absorption)
  • Chia seeds — 5.0 g ALA per 30 g

Recommendation: Aim for 2 portions of oily fish per week plus daily plant sources. If you don't eat fish, consider an algae-based omega-3 supplement (providing EPA/DHA directly).

Turmeric and Curcumin

Turmeric's active compound, curcumin, is one of the most extensively studied natural anti-inflammatory agents. It works by blocking NF-ÎºB — a master regulator of inflammation — and inhibiting COX-2 and LOX enzymes (similar mechanisms to NSAIDs like ibuprofen). A 2016 systematic review and meta-analysis published in the Journal of Medicinal Food concluded that 1,000 mg/day of curcumin significantly reduced pain and improved function in knee OA patients.

Key considerations:

  • Curcumin has poor bioavailability on its own — pairing with black pepper (piperine) increases absorption by up to 2,000%
  • Study curcumin products differ from cooking turmeric — ask a clinician or pharmacist before using concentrated supplements
  • Some trials show curcumin provides comparable pain relief to diclofenac with fewer side effects
  • Consult your doctor if taking blood thinners or diabetes medication, as curcumin may interact

Ginger

Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols — bioactive compounds with anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties. A 2015 meta-analysis of 5 randomised controlled trials found that ginger supplementation (500–1,000 mg/day) significantly reduced OA pain compared to placebo. Fresh ginger can be used in cooking (1–2 cm fresh root daily) or as a tea.

Berries and Antioxidant-Rich Foods

Berries — particularly blueberries, strawberries, cherries and blackcurrants — are rich in anthocyanins, powerful antioxidants that reduce oxidative stress and inflammation. Tart cherry juice has been specifically studied for gout, where it has been shown to reduce uric acid levels and flare frequency. Other antioxidant-rich foods include dark leafy greens (kale, spinach), beetroot, sweet potatoes and dark chocolate (70%+ cocoa).

Foods That May Worsen Arthritis

While individual responses vary, certain foods are consistently associated with increased inflammation and worsened arthritis symptoms:

  • Processed and ultra-processed foods — ready meals, crisps, biscuits, processed meats (bacon, sausages, ham) — high in advanced glycation end products (AGEs) that promote inflammation
  • Added sugars — fizzy drinks, sweets, cakes — trigger inflammatory cytokine release
  • Refined carbohydrates — white bread, white pasta, pastries — spike blood sugar and insulin, promoting inflammation
  • Excessive alcohol — increases uric acid (worsens gout) and systemic inflammation
  • Excessive omega-6 fatty acids — found in sunflower oil, corn oil and many processed foods — when consumed in excess relative to omega-3, these promote pro-inflammatory pathways
  • Trans fats — hydrogenated oils found in some margarines and commercial baked goods
  • Excessive red meat — particularly processed meats, which contain nitrites and saturated fats

Supplements: What the Evidence Says

Glucosamine and Chondroitin

These are the most widely used OA supplements in the UK. Evidence is mixed: a 2018 Cochrane review found glucosamine provides small, uncertain benefits for pain compared to placebo. Chondroitin alone showed similarly modest effects. Combined glucosamine/chondroitin may offer slightly better outcomes, but the evidence is not strong enough for NICE to recommend routine use.

Collagen (Hydrolysed)

Emerging research suggests hydrolysed collagen peptides (10 g/day) may modestly reduce joint pain and stiffness in OA. A 2019 meta-analysis in International Orthopaedics found statistically significant improvements in pain and function, though effect sizes were small. Collagen is generally well-tolerated.

Vitamin D

Vitamin D deficiency is extremely common in the UK (affecting up to 1 in 5 adults) and is associated with worse arthritis outcomes. The health service recommends all UK adults take a 10 mcg (400 IU) vitamin D supplement daily during autumn and winter. People with inflammatory arthritis may benefit from higher doses (discuss with your doctor).

Fish Oil (Omega-3 Supplements)

If you don't consume enough oily fish, a high-quality fish oil supplement providing 1–3 g of combined EPA/DHA daily is the most well-evidenced supplement for arthritis. Look for purified, sustainably sourced products with high EPA content. Algae-based alternatives are equally effective for vegetarians and vegans.

Sample 7-Day Anti-Inflammatory Meal Plan

This plan follows Mediterranean diet principles and provides approximately 1,800–2,000 kcal/day:

Day 1

  • Breakfast: Overnight oats with blueberries, walnuts, chia seeds and honey
  • Lunch: Mediterranean salad with chickpeas, roasted peppers, feta, olives, extra virgin olive oil dressing
  • Dinner: Baked salmon with sweet potato, broccoli and turmeric-ginger sauce
  • Snack: Apple slices with almond butter

Day 2

  • Breakfast: Spinach and mushroom omelette with wholemeal toast
  • Lunch: Lentil and vegetable soup with crusty wholegrain bread
  • Dinner: Grilled mackerel with quinoa tabbouleh and roasted courgettes
  • Snack: Handful of mixed nuts and dried cranberries

Day 3

  • Breakfast: Greek yoghurt with strawberries, ground flaxseed and granola
  • Lunch: Avocado and smoked salmon on rye bread with cherry tomatoes
  • Dinner: Chicken and vegetable stir-fry with ginger, garlic and brown rice
  • Snack: Hummus with carrot and cucumber sticks

Day 4–7

Continue rotating fish (2–3 times), lean poultry, legume-based meals and plenty of colourful vegetables. Include turmeric, ginger and garlic regularly. Use extra virgin olive oil for cooking and dressings. Stay hydrated with water, green tea and ginger tea.

Gut Health and Arthritis

Emerging research links the gut microbiome to inflammatory arthritis. An imbalanced gut microbiome (dysbiosis) may trigger or worsen autoimmune responses in conditions like RA and PsA. To support gut health:

  • Eat 30+ different plant foods per week — diversity feeds diverse beneficial bacteria
  • Include fermented foods — kefir, sauerkraut, kimchi, live yoghurt, miso
  • Consume prebiotic fibre — garlic, onions, leeks, asparagus, bananas, oats
  • Limit artificial sweeteners and emulsifiers — these may disrupt gut bacteria

Weight Management for Joint Health

Maintaining a healthy weight is arguably the most impactful dietary intervention for OA. Evidence-based strategies include:

  • Focus on nutrient-dense, high-satiety foods — vegetables, protein, wholegrains and healthy fats keep you fuller for longer
  • Avoid crash diets — they lead to muscle loss, which worsens joint instability
  • Aim for gradual weight loss — 0.5–1 kg per week is sustainable and preserves muscle mass
  • Combine dietary changes with regular low-impact exercise — walking, swimming, cycling
  • Consider portion control rather than food restriction — using smaller plates and mindful eating techniques

The NICE guidelines for OA (NG226) specifically recommend weight loss as a first-line treatment alongside exercise, stating it should be offered before medication.

Practical Tips for UK Shoppers

  • Budget-friendly options — tinned fish (sardines, mackerel), frozen berries, dried lentils and tinned chickpeas are just as nutritious as fresh alternatives
  • Read labels — look for traffic-light labels; aim for green on fat, sugar and salt
  • Buy seasonal UK produce — cheaper and more nutritious; farmer's markets often have better value
  • Batch cooking — prepare soups, stews and curries in bulk and freeze portions
  • Joint-friendly cooking — use electric can openers, lightweight pans and adaptive kitchen utensils from organisations like the Arthritis Action or OT referral

Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie Recipe

Beet & Berry Anti-Inflammatory Smoothie (serves 1):

  • 1 small cooked beetroot (peeled, chopped)
  • 1 cup frozen mixed berries
  • 1 banana
  • 1-inch fresh ginger (grated)
  • 1 tbsp ground flaxseed
  • 1 cup unsweetened almond milk or oat milk
  • Optional: 1 tsp turmeric powder + pinch black pepper

Blend until smooth. This provides omega-3 (flaxseed), betalains (beetroot), anthocyanins (berries), gingerols (ginger) and curcumin (turmeric) — a powerhouse of anti-inflammatory compounds in one glass.

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide is based on evidence from NICE guidelines (NG226), systematic reviews published in Nutrients, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases, British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology, Journal of Medicinal Food, and guidance from the British Dietetic Association. Statistics cited are from the most recent publications available as of 2024. This information is for educational purposes only. Always consult a registered dietitian or your GP before making significant dietary changes, especially if you take medication.

How do Conventional DMARDs and Biologics compare?

For rheumatoid, psoriatic and axial spondyloarthritis, DMARDs and biologics are the two families of medicines that actually change the disease. They are not painkillers — they suppress the immune activity driving joint damage. This guide compares them for UK patients navigating UK healthcare rheumatology.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

For rheumatoid, psoriatic and axial spondyloarthritis, DMARDs and biologics are the two families of medicines that actually change the disease. They are not painkillers — they suppress the immune activity driving joint damage. This guide compares them for UK patients navigating UK healthcare rheumatology.

Conventional DMARDs

  • How it works: Broadly damp down the immune system. Methotrexate is the anchor drug; others include sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide.
  • Best for: First-line treatment for rheumatoid, psoriatic and juvenile arthritis. Often used long-term.
  • Common side-effects: Nausea, mouth ulcers, hair thinning, raised liver enzymes, low blood counts. Reversible with dose changes.
  • UK healthcare availability: Freely prescribed on the UK healthcare system, usually started by rheumatology and monitored with regular blood tests.
  • Typical UK cost: Very cheap — methotrexate tablets cost the UK healthcare system pennies per week.

Biologics

  • How it works: Target one specific step of the immune response — TNF, IL-6, IL-17, JAK, B cells — using engineered proteins or small molecules.
  • Best for: People whose disease stays active despite two conventional DMARDs, or who cannot tolerate them.
  • Common side-effects: Increased infection risk, injection-site reactions; specific classes carry other risks (e.g. shingles, cardiovascular).
  • UK healthcare availability: Prescribed by rheumatology under NICE-approved criteria after DMARD failure, monitored by hospital.
  • Typical UK cost: £8,000–£15,000+/year — usually free to eligible UK healthcare patients; biosimilars have reduced the price significantly.

How the two families really differ

Conventional DMARDs are old-school immune suppressants: they slow down a wide range of immune activity, which is why they work but also why they need blood monitoring. Methotrexate — the most-used arthritis medicine in the world — is safe and effective for most people at once-weekly doses.

Biologics are precision tools. Instead of dampening the whole immune system, they block one signal — for example TNF-Î± (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab), IL-6 (tocilizumab), IL-17 (secukinumab) or B-cells (rituximab). Newer 'targeted synthetic DMARDs' (JAK inhibitors like tofacitinib and baricitinib) are tablets rather than injections but work in the same targeted way.

How the UK healthcare system decides who gets what

NICE sets clear criteria. For rheumatoid arthritis, biologics are approved after a person has failed to respond to at least two conventional DMARDs (one of which is usually methotrexate) and still has moderate to severe disease activity — measured by DAS28 score. Similar rules apply to psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis.

This means most UK patients start on methotrexate, add hydroxychloroquine or sulfasalazine, and only move to biologics if disease activity stays high. It's not a matter of newer being 'better' — for a large minority of patients, DMARDs alone give excellent control.

Side-effect trade-offs

DMARDs need regular blood tests (fortnightly at start, then every 8–12 weeks) to catch liver, kidney or blood-count problems early. Common day-to-day side-effects — nausea, mouth ulcers, tiredness the day after methotrexate — often improve with folic acid, dose splitting or an anti-sickness tablet.

Biologics have lower rates of these particular issues but a higher risk of serious infection, TB reactivation and, for some classes, shingles or blood clots. That's why patients are screened for TB, hepatitis and vaccinated before starting, and told to hold doses during active infections.

Cost and access

For the individual patient, both are free on the UK healthcare system if criteria are met (though there's a prescription charge in England for DMARD tablets unless you're exempt). To the UK healthcare system, however, biologics cost thousands per patient per year — mitigated significantly by the rise of biosimilars, which are cheaper 'generic' versions with equivalent effect.

Privately, methotrexate and other DMARDs can be prescribed for a few pounds a month; biologics privately cost hundreds to a few thousand a month, so almost all UK patients access them through the UK healthcare system.

Which is 'better'?

For most newly-diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis, methotrexate remains the anchor drug — often combined with a short course of steroids to bridge until it kicks in. Roughly half of patients get durable low disease activity or remission on DMARDs alone.

For those with persistent activity or specific features (like severe skin psoriasis or axial disease), biologics are transformative and now expected in the UK healthcare system treatment pathway. Increasingly, rheumatologists tailor the choice of biologic to the disease pattern and personal factors like pregnancy, cardiovascular risk and needle tolerance.

At a glance

Conventional DMARDsBiologics
Type of medicineBroad immune suppressantsTargeted immune blockers
First-line?YesAfter DMARD failure
How givenTablets or weekly injectionInjection or infusion (some tablets)
MonitoringRegular bloodsScreening + infection watch
UK healthcare cost/yearUnder £100£8,000–£15,000+
Access on NHSFreely prescribedNICE criteria required

Key takeaways

  • Most UK patients start on methotrexate — cheap, effective, and well understood.
  • Biologics come in after two DMARDs haven't controlled disease.
  • Both need infection awareness, but biologics carry a higher infection risk.
  • Biosimilars have made biologics far more affordable for the UK healthcare system.
  • The goal for either family is remission or low disease activity, not just pain relief.

Talk to your clinician

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Conventional DMARDs and Biologics with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

Pillar Guide

NICE-aligned home physio routines for knees, hips, hands and more — free from Living With Arthritis (charity 1218461). Start gently, progress safely.

Exercise is the single most effective non-drug treatment for arthritis. UK NICE guidelines (NG226) put it ahead of medication for osteoarthritis. Aim for 150 minutes of low-impact aerobic activity per week (walking, swimming, cycling), plus two sessions of strength work and a flexibility practice such as tai chi. Start short, build gradually, and pick activities you enjoy.

What exercise is best for arthritis?

NICE places exercise first-line for osteoarthritis: combine low-impact aerobic activity (walking, cycling, swimming) with strengthening two or more days a week and flexibility work. Moderate discomfort that settles within 24 hours is expected; reduce intensity if pain stays high overnight or joints swell.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Frequently asked questions

Why Exercise Is the Best Medicine for Arthritis

If arthritis exercise could be packaged into a pill, it would be hailed as a miracle drug. The evidence is overwhelming: regular, appropriate physical activity is the single most effective non-pharmacological treatment for arthritis. NICE guidelines (NG226) place exercise ahead of medication in the treatment hierarchy for osteoarthritis, and the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy describes it as "the most important thing you can do" for joint health.

Despite this, research shows that over 60% of adults with arthritis in the UK are insufficiently active (Sport England, 2023). Fear of worsening symptoms, lack of guidance and misinformation ("rest is best") are the primary barriers. In reality, not exercising is far more harmful: inactivity leads to muscle weakening, joint stiffness, weight gain, cardiovascular decline and worsened pain — creating a vicious cycle of deconditioning.

Benefits of regular exercise for arthritis include:

  • Pain reduction — exercise releases endorphins (natural painkillers) and reduces inflammatory markers
  • Improved joint mobility — regular movement prevents stiffness and maintains range of motion
  • Stronger muscles — muscles act as shock absorbers, protecting and stabilising joints
  • Weight management — every 1 kg lost reduces knee load by 4 kg per step
  • Better sleep — physical activity improves sleep quality, which in turn reduces pain perception
  • Improved mental health — exercise reduces depression and anxiety by up to 30% (WHO, 2022)
  • Cardiovascular protection — vital for people with inflammatory arthritis who have increased heart disease risk
  • Reduced fatigue — counterintuitively, regular exercise reduces the chronic fatigue associated with RA

Joint exercise index (start here)

Jump to the free joint-specific home routines:

  • Free knee exercises for osteoarthritis UK — 8-move NICE-aligned routine
  • Hip exercises for osteoarthritis — 8-move physio-aligned routine
  • Exercise hub — interactive library by joint
  • Can exercise make osteoarthritis worse? — safety evidence
  • Free arthritis resources UK — guides, home physio and tools (charity 1218461)

Types of Exercise for Arthritis

A balanced arthritis exercise programme should include three types of activity:

1. Aerobic (Cardiovascular) Exercise

Low-impact aerobic exercise improves cardiovascular fitness, helps manage weight, reduces inflammation and boosts mood. The health service recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week (or 75 minutes of vigorous activity). For people with arthritis, suitable options include:

  • Walking — the most accessible exercise; start with 10–15 minutes and gradually increase. Nordic walking (with poles) may improve comfort and confidence for some people, but evidence on its effect on knee loading is mixed.
  • Swimming and water aerobics — buoyancy reduces joint load by up to 90%, making it ideal for painful joints. Many the public health service and local authority pools offer arthritis-specific sessions
  • Cycling — stationary or outdoor; very low joint impact. Excellent for knee OA
  • Elliptical trainer — smooth, controlled movement without impact
  • Rowing — full-body workout with minimal joint jarring

Tip: Start at a level you can manage and build up gradually. The "talk test" is useful — if you can hold a conversation while exercising, the intensity is appropriate. If joints are sore for more than 2 hours after exercise, you may have done too much.

2. Strength (Resistance) Training

Strengthening the muscles around affected joints is critical. Strong muscles absorb shock, reduce load on joints and improve stability. A 2021 Cochrane review found that resistance training significantly reduces pain and improves function in knee OA, with effects comparable to or better than most medications.

Key exercises by joint:

Knee exercises

Full free programme: Free knee exercises for osteoarthritis UK.

  • Straight-leg raises — lie on your back, keep one leg bent and slowly raise the other, hold 5 seconds. 3 sets of 10.
  • Wall squats — lean against a wall and slide down to a comfortable squat (30–45°), hold 10 seconds. 3 sets of 5–10.
  • Step-ups — using a low step (15–20 cm), step up and down slowly. 2 sets of 10 per leg.
  • Terminal knee extensions — seated, slowly straighten your knee against resistance (using a resistance band or ankle weight). 3 sets of 10.

Hip exercises

Full free programme: Hip exercises for osteoarthritis.

  • Bridges — lie on your back with knees bent, lift hips toward the ceiling, hold 5 seconds. 3 sets of 10.
  • Clamshells — lie on your side with knees bent, keep feet together and open the top knee like a clamshell. 3 sets of 15.
  • Side-lying leg raises — lie on your side, raise the top leg slowly, hold 3 seconds. 3 sets of 10.
  • Seated hip flexion — seated, lift one knee toward your chest, hold 5 seconds. 2 sets of 10.

Hand and wrist exercises

  • Finger spreads — spread fingers wide, hold 5 seconds, relax. 10 repetitions.
  • Fist making — slowly make a fist, hold 5 seconds, release and spread. 10 repetitions.
  • Thumb touches — touch each fingertip to thumb in turn. 5 cycles per hand.
  • Wrist circles — slow circles in both directions. 10 each way.
  • Putty squeezing — therapeutic putty or stress ball. 2 minutes per hand.

Shoulder exercises

  • Pendulum swings — lean forward, let arm hang and gently swing in small circles. 1 minute each direction.
  • Wall walks — face a wall and "walk" your fingers up the wall as high as comfortable. 10 repetitions.
  • External rotation with band — elbow at side, rotate forearm outward against resistance. 3 sets of 10.

3. Flexibility and Range of Motion

Gentle stretching maintains joint flexibility, reduces stiffness and improves comfort. Best practices include:

  • Stretch daily, ideally when joints are warm (after a bath/shower or light activity)
  • Hold each stretch for 15–30 seconds; never bounce
  • Breathe normally and relax into the stretch; stop if you feel sharp pain
  • Yoga and tai chi are excellent structured flexibility programmes — both have strong evidence for arthritis benefit. Tai chi in particular has been shown to reduce pain, improve balance and reduce fall risk in older adults with OA (a 2019 BMJ meta-analysis found tai chi as effective as standard physiotherapy for knee OA)

Chair-Based Exercises

For people with significant mobility limitations or during flare-ups, chair-based exercises provide an excellent way to stay active:

  • Seated marching — lift alternate knees for 1–2 minutes
  • Seated leg extensions — straighten one knee, hold 5 seconds, lower. 10 per leg
  • Seated arm raises — lift arms to shoulder height and lower. 10 repetitions
  • Ankle circles — lift one foot and circle the ankle. 10 each direction
  • Seated trunk rotations — hands on thighs, gently rotate upper body left and right. 10 each side

These exercises are also ideal for office workers who need to combat prolonged sitting, which worsens joint stiffness.

Water-Based Exercise (Hydrotherapy)

Exercising in warm water (typically 33–36°C) is one of the most effective environments for arthritis exercise. Benefits include:

  • Buoyancy — water supports up to 90% of body weight, dramatically reducing joint load
  • Warmth — warm water relaxes muscles and increases blood flow to joints
  • Resistance — water provides natural resistance for strengthening without weights
  • Pain relief — hydrostatic pressure reduces swelling

The health service provides hydrotherapy at some hospitals (referral via GP or physiotherapist). Many local authority pools and leisure centres also offer warm-water sessions. Organisations like Swim England and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) maintain directories of arthritis-friendly swimming sessions.

Exercising During Flare-Ups

A common question is whether to exercise during a flare-up. The answer is: yes, but modify. During active flares:

  • Reduce intensity and duration — do gentle range-of-motion exercises rather than strengthening or aerobic work
  • Focus on affected joints — gentle stretching and movement to prevent stiffness
  • Use ice after exercise — 10–15 minutes to reduce inflammation
  • Listen to your body — pain during exercise that worsens or persists for more than 2 hours suggests you've overdone it
  • Avoid complete rest — prolonged inactivity during flares leads to muscle wasting and longer recovery times

Getting Started: A Progressive Programme

Weeks 1–2: Foundation

  • 5–10 minutes of gentle walking or chair exercises, 3 times per week
  • Basic stretches for affected joints (5 minutes daily)
  • Focus on establishing the habit, not intensity

Weeks 3–4: Building

  • 15–20 minutes of walking or swimming, 4 times per week
  • Add 2 strengthening exercises per affected joint area
  • Continue daily stretches

Weeks 5–8: Progressing

  • 20–30 minutes of aerobic activity, 5 times per week
  • Full strengthening routine (3 sets, 10 reps), 2–3 times per week
  • Consider joining a group class (tai chi, yoga, aqua aerobics)

Weeks 9+: Maintenance

  • 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity per week
  • Strength training 2–3 times per week
  • Daily flexibility work
  • Variety — mix activities to prevent boredom and overuse

Safety Guidelines

  • Warm up for 5 minutes before strengthening or vigorous activity
  • Cool down with gentle stretches afterwards
  • Use the 2-hour pain rule — if joint pain is worse 2 hours after exercise, reduce intensity next time
  • Avoid high-impact activities during flares — running, jumping, contact sports
  • Wear supportive footwear — proper shoes reduce knee and hip strain
  • Stay hydrated — dehydration can worsen joint stiffness
  • Consult a physiotherapist — for a personalised programme, especially if you're newly diagnosed or post-surgery

UK Exercise Resources

  • Living With Arthritis — free exercise programmes for every major joint
  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) — exercise guides and video library at arthritis-uk.org
  • UK Health Fitness Studio — free exercise videos at NHS services
  • Chartered Society of Physiotherapy — find a physiotherapist at csp.org.uk
  • We Are Undefeatable — campaign supporting people with long-term conditions to be active

This guide is based on NICE guidelines (NG226), Cochrane systematic reviews of exercise interventions for OA and RA, the public health service physical activity guidelines, Sport England Active Lives survey data, and guidance from the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy and British Society for Rheumatology. Statistics cited are from the most recent publications available as of 2024. This information is for educational purposes only. Consult a physiotherapist or GP before starting a new exercise programme, particularly if you have severe or unstable joint disease.

How can older adults prevent falls?

Strength and balance training (tai chi, Otago programme) cuts falls by around 30%. Also: home hazard checks, medication review, eye tests every 2 years and vitamin D 10 mcg/day. Contact your GP or UK healthcare falls clinic if you've fallen twice in a year.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

How can older adults with arthritis prevent falls?

Fall prevention usually combines strength and balance exercise, a medication and vision review, suitable footwear, and changes to hazards at home. Ask a GP, physiotherapist or local falls service for an individual assessment if you have fallen, feel unsteady or are worried about falling.

Medically reviewed by Maxwell

First Contact Practitioner • HCPC PH128483 • Last updated June 2026

Reviewer details and the site's clinical review process are documented in our editorial standards.

1. Understanding fall risk in arthritis

One in three adults over 65 falls each year — more for those with arthritis. Risk factors cluster: muscle weakness, balance loss, slower reactions, joint pain altering gait, medications causing dizziness, vision changes and environmental hazards. Addressing several at once works best.

2. Home safety: the checklist

  • Remove loose rugs or secure them with non-slip backing
  • Install grab rails by the toilet, shower and front door
  • Fit bright lighting on stairs and night-lights between bed and bathroom
  • Wear supportive, well-fitting footwear indoors — not slippers without grip
  • Keep frequently-used items within easy reach to avoid stretching or stooping
  • Use a stairlift or banister on both sides for steep stairs

3. Balance and proprioception training

Balance is trainable at any age. Start with simple drills at a kitchen counter: stand on one leg 10 seconds (build to 30), heel-to-toe walking, weight shifts. Tai chi reduces falls by around 20% and is suitable for most older adults — see our tai chi for balance guide.

4. Strength training to prevent falls

Strong legs catch you when balance fails. Prioritise quadriceps (sit-to-stand, step-ups), glutes (bridges, sideways leg lifts), calves (heel raises) and core (gentle planks at a counter). Two sessions per week, building from 1 to 3 sets of 10–12.

5. When a fall happens: immediate response and recovery

Stay calm and check for pain or injury before moving. If you may be injured, feel unwell or cannot get up safely, use a phone or pendant alarm and keep warm while you wait for help. Call 999 for a serious injury or emergency. Tell your GP or another healthcare professional about a fall so they can consider strength, medication, vision and home hazards.

Frequently asked questions

Why do older adults with arthritis fall more often?

Arthritis reduces muscle strength, joint stability and balance reactions. Pain alters walking patterns, medications can cause dizziness, and reduced activity erodes confidence — together raising fall risk substantially.

What exercise helps prevent falls?

Programmes that combine progressive strength and balance work are commonly used for people at risk of falls. The best programme is one matched to your health, mobility and current balance.

Are walking aids a sign of giving up?

No. A correctly fitted stick or frame increases confidence, reduces falls and lets you stay active longer. They are tools — not failures.

What should I do immediately after a fall?

Check for pain or injury before trying to move. If you may be injured, feel unwell or cannot get up safely, use a phone or pendant alarm and keep warm while you wait for help. Call 999 for a serious injury or emergency.

Do certain medications increase fall risk?

Yes. Sedatives, sleeping tablets, blood pressure medications and some painkillers can cause dizziness. Ask your GP for a medication review if you have fallen.

Should I get a home safety check?

A home assessment can identify hazards and useful equipment. Availability and referral routes vary, so ask your GP, local council or UK healthcare service whether an occupational therapy or falls assessment is available locally.

Pillar Guide

A plain-English UK guide to dosing, monitoring, side effects and how febuxostat compares with allopurinol.

Febuxostat (Adenuric) is a daily tablet that lowers uric acid to prevent gout attacks. Used when allopurinol isn't tolerated or strong enough, it gradually dissolves the crystal deposits in joints that drive flares. This guide explains how it works, what to expect, and how to get the most from it.

Febuxostat for gout: an overview

Gout is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis, affecting around 1 in 40 adults in the UK. It happens when uric acid in the blood rises high enough to form sharp crystals inside joints — most often the big toe, but also the ankle, knee, wrist and fingers. The body's immune response to these crystals causes the sudden, severe pain of a gout attack.

Febuxostat (sold as Adenuric in the UK and Uloric in the US) is a urate-lowering therapy: it doesn't treat the pain of an attack, but taken every day it lowers the level of uric acid in the blood, gradually dissolves the crystal deposits already in the joints, and over time prevents new attacks.

It is one of two main long-term gout medications used in the UK, the other being allopurinol. Both work by blocking xanthine oxidase, the enzyme that produces uric acid. Febuxostat is a more targeted blocker and is the recommended option when allopurinol has not worked, has caused side effects, or cannot be dosed high enough because of reduced kidney function.

How febuxostat works

Uric acid is a normal waste product made when the body breaks down purines — chemicals found in cells and in some foods. Most people clear it efficiently through the kidneys. In gout, either too much uric acid is produced, too little is excreted, or both.

Febuxostat blocks the xanthine oxidase enzyme so the body produces less uric acid in the first place. Blood levels begin to fall within 24–48 hours, and most people reach the recommended target of below 360 µmol/L (6 mg/dL) within 4–8 weeks of starting treatment.

Once uric acid is below this threshold for long enough, the crystal deposits in the joints — and the larger lumps known as tophi under the skin — slowly dissolve. This is what protects against future attacks and reverses long-term joint damage.

Who febuxostat is for

NICE guidance (TA164) recommends febuxostat for adults with chronic gout where uric acid crystal deposition has already caused damage and where allopurinol is either contraindicated or not tolerated. In practice, your GP or rheumatologist may consider febuxostat if:

  • You have had two or more gout attacks in a year
  • You have tophi (firm lumps of urate crystals under the skin)
  • You have urate kidney stones
  • You have chronic kidney disease that limits allopurinol dosing
  • You experienced a rash, raised liver enzymes or other side effects on allopurinol
  • Your uric acid level remains above target despite maximum allopurinol

How clinicians typically monitor febuxostat

UK labels and BNF summaries describe common starting strengths (often discussed as 80 mg once daily, sometimes increased toward 120 mg if uric acid remains above target). Your rheumatology team sets your dose — do not start, increase or stop febuxostat based on this educational page. Follow the SmPC / patient leaflet they give you.

Your prescriber will usually arrange:

  • A blood test for uric acid at 2–4 weeks, then every 3–6 months
  • A blood test for liver function at 2 months and then yearly
  • A discussion about flare prophylaxis with colchicine or a low-dose NSAID for the first 3–6 months

It is essential to keep taking febuxostat every day, including during a gout attack. Stopping and starting urate-lowering therapy causes the uric acid level to swing, which triggers more attacks.

Side effects and safety

Most people tolerate febuxostat well. The most common side effects are mild and short-lived:

  • Nausea, diarrhoea or stomach discomfort
  • Headache
  • Mildly raised liver enzymes on blood tests
  • A mild rash

Less common but more serious risks include:

  • Cardiovascular events — large trials have shown a small increase in heart-related events in people with established heart or vascular disease. The European Medicines Agency advises caution in this group; allopurinol is usually preferred unless not tolerated.
  • Severe skin reactions — including Stevens–Johnson syndrome. Stop the medication and seek urgent medical advice if a rash spreads or blisters appear.
  • Liver injury — rare but reported. Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or persistent abdominal pain.

Febuxostat vs allopurinol: which is better?

For most newly diagnosed gout, allopurinol is first-line: it is cheaper, has decades of safety data, and is effective for the majority. Febuxostat is reserved for the situations listed above.

Head-to-head trials show febuxostat lowers uric acid at least as effectively as allopurinol, and often faster. It does not need dose adjustment in mild-to-moderate kidney disease, which is a major practical advantage. The trade-off is the cardiovascular signal in high-risk patients and the higher prescription cost.

Lifestyle alongside febuxostat

Medication does the heavy lifting in lowering uric acid, but diet and lifestyle reduce the burden and protect kidney function:

  • Limit alcohol — especially beer (high in purines) and spirits
  • Cut sugary drinks — fructose raises uric acid as much as alcohol
  • Reduce red meat, offal and shellfish — the highest-purine foods
  • Drink 2 litres of water a day to help the kidneys clear urate
  • Lose excess weight gradually — crash dieting and fasting raise uric acid temporarily
  • Eat low-fat dairy and cherries — both associated with lower flare risk

For a full anti-inflammatory eating pattern that supports gout and other forms of arthritis, see our foods to avoid with arthritis guide.

When to seek urgent help

  • A spreading rash, blistering, or peeling skin — stop febuxostat and contact a doctor immediately.
  • Chest pain, breathlessness or signs of stroke — call 999.
  • Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or persistent right-sided abdominal pain — possible liver injury.
  • A gout attack that doesn't settle within a week on usual treatment — speak to your GP about flare control.

Key takeaways

  • Febuxostat lowers uric acid by blocking xanthine oxidase, gradually dissolving crystal deposits in joints.
  • It is used when allopurinol is not tolerated or not effective, and when kidney function limits allopurinol dosing.
  • Target uric acid is below 360 µmol/L (300 µmol/L in severe gout with tophi).
  • Take it every single day — including during a flare — and pair it with colchicine for the first 3–6 months.
  • Watch for skin reactions, liver changes and cardiovascular risk in people with established heart disease.
  • Diet, alcohol and weight management amplify the benefit but do not replace daily medication.
