How do Allopurinol and Febuxostat compare?

Allopurinol and febuxostat are the two urate-lowering drugs used long term to prevent gout attacks in the UK. Both lower blood uric acid by blocking xanthine oxidase, but they differ in effectiveness at standard doses, cardiovascular safety, kidney handling and UK healthcare availability. This guide explains what NICE and the British Society for Rheumatology actually recommend, how each drug performs in practice, and when febuxostat is the sensible second choice.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Allopurinol and febuxostat are the two urate-lowering drugs used long term to prevent gout attacks in the UK. Both lower blood uric acid by blocking xanthine oxidase, but they differ in effectiveness at standard doses, cardiovascular safety, kidney handling and UK healthcare availability. This guide explains what NICE and the British Society for Rheumatology actually recommend, how each drug performs in practice, and when febuxostat is the sensible second choice.

Allopurinol

  • How it works: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor. Lowers uric acid production. Standard first-line urate-lowering therapy in UK guidelines, titrated from 100 mg up to 900 mg/day to hit a target serum urate below 300–360 Âµmol/L.
  • Best for: Almost everyone starting long-term gout treatment. Effective, cheap, well studied over 60+ years, and safe for most people with mild to moderate kidney impairment when titrated slowly.
  • Common side-effects: Rash (common), rare but serious hypersensitivity syndrome (higher risk in people of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry with the HLA-B*5801 gene), mildly deranged liver enzymes. Acute gout flares in the first weeks of treatment.
  • UK healthcare availability: First-line urate-lowering therapy on the UK healthcare system per NICE NG219 (2022) and BSR guidance. Available on standard UK healthcare prescription.
  • Typical UK cost: Approximately £1–£3 per month at standard doses. Free with an UK healthcare prescription exemption.

Febuxostat

  • How it works: A newer, non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor. Licensed doses in the UK are 80 mg or 120 mg once daily. More potent per milligram than allopurinol, so a fixed dose often reaches target serum urate faster.
  • Best for: People who cannot tolerate allopurinol, those who fail to reach target urate on maximum allopurinol, and some patients with significant renal impairment where allopurinol dose titration is limited.
  • Common side-effects: Liver enzyme rise, nausea, headache, rash, and acute flares during initiation. A large cardiovascular safety trial (CARES, 2018) raised concerns about higher cardiovascular death rates versus allopurinol, though a later trial (FAST, 2020) in a UK/European population did not confirm this.
  • UK healthcare availability: Second-line on the UK healthcare system. NICE TA164 restricts it to patients intolerant of allopurinol or in whom allopurinol is contraindicated. Not first-choice.
  • Typical UK cost: Roughly £13–£20 per month for 80 mg tablets. Free with an UK healthcare prescription exemption.

What UK guidelines actually say

NICE NG219 (2022) and the British Society for Rheumatology are clear: allopurinol is first-line urate-lowering therapy for essentially all UK adults with gout who need long-term treatment. Febuxostat sits as a second-line option, reserved for people who cannot tolerate allopurinol or in whom it is contraindicated.

This is not because febuxostat is a worse drug — it isn't. It reflects cost, decades of allopurinol safety data, and the unresolved cardiovascular question from the CARES trial. If allopurinol is well tolerated and reaches the target serum urate, there is no reason to switch.

Effectiveness — reaching the target urate

The whole point of urate-lowering therapy is to drop serum urate below 300–360 Âµmol/L (5–6 mg/dL) and keep it there. Below that threshold, existing urate crystals in joints slowly dissolve and new attacks become rare.

At its full titrated dose (up to 900 mg/day, though most UK patients reach target on 300–500 mg), allopurinol gets 70–80% of people to target. The problem is that many are left under-treated on 100–300 mg because their GP doesn't titrate high enough.

Febuxostat at 80 mg or 120 mg once daily reaches target urate in more people at a fixed dose than allopurinol 300 mg does — but the fair comparison is against properly titrated allopurinol, and there the difference narrows significantly.

The cardiovascular question

The CARES trial (published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018) enrolled US patients with gout and pre-existing cardiovascular disease. Febuxostat and allopurinol prevented similar numbers of cardiovascular events overall, but there was a higher rate of cardiovascular death and all-cause death in the febuxostat group. This prompted the MHRA to issue a warning and the EMA to update the label.

The FAST trial (Lancet, 2020) was a UK, Danish and Swedish study of over 6,000 patients. It did not find a higher cardiovascular death rate on febuxostat versus allopurinol, which reassured many UK rheumatologists. Current UK practice treats febuxostat as safe in people without severe pre-existing cardiovascular disease, but avoids it in those with a history of major cardiovascular events where allopurinol is a reasonable alternative.

When allopurinol is not suitable

The main reasons a UK patient ends up on febuxostat are: a previous allopurinol rash or hypersensitivity, inability to reach target urate on the maximum tolerated allopurinol dose, or significant renal impairment where allopurinol titration is capped.

People of Han Chinese, Thai or Korean ancestry are offered HLA-B*5801 testing before starting allopurinol because that gene raises the risk of severe cutaneous reactions (Stevens–Johnson syndrome). A positive test is a clear indication for febuxostat instead.

Kidney disease — a real difference

Allopurinol needs careful dose reduction in moderate to severe chronic kidney disease. UK guidance now allows titration up in CKD, but slowly and with close monitoring. In practice many patients with CKD are under-dosed.

Febuxostat needs no dose adjustment in mild to moderate renal impairment and only cautious use in severe CKD. That makes it a practical option for patients where allopurinol titration keeps hitting a ceiling.

Starting either drug — the flare paradox

Both drugs frequently trigger gout attacks in the first weeks of treatment as urate crystals start to dissolve and shed from joints. This is expected, not a treatment failure. UK guidance recommends covering the first 3–6 months of urate-lowering therapy with a low-dose colchicine (usually 500 micrograms once or twice daily) or a low-dose NSAID if colchicine is not tolerated.

The most common reason people stop urate-lowering therapy is stopping in the middle of an early flare. If your urate is coming down, do not stop the drug — that's when the flares are most likely, but also when the long-term benefit is beginning.

So which should you take?

For almost all UK adults with gout, allopurinol first — titrated properly to hit a serum urate target below 360 Âµmol/L. This is the NICE- and BSR-recommended route, it is far cheaper, and it has the longest safety record.

Febuxostat is the right answer if you cannot tolerate allopurinol, if you have failed to reach target on the highest allopurinol dose you can take, or if kidney disease is limiting how high your allopurinol can go. In those situations it is often the drug that finally gets your urate under control.

  • Febuxostat is a useful alternative in significant kidney disease where allopurinol titration is limited.
  • Do not stop urate-lowering therapy during an early flare — that's when it's starting to work.

How is frailty managed with arthritis?

Frailty and arthritis together respond to comprehensive geriatric assessment: strength training, protein-rich diet, medication review, hearing/vision checks and social connection. Ask your GP for a formal frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale) review.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

What is frailty and can it be reversed?

Frailty is a state of reduced physical reserve common in older adults with arthritis. The good news: mild and moderate frailty can be reversed with progressive strength training, adequate protein, social engagement, mood support and treatment of underlying conditions. Early intervention is most effective.

Medically reviewed by Maxwell

First Contact Practitioner • HCPC PH128483 • Last updated June 2026

Reviewer details and the site's clinical review process are documented in our editorial standards.

1. What is frailty and how does it connect to arthritis?

Frailty is a clinical syndrome of reduced reserve across multiple body systems — muscle, bone, balance, cognition and immunity. Adults with arthritis are at higher risk because chronic pain reduces activity, accelerating muscle loss (sarcopenia) and balance decline.

Around 10% of people aged 65+ in the UK are living with frailty, rising to 25–50% over 85. The Clinical Frailty Scale, gait speed and grip strength help clinicians identify who is pre-frail or frail.

2. The five pillars of frailty prevention

  • Strength: progressive resistance training 2–3 times per week.
  • Nutrition: 1.0–1.2 g/kg protein/day plus vitamin D, calcium and adequate calories.
  • Cognition: regular mental stimulation, reading, puzzles, learning.
  • Mood: identify and treat depression and anxiety early.
  • Social connection: isolation doubles frailty risk — community, family and groups protect.

3. Exercise for frailty: safe progressions

Start seated. Sit-to-stand from a chair (aim for 10–15 reps), heel raises, knee extensions with ankle weights, and resistance band rows build the legs and trunk safely. Add balance work — single-leg standing at a counter — once strength returns.

See our exercise hub for progressions.

4. Nutrition strategies for muscle preservation

Spread protein across meals: 25–30 g per meal triggers muscle protein synthesis better than one large serving. Sources include eggs, Greek yoghurt, fish, lean meat, beans and tofu. Pair with vitamin D (10 Âµg/day October–March, UK healthcare guidance) and adequate calories.

Read our diet hub and foods to avoid with arthritis.

5. When to ask for help: red flags and support services

  • Unintentional weight loss greater than 5% in 12 months
  • More than one fall in 12 months
  • New or worsening exhaustion most days
  • Struggling with dressing, washing or shopping
  • Slower walking pace (under 0.8 m/s)

Speak to your GP, who can refer to community physiotherapy, falls clinics and social prescribing.

6. What families are looking for

Many adult children begin researching frailty after a parent has a fall, loses weight or struggles with day-to-day tasks. The most effective interventions are preventative rather than reactive — nutritional support, balance and strength work, home safety changes and assistive technology — and the earlier they start, the better the outcome.

A community geriatric or occupational therapy assessment is the highest-value starting point: it pulls together the medical, functional and home-environment picture and signposts the right combination of services and equipment.

Common frailty solutions

  • High-protein supplements and fortified foods to counter sarcopenia
  • Vitamin D and other targeted nutritional intervention
  • Medical alert systems, personal alarms and fall detectors
  • Home modifications — grab rails, ramps, improved lighting, removing trip hazards
  • Geriatric assessments (Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment) and frailty case management
  • Balance, resistance and tai chi programmes — group or one-to-one

Educational information only — we don't endorse specific brands or providers. Speak to your GP, community physiotherapy or social services for personalised recommendations.

Frequently asked questions

What is frailty?

Frailty is a clinical state of reduced reserve and resilience across multiple body systems, leaving older adults more vulnerable to falls, hospital admission and slower recovery.

Does arthritis cause frailty?

Arthritis does not directly cause frailty, but pain, inflammation and inactivity accelerate muscle loss and reduce function — pushing people into pre-frail or frail states earlier.

Can frailty be reversed?

Yes. Mild and moderate frailty often improves with progressive resistance training, adequate protein (1.0–1.2 g/kg/day), social engagement and treatment of underlying conditions.

How is frailty measured?

Clinicians use tools such as the Clinical Frailty Scale, gait speed (<0.8 m/s), grip strength and the Fried phenotype (weakness, slowness, exhaustion, low activity, weight loss).

What exercise is safest for frail older adults?

Supervised seated strength work, sit-to-stand repetitions, resistance bands and balance drills — progressed gradually. Avoid high-impact loading until strength returns.

When should I ask for help?

Speak to your GP if you notice unintentional weight loss, more than one fall in 12 months, exhaustion, or struggling with daily tasks like dressing or shopping.

/guides/health-services:
Pillar Guide

How to access free arthritis care through the public health service — from your first GP visit to specialist rheumatology, physiotherapy and joint replacement surgery.

Arthritis care in the UK is free at the point of use. Most journeys start with a GP, who may refer you to a First Contact Physiotherapist, a rheumatology clinic or an orthopaedic team. This guide explains how each service works, typical waiting times, and what to do while you wait for an appointment.

Overview of Arthritis Services

The National Health Service provides a comprehensive framework of arthritis care across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. From initial GP consultations through to specialist rheumatology clinics, joint replacement surgery and community rehabilitation, the public health service offers a multi-layered system of support. Understanding how to navigate this system effectively can dramatically improve your experience and outcomes.

In England alone, musculoskeletal (MSK) conditions account for approximately 30% of all GP consultations (public health data, 2023). The health service spends an estimated £10.2 billion annually on musculoskeletal care, making it one of the largest areas of healthcare expenditure. Despite this, waiting times for rheumatology appointments have increased significantly since 2020, with some areas reporting waits of 6–12 months for a first specialist appointment.

Your GP and First Contact Physiotherapists

Your journey through the arthritis care pathway typically begins with your General Practitioner (GP). GPs are trained to assess joint pain, order initial blood tests and imaging, prescribe first-line medications, and refer to specialists when necessary.

However, one of the most significant recent developments in the public health service musculoskeletal care is the introduction of First Contact Practitioners (FCPs). These are specialist physiotherapists embedded within GP practices who can assess, diagnose and manage musculoskeletal conditions — including arthritis — without requiring a GP referral. Since 2019, the public health service has trained and deployed over 4,000 FCPs across England as part of the Additional Roles Reimbursement Scheme (ARRS).

FCPs can:

  • Assess your joint symptoms on the same day or within days
  • Order X-rays and blood tests
  • Provide exercise programmes and self-management advice
  • Refer directly to rheumatology, orthopaedics or other specialists
  • Prescribe certain medications (if qualified as an independent prescriber)

To access an FCP, simply contact your GP practice and ask to book an appointment with the musculoskeletal physiotherapist or first contact practitioner. Not all practices have one, but the number is growing rapidly.

Getting a Rheumatology Referral

If your GP or FCP suspects an inflammatory type of arthritis (such as RA, PsA or ankylosing spondylitis), they should refer you to a rheumatologist — a hospital-based consultant who specialises in inflammatory joint diseases. NICE guidelines (NG100) state that suspected RA should be referred urgently, ideally within 3 working days, because early treatment with DMARDs within the first 12 weeks of symptom onset significantly improves long-term outcomes.

What to expect at your first rheumatology appointment:

  • A thorough clinical examination of your joints
  • Review of blood tests (CRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP antibodies)
  • Possible ultrasound scan of affected joints (increasingly done in clinic)
  • Discussion of treatment options, typically starting with methotrexate for RA
  • Goal-setting using a treat-to-target approach (aiming for low disease activity or remission)

The national standard for rheumatology is an 18-week referral-to-treatment (RTT) target. However, actual waiting times vary considerably by region. As of 2024, the average wait for a rheumatology first appointment in England is approximately 14 weeks, but some Integrated Care Boards (ICBs) report waits exceeding 26 weeks.

Tips for faster access:

  • Ask your GP to mark the referral as urgent if inflammatory arthritis is suspected
  • Request a choose and book appointment — you may find shorter waits at a hospital further away
  • Some local health trusts offer triage services where a rheumatology nurse reviews referrals and fast-tracks urgent cases
  • Check if your area has an Early Inflammatory Arthritis (EIA) clinic — these are dedicated rapid-access services

Public Health Physiotherapy for Arthritis

Physiotherapy is a cornerstone of arthritis management and is available free through the public health service. NICE guidelines recommend exercise therapy as a first-line treatment for osteoarthritis, ahead of medication. public health physiotherapy services include:

  • Individual assessment — a physiotherapist evaluates your mobility, strength, pain and function
  • Tailored exercise programmes — specific to your joints and condition
  • Group exercise classes — many local health trusts run arthritis-specific group sessions
  • Hydrotherapy — warm-water exercise sessions available at some hospitals
  • Manual therapy — hands-on treatment for joint mobilisation
  • Education and self-management — teaching you to manage symptoms independently

Access is via GP or FCP referral, or in some areas through self-referral. The health service website (NHS services) lists self-referral physiotherapy services near you. Waiting times for public health physiotherapy typically range from 4–12 weeks.

Public Pain Management Programmes

For people with chronic arthritis pain that hasn't responded adequately to standard treatments, the public health service offers multidisciplinary pain management programmes (PMPs). These are typically run by a team including a pain consultant, psychologist, physiotherapist and occupational therapist.

PMPs focus on:

  • Understanding pain — pain neuroscience education
  • Pacing and activity management — avoiding boom-bust cycles
  • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) — changing unhelpful pain-related thoughts and behaviours
  • Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) — psychological flexibility
  • Graded exercise — building activity levels safely
  • Medication review — optimising or reducing pain medication

Referral is typically through your GP or rheumatologist. PMPs are available in most the public health service regions, though waiting times can be 6–18 months.

Joint Replacement Surgery through the public health service

When conservative treatments fail to adequately manage pain and function, joint replacement surgery may be recommended. The health service performs over 160,000 hip and knee replacements annually, making them among the most common and successful operations in the public health service (NJR, 2024).

Key facts about the public health service joint replacement:

  • Success rates — over 95% of patients report significant pain reduction; 90% of knee replacements last 15+ years
  • Eligibility — based on clinical need, not age; assessed by orthopaedic surgeon
  • Waiting times — the public health service target is 18 weeks, but actual waits average 6–12 months in 2024
  • Prehabilitation — many trusts now offer "prehab" programmes to optimise fitness before surgery
  • Recovery — most patients return to normal activities within 3–6 months
  • Cost — fully funded through the public health service; no charge to the patient

The National Joint Registry (NJR) tracks every joint replacement performed in England, Wales, Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man, ensuring quality and safety monitoring.

Medications Available through the public health service

The health service provides all medically necessary arthritis medications at standard prescription cost (currently £9.90 per item in England as of 2024; free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). Key medications include:

  • Paracetamol and NSAIDs — first-line pain relief
  • Corticosteroids — short courses for flares, injections for localised inflammation
  • DMARDs — methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide
  • Biologics — adalimumab (Humira), etanercept (Enbrel), rituximab, tocilizumab, secukinumab
  • JAK inhibitors — tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib

If you take regular prescribed medication, a Prescription Prepayment Certificate (PPC) can save significant money. A 12-month PPC costs £111.60 (2024) and covers unlimited prescriptions — worthwhile if you have more than 11 items per year.

Mental Health Support Through the Public Health System

The health service recognises the profound impact of chronic pain on mental health. Services available include:

  • IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies) — free CBT and counselling, self-referral available at NHS services
  • Public health pain psychology — specialist psychologists within pain management teams
  • Social prescribing — link workers who connect you with community activities, support groups and local services
  • Crisis support — 111 helpline (option 2 for mental health crisis) or Samaritans 116 123

Differences Across the UK Nations

Healthcare is devolved in the UK, meaning services differ between England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland:

  • Scotland — Scotland's health service provides free prescriptions for all. Musculoskeletal services are managed through Health Boards. The Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN) publishes its own clinical guidelines.
  • Wales — Wales's health service also provides free prescriptions. Arthritis care is delivered through Local Health Boards. Wales has invested in community musculoskeletal services.
  • Northern Ireland — Free prescriptions. Services delivered through Health and Social Care (HSC) trusts. Waiting times have historically been longer than England.
  • England — Standard prescription charges apply (unless exempt). Services commissioned by Integrated Care Boards (ICBs). Most FCPs are deployed here.

How to Get the Most From Arthritis Services

  • Prepare for appointments — write down your symptoms, questions and medication list
  • Ask about self-referral — for physiotherapy, IAPT and some community services
  • Use the public health service online services — book appointments, order repeat prescriptions and view records through the public health service App
  • Request a care plan — if you have a long-term condition, you're entitled to an annual review and personalised care plan
  • Know your rights — the public health service Constitution gives you the right to treatment within 18 weeks of referral
  • Consider Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS) — if you're unhappy with your care
  • Join a support group — many local health trusts partner with Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) to run hospital-based support groups

How do Heat therapy and Cold therapy compare?

Heat and cold are the oldest self-management tools we have for joint pain, and — done properly — they remain some of the most useful. This guide explains when to reach for a hot water bottle versus a bag of frozen peas, based on UK healthcare pain-service advice and the arthritis charity guidance most physiotherapists follow.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Heat and cold are the oldest self-management tools we have for joint pain, and — done properly — they remain some of the most useful. This guide explains when to reach for a hot water bottle versus a bag of frozen peas, based on UK healthcare pain-service advice and the arthritis charity guidance most physiotherapists follow.

Heat therapy

  • How it works: Warms tissue, relaxes muscle spasm, increases blood flow and gates the transmission of pain signals.
  • Best for: Stiff, aching joints, morning stiffness in rheumatoid or ankylosing spondylitis, and muscle-driven low back pain.
  • Common side-effects: Burns if too hot or applied too long; should be avoided over active flares, broken skin or reduced sensation.
  • UK healthcare availability: Recommended by UK healthcare pain services and physiotherapists as a self-care measure.
  • Typical UK cost: £5–£20 for a wheat bag, hot water bottle or reusable heat pad.

Cold therapy

  • How it works: Reduces tissue temperature, narrows blood vessels, slows nerve conduction and damps down inflammation.
  • Best for: Swollen, warm, red joints in inflammatory flares, gout attacks and after activity that has aggravated a joint.
  • Common side-effects: Frostbite or nerve irritation if applied direct to skin or for too long; not for Raynaud's or poor circulation.
  • UK healthcare availability: Recommended for acute inflammatory flares by UK healthcare and rheumatology teams.
  • Typical UK cost: £0 (frozen peas!) to £15 for a reusable gel pack.

What heat and cold actually do

Heat opens up local blood vessels, brings warm blood to stiff tissue and helps muscles relax. It also reduces the sensitivity of pain receptors — a temporary but real effect. That's why a hot shower in the morning is often the single most helpful thing for rheumatoid or ankylosing spondylitis stiffness.

Cold does the opposite: it narrows blood vessels, slows chemical activity in inflamed tissue and numbs the area. That makes it best for the swollen, throbbing, warm joint you get in a gout attack or a rheumatoid flare.

Simple rule of thumb

If the joint is stiff and achy, choose heat. If it is hot, swollen and angry, choose cold. If it's both — say, an osteoarthritic knee that's been overused — most people find alternating heat and cold sessions helps.

This isn't a hard rule. Some people with rheumatoid arthritis prefer heat even during flares because the muscle-relaxing effect outweighs the mild pro-inflammatory effect. Trust your own body.

How to use each one safely

For heat: aim for pleasantly warm, not scalding. 15–20 minutes at a time, with a towel or clothing between skin and the heat source. Never sleep with an electric blanket or heat pad on. Avoid heat on skin with reduced sensation (from neuropathy or after some steroid injections).

For cold: wrap an ice pack or bag of frozen peas in a thin tea towel — never straight onto the skin. 10–15 minutes maximum, with at least an hour off between applications. Skip cold on numb areas, on Raynaud's-affected fingers, or if you have poor circulation.

What the evidence says

Systematic reviews consistently show that superficial heat provides small but meaningful short-term pain relief in osteoarthritis, low back pain and rheumatoid arthritis. Cold has a weaker evidence base but is repeatedly shown to reduce pain and swelling after acute flares, and after exercise that has stirred up a joint.

Neither modality changes the underlying disease. They are self-management tools that make daily life more bearable and can reduce reliance on painkillers — a genuinely useful thing given NSAID risks in older adults.

Combining with other self-care

Heat before exercise or stretching can help you move further; cold afterwards can settle any post-exercise swelling. Many physiotherapists teach this 'heat-move-cold' routine for stubborn joints.

Contrast bathing — alternating warm and cold water — is popular anecdotally for hand and foot arthritis, though evidence is limited. If it feels good and skin tolerates it, it's harmless.

At a glance

Heat therapyCold therapy
Best on stiff jointsYesNo
Best on hot, swollen jointsNoYes
Typical session15–20 min10–15 min
Cost£5–£20£0–£15
Avoid ifReduced sensation, over broken skinRaynaud's, poor circulation

Key takeaways

  • Stiff and achy â†’ heat. Hot and swollen â†’ cold.
  • Always use a barrier between skin and heat/ice; never sleep on either.
  • Heat before movement, cold after can be a helpful routine.
  • Both reduce pain temporarily; neither changes the disease.
  • Stop and seek advice if pain increases or skin reacts.

Talk to your clinician

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Heat therapy and Cold therapy with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

What are the best hip exercises for osteoarthritis?

Educational information for people in the UK living with arthritis — not a diagnosis or personal medical advice. Check medicines and exercises with your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111. See our medical disclaimer, editorial standards and claims policy.

Hip osteoarthritis responds to targeted strength and mobility work. UK NICE guidance (NG226) puts structured exercise ahead of medication as the first-line treatment. This guide gives you eight evidence-based hip exercises, a warm-up, a sensible weekly plan and clear rules for flare-ups — everything you need to start at home today.

Who this routine is for

This routine is for adults with hip osteoarthritis (OA), or long-standing hip or groin pain that a GP or physiotherapist has said is likely to be OA. It suits people starting out, people on a physiotherapy waiting list, and people preparing for a hip replacement. It is general guidance, not a personal prescription. If a physiotherapist has given you exercises, do theirs first.

Hip OA often shows up as pain in the groin, buttock or front of the thigh, sometimes spreading to the knee. Stiffness is common when you first get up or after sitting, and everyday tasks such as putting on socks, getting in and out of the car, or climbing stairs can become harder.

Why exercise helps a hip with osteoarthritis

NICE guideline NG226 (2022) recommends therapeutic exercise, tailored to the person, as a core treatment for everyone with osteoarthritis, combining local muscle strengthening with general aerobic fitness. The NHS also lists regular exercise and losing weight if you are overweight among the main ways to manage OA symptoms.

  • Stronger hip muscles. The buttock muscles (gluteals) keep the pelvis level when you walk and take load off the joint. They weaken quickly when the hip hurts.
  • Better movement. Hip OA tends to reduce how far the hip bends, turns and moves backwards. Regular movement helps keep what you have.
  • Easier everyday tasks. Sit-to-stands and squats rehearse the exact movements needed to get out of chairs, cars and the bath.
  • Less pain over time. Over 6 to 12 weeks, regular exercise can make the hip less sensitive, as well as stronger.

Built up gradually, exercise does not speed up hip damage. Our guide to whether exercise can make osteoarthritis worse explains why.

Before you start: safety check

Speak to a GP or physiotherapist before starting if you have:

  • had a fall and now have hip pain, or cannot put weight on the leg
  • had hip surgery, including a replacement, in the last few months
  • a hip that is suddenly very painful with a high temperature or feeling unwell
  • pain that is getting quickly worse, or night pain that does not ease when you change position
  • heart or lung problems that limit activity

The 4/10 pain rule. Mild discomfort during or after exercise, up to about 4 out of 10, that settles back to your usual level within 24 hours, is acceptable. If pain goes higher or lasts into the next day, make the exercise smaller next time rather than stopping altogether.

Warm-up (2–3 minutes)

  • Marching on the spot while holding a worktop: 60 seconds.
  • Gentle leg swings: hold on and swing one leg slowly forward and back, within comfort. 10 each side.
  • Hip circles: hands on hips, make small slow circles with the pelvis. 5 each way.

The core routine: 8 hip exercises for osteoarthritis

For each strength exercise, aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions, unless shown otherwise. Move slowly, breathe out as you push, and rest 30 to 60 seconds between sets. If you are new to exercise, start with one set.

1. Side-lying hip abduction

Lie on your less painful side with your head supported and the bottom knee bent. Keep the top leg straight and in line with your body, toes pointing forward. Lift the top leg up to about 30 cm, hold for 2 seconds, and lower slowly. 8 to 12 each side. Easier: do it standing, holding a worktop, lifting the leg out to the side. If lying on one side hurts, use the standing version.

2. Clamshell

Lie on your side with hips and knees bent and feet together. Keeping your feet touching, lift the top knee as far as is comfortable without rolling your pelvis back. Lower slowly. 10 to 15 each side. Harder: loop a light resistance band just above the knees.

3. Glute bridge

Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart. Squeeze your buttocks and lift your hips until your body is in a line from shoulders to knees. Hold for 3 seconds and lower slowly. 8 to 12 repetitions. Easier: lift only a little way. Harder: hold for 5 seconds, or straighten one leg while lifted.

4. Standing hip extension

Stand facing a worktop and hold on. Keeping your back straight and knee straight, take one leg backwards a little way, squeezing the buttock. Do not lean forward. Return slowly. 8 to 12 each leg.

5. Sit-to-stand

Sit near the front of a firm chair with feet slightly behind your knees. Lean forward, push through both feet evenly and stand up, then sit down slowly with control. Use the armrests at first. 8 to 12 repetitions. Easier: a higher chair or cushion. Harder: arms crossed or a slow 3-second lowering.

6. Mini squat

Stand holding a worktop, feet hip-width apart. Push your bottom back and bend your knees slightly, as if starting to sit, keeping your chest up. Go only as far as is comfortable and stand up. 8 to 12 repetitions.

7. Standing hip flexion (marching)

Stand holding a worktop. Lift one knee up in front of you towards hip height, or as high as is comfortable, keeping your back upright. Lower slowly. Alternate legs, 8 to 12 each side. Easier: seated marching.

8. Cool-down stretches: hamstring and hip flexor

Hamstring: sit near the front of a chair with one leg straight, heel on the floor. Keeping your back straight, lean forward from the hips until you feel a stretch at the back of the thigh. Hold 20 to 30 seconds, twice each side.

Hip flexor: stand side-on to a worktop. Step one foot back, keep your back upright and gently tuck your bottom under until you feel a stretch at the front of the back hip. Hold 20 to 30 seconds, twice each side.

Choose your starting level

LevelWho it suitsWhat to do
GentleVery painful hip, new to exercise, after a flareExercises 3 (small), 5 (with hands), 7 (seated) and 8. One set each, most days.
StandardCan walk for 10 minutes and manage stairsAll 8 exercises, 2 sets, 3 days a week, plus walking, cycling or swimming on other days.
ProgressingStandard level feels easy for 2 weeks3 sets, harder versions, resistance bands or light weights, longer aerobic sessions.

A sensible weekly plan

  • Strength routine: 2 to 3 sessions a week on non-consecutive days, 15 to 25 minutes.
  • Aerobic activity: walking, cycling (static or outdoor), swimming or water exercise on other days, building towards the UK Chief Medical Officers' target of 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
  • Daily movement: a few minutes of marching, hip circles and stretches, and breaking up long spells of sitting.
  • Balance: tai chi or simple balance exercises once or twice a week, which also help prevent falls.

Water exercise suits many people with hip OA because the water supports your weight. See our guide to swimming exercises for hip osteoarthritis.

How to progress

Move up when you can complete the top of the rep range with good form, and your hip settles within 24 hours, for three sessions in a row. Change one thing at a time: add repetitions, then a set, then a harder version, then light resistance. If you have a flare after progressing, drop back for a week, then try again.

ExerciseStarting versionNext stepLater
AbductionStanding, holding onSide-lyingBand around ankles
BridgeSmall liftFull lift, 3-second holdSingle leg
Sit-to-standHigh chair, handsStandard chair, no handsSlow lowering, holding a weight
SquatQuarter range, holding onDeeper, light holdHolding a light weight

Everyday tips for a painful hip

  • Stairs: lead with the less painful leg going up and the painful leg going down, holding the rail.
  • Walking stick: held in the hand opposite the painful hip, a stick can reduce load on the joint. Ask a physiotherapist to check the height.
  • Chairs: a firm, higher chair is easier to get out of. Cushions or chair raisers can help.
  • Socks and shoes: long-handled shoe horns and sock aids reduce bending. An occupational therapist can advise on equipment.
  • Sleep: a pillow between the knees when lying on your side can ease night-time hip pain.
  • Weight: if you are overweight, losing some weight can reduce the load through your hips.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Doing too much on a good day. A big burst of activity often leads to a flare. Keep to your plan and build up steadily.
  • Letting the pelvis tip or twist. In side-lying lifts and clamshells, keep your hips stacked and move only the leg. Fewer good repetitions beat many sloppy ones.
  • Holding your breath. Breathe out as you lift or push.
  • Stopping when it gets easier. Strength fades within weeks if you stop. Keep at least two sessions a week going long term.
  • Only stretching. Stretches help stiffness, but strengthening is what builds support around the hip.

Flare-ups, prehab and hip replacement

During a flare, drop to the gentle level: small bridges, seated marching, gentle stretches and short, flat walks. Warmth often helps a stiff hip. Build back up over a week or two rather than resting completely, as long rest makes muscles weaker.

If a hip replacement is being considered, continue this routine. Stronger muscles and better fitness before surgery can help you recover.

After a hip replacement, follow your surgical team's exercises and any advice about positions to avoid. Only return to a general routine like this when your physiotherapist or surgeon says it is suitable.

NHS physiotherapy and group programmes

In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS physiotherapy without seeing a GP first; check your GP practice or local NHS website. Some areas run group exercise and education programmes for knee and hip pain, such as ESCAPE-pain. For more options, including water-based and seated exercise, see our exercise hub. Knee pain often comes alongside hip OA; our knee exercises for osteoarthritis can be combined with this routine.

Stop rules and when to get medical help

Stop the session if you get: sharp or stabbing pain, a feeling of the hip catching or giving way, pain that keeps increasing as you go, or pins and needles or numbness down the leg.

  • Call 999 for chest pain, severe breathlessness or feeling faint during exercise that does not settle with rest.
  • Go to A&E if you fall and cannot put weight on your leg, or the leg looks shorter or turned outwards.
  • Call NHS 111 urgently if your hip becomes suddenly very painful with a high temperature, or a hip replacement becomes hot, swollen and painful.
  • See your GP or physiotherapist if pain is steadily getting worse, night pain is disturbing your sleep most nights, you are limping more, or you are not improving after 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise.

Your next step

Choose your level and try three of the exercises today. Add the others over the next two weeks, and note how your hip feels the next morning. Most people need 6 to 12 weeks of regular practice to notice real change, so be patient and keep going.

For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111. See our medical disclaimer, editorial standards and claims policy.

Free knee exercises for osteoarthritis in the UK. NICE guidance (NG226) puts structured exercise ahead of medication as first-line treatment. This guide gives you eight evidence-based moves — quad sets, straight-leg raise, sit-to-stand, mini squat, step-ups, hamstring curl, calf raise and gentle ROM — plus a weekly plan and clear rules for flares.

Who this routine is for

This routine is for adults with knee osteoarthritis (OA), or long-standing knee pain that a GP or physiotherapist has said is likely to be OA. It also suits people waiting for an NHS physiotherapy appointment, people who have been told they are "not ready" for surgery yet, and people preparing for a knee replacement. It is general guidance, not a personal prescription. If a physiotherapist has already given you exercises, do theirs first and use this page to fill in gaps.

NICE guideline NG226 (2022) recommends therapeutic exercise, tailored to the person, as a core treatment for everyone with osteoarthritis. That means local muscle strengthening around the joint plus general aerobic fitness. NICE also advises against routinely offering paracetamol or weak opioids for OA, and against glucosamine and strong opioids, which puts even more weight on exercise, weight management and self-help as the foundations of care.

Why exercise helps a knee with osteoarthritis

Knee OA makes the joint stiffer and more painful, especially on stairs, when rising from a chair and after sitting still. The muscles that protect the knee, particularly the quadriceps at the front of the thigh, weaken quickly when the knee hurts. Weaker muscles mean the joint absorbs more load, which can mean more pain, and so the cycle continues. A targeted routine breaks that cycle.

  • Muscle support. Stronger quadriceps, hamstrings, hip and calf muscles share the work the joint would otherwise do on its own.
  • Joint health. Cartilage has no blood supply of its own. Regular, moderate loading and movement help keep it nourished.
  • Less stiffness. Moving the knee through its range regularly helps limit the stiffness that builds up after rest.
  • Calmer pain system. Over 6 to 12 weeks, regular exercise can reduce how sensitive the knee feels, as well as improving strength.
  • Confidence. Practising sit-to-stands and steps in a controlled way makes everyday tasks feel less risky.

Exercise does not wear the joint out faster when it is built up sensibly. Our guide to whether exercise can make osteoarthritis worse explains the evidence in more detail.

Before you start: safety check

Most people with knee OA can start this routine safely at home. Speak to a GP or physiotherapist before starting if you have:

  • a recent fall, injury or suspected fracture
  • a knee that is suddenly hot, red and swollen, especially with a high temperature or feeling unwell
  • a knee that locks (gets stuck) or repeatedly gives way
  • pain that wakes you every night or is getting quickly worse
  • had knee surgery, including a replacement, in the last few months
  • heart or lung problems that limit what you can do

The 4/10 pain rule. Many physiotherapists use a simple guide: mild discomfort during or after exercise, up to about 4 out of 10, that settles back to your usual level within 24 hours, is acceptable. If pain goes higher, lasts into the next day, or the knee swells more, do less next time: fewer reps, a smaller movement, or a lower step. Do not stop moving altogether.

Warm-up (2–3 minutes)

  • Marching on the spot or seated marching: 60 seconds, lifting knees to a comfortable height.
  • Seated knee swings: sit tall and gently swing one lower leg forward and back. 10 each side.
  • Ankle pumps: point and flex both feet 20 times.

The core routine: 8 knee exercises for osteoarthritis

For each strength exercise, aim for 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions unless shown otherwise. Move slowly, breathe out as you push, and stop a couple of repetitions before you are too tired to keep good form. Rest 30 to 60 seconds between sets. If you are new to exercise, start with one set of each.

1. Quad sets (thigh tightening)

Sit or lie with your leg straight and a small rolled towel under the knee. Tighten the muscle at the front of the thigh to press the back of the knee down into the towel. Hold for 5 seconds, relax. Build up to 10 holds of 10 seconds. Good for: bad days, early after a flare and as a starting point if other exercises hurt.

2. Straight-leg raise

Lie on your back with one knee bent and foot flat. Tighten the thigh of the straight leg, then lift it to the height of the bent knee. Hold for 2 to 3 seconds and lower slowly. 8 to 12 each leg. Easier: lift only a few centimetres. Harder: add a light ankle weight once 3 sets of 12 feel easy.

3. Sit-to-stand

Sit near the front of a firm chair with feet hip-width apart and slightly behind your knees. Lean forward, push through your feet and stand up, then sit back down slowly. Use your hands on the armrests at first. 8 to 12 repetitions. Easier: use a higher chair or add a cushion. Harder: arms crossed, a lower chair, or a slow 3-second lowering.

4. Mini squat

Stand holding a worktop, feet hip-width apart. Bend your knees and hips slightly as if starting to sit, keeping your weight through your heels and knees in line with your toes. Go only as far as is comfortable, often 10 to 20 cm, then stand up. 8 to 12 repetitions.

5. Step-ups

Using the bottom stair with a banister, step up with one foot, bring the other up, then step down with control. Lead with the stronger leg first if one is more painful. 8 to 10 each leg. Easier: use a lower step or a thick book. Harder: slow the step down.

6. Standing hamstring curl

Hold a chair back. Bend one knee to bring the heel towards your bottom without moving the thigh forward. Lower slowly. 8 to 12 each leg. Harder: add a light ankle weight or resistance band.

7. Calf raise

Hold a worktop with both hands. Rise up onto the balls of your feet, pause, and lower slowly. 10 to 15 repetitions. Harder: one leg at a time.

8. Knee bend and straighten (range of movement)

Sit on a chair. Slide one foot back under the chair to bend the knee as far as is comfortable, hold for a few seconds, then slide it forward and straighten the knee fully, tightening the thigh. 10 slow repetitions each leg. Do this daily, including on flare days.

Choose your starting level

LevelWho it suitsWhat to do
GentleVery painful knees, new to exercise, recovering from a flareExercises 1, 2, 3 (with hands) and 8. One set each, daily or most days.
StandardCan manage stairs and short walksAll 8 exercises, 2 sets, 3 days a week, plus walking on other days.
ProgressingStandard level feels easy for 2 weeks3 sets, harder versions, light weights or bands, plus longer walks or cycling.

A sensible weekly plan

DayActivity
MondayStrength routine (15–25 minutes)
TuesdayWalk, cycle or swim (10–30 minutes)
WednesdayStrength routine
ThursdayWalk, cycle or swim; daily knee bends
FridayStrength routine
WeekendSomething you enjoy: a longer walk, gardening, a class, or rest

The UK Chief Medical Officers recommend adults build up to at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus strengthening on at least two days. Build up gradually; small, regular amounts count. Our guide to walking with arthritis explains how to build up walking safely.

How to progress

Move up when you can do the top of the rep range with good form, and your knee settles within 24 hours, for three sessions in a row. Change only one thing at a time:

  1. add repetitions (up to 12 to 15)
  2. add a set
  3. make the exercise harder (lower chair, slower lowering, one leg)
  4. add light resistance (ankle weights or a band)

Expect ups and downs. If a harder version causes a flare-up, go back a step for a week and try again.

Everyday tips that protect the knee

  • Stairs: "up with the good, down with the bad". Lead with the less painful leg going up and the more painful leg going down, and use the rail.
  • Footwear: cushioned, supportive shoes with a thick, flexible sole help many people. Insoles and braces are not needed by everyone, but some people find them helpful; ask your physiotherapist.
  • Walking aids: a stick held in the hand opposite the painful knee can reduce load. Ask a physio to check the height.
  • Weight: if you are overweight, NICE says any amount of weight loss is likely to help knee OA.
  • Break up sitting: stand and move every 30 to 60 minutes to limit stiffness.

Flare-ups, prehab and knee replacement

During a flare (a few days of more pain, warmth or swelling), drop to the gentle level: quad sets, knee bends and short, flat walks. Use a wrapped ice pack for 10 to 15 minutes on a warm, swollen knee. Build back up over a week or two rather than resting completely.

If a knee replacement is being considered, carry on with this routine as "prehab". Going into surgery with stronger muscles and good knee straightening can help recovery.

After a knee replacement, follow your surgical team's exercise programme. Only return to a general routine like this one when your physiotherapist or surgeon says it is suitable.

Group programmes and NHS physiotherapy

In many areas you can refer yourself to NHS musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy without seeing a GP. Ask your GP practice or check your local NHS website. Some areas also offer group exercise and education programmes for knee and hip pain, such as ESCAPE-pain, through NHS services or leisure centres. For other activities that suit knees, see our exercise hub.

Stop rules and when to get medical help

Stop the session and rest if you get: sharp or stabbing pain, the knee locking or giving way, sudden new swelling, or pain that keeps increasing as you go.

  • Call 999 if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness, or feel faint during exercise and it does not settle with rest.
  • Call NHS 111 or go to A&E if your knee suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially with a high temperature, or you cannot put weight on it after a fall or twist.
  • Get urgent advice the same day if your calf is painful, swollen and warm, as this can be a sign of a blood clot.
  • See your GP or physiotherapist if pain is getting steadily worse over weeks, the knee keeps giving way or locking, pain wakes you every night, or you are not improving after 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise.

Your next step

Pick your level from the table above and do two of the exercises today. Add the rest over the next fortnight. Note how your knee feels the morning after each session. Most people need 6 to 12 weeks of regular exercise to notice a real difference in strength and pain, so keep going even if progress feels slow at first.

/guides/knee-replacement-surgery:
Pillar Guide

From deciding on surgery to post-operative recovery — an evidence-based walk-through of every stage, written for UK patients.

Knee replacement is one of the most successful operations performed in the UK, with one of the most commonly performed joint operations in the UK. Many patients gain substantial pain relief and improved mobility over the following months — individual outcomes vary. This guide explains who benefits, how to prepare, what to expect in hospital, and what realistic recovery looks like week by week.

A Patient's Guide to Knee Replacement Surgery

Knee replacement — known clinically as knee arthroplasty — is one of the most successful and well-studied operations performed in the UK. Around 110,000 knee replacements are carried out each year in England, Wales and Northern Ireland (National Joint Registry, 2023), and the great majority of patients report substantial pain relief and improved mobility within a year of surgery.

This guide walks you through every stage of the patient journey: deciding whether surgery is right for you, what to expect in hospital, how to prepare your home, and the realities of recovery. It is written for UK patients and reflects current NICE guidance (NG226) and Royal College of Surgeons standards.

When to Consider Knee Replacement

Knee replacement is recommended when conservative treatments no longer control pain and disability. Typical triggers include:

  • Pain that disturbs sleep — waking at night or being unable to find a comfortable position
  • Reduced walking distance — struggling to walk for more than 20–30 minutes
  • Difficulty with stairs, getting out of a chair, or driving
  • Persistent stiffness and visible deformity (bow-leg or knock-knee)
  • X-ray evidence of advanced arthritis — narrowed joint space, bone spurs, bone-on-bone contact
  • Symptoms not improving after 3–6 months of weight loss, physiotherapy, analgesia and (where appropriate) steroid injections

If these apply, ask your GP for an orthopaedic referral. You may also want to read our companion guide on knee arthritis and managing the wait for surgery.

Types of Knee Replacement

Total Knee Replacement (TKR)

The whole joint surface is replaced — the lower end of the femur, the top of the tibia, and usually the underside of the patella. TKR accounts for around 90% of UK knee replacements. Implants are typically cobalt-chromium and polyethylene, fixed with bone cement.

Partial (Unicompartmental) Knee Replacement

Only the damaged compartment (usually the inner side) is resurfaced. Recovery is faster and the knee feels more "natural", but it suits only around 1 in 4 patients — those with arthritis confined to one compartment and intact ligaments.

Patellofemoral Replacement

Resurfaces only the kneecap and its groove. Used for isolated kneecap arthritis — about 1–2% of cases.

Revision Knee Replacement

A second operation if the original implant loosens, wears out or becomes infected. Revisions are technically harder, take longer to recover from, and are best done in specialist centres.

Preparing for Surgery (Prehabilitation)

"Prehab" — getting fitter before surgery — has strong evidence for shorter hospital stays and faster recovery. UK enhanced recovery programmes recommend:

  • Quadriceps and glute strengthening — straight-leg raises, mini-squats, step-ups (3–4 sessions per week for 6+ weeks)
  • Aerobic conditioning — cycling, swimming, or aqua-walking
  • Weight loss — a BMI under 35 reduces complication risk; many trusts now require BMI optimisation
  • Stopping smoking at least 8 weeks before surgery — smoking doubles wound infection risk
  • Reducing alcohol to under 14 units per week
  • Optimising chronic conditions — diabetes (HbA1c < 69 mmol/mol), blood pressure, anaemia
  • Dental check-up — untreated dental infection is a known source of implant infection

You will usually attend a pre-operative assessment clinic 2–6 weeks before surgery for blood tests, ECG, MRSA swabs, and an anaesthetic review.

Preparing Your Home

A small amount of planning makes early recovery far easier:

  • Move frequently used items to waist height — no bending or reaching
  • Set up a recovery base downstairs if possible, with a firm chair (knee at 90°), footstool, and bedside table
  • Remove trip hazards — loose rugs, trailing cables, clutter on stairs
  • Buy or borrow a raised toilet seat, long-handled shoe horn, sock aid, grabber and shower stool
  • Batch-cook and freeze meals for the first 2–3 weeks
  • Arrange help with shopping, pets, laundry and childcare for at least 2 weeks
  • Tell family you will not be driving for around 6 weeks

What Happens in Hospital

Most UK hospital trusts now follow an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathway. A typical timeline:

Day of Surgery

You arrive fasted (usually from midnight, or as instructed). Anaesthetic is most often spinal with sedation, which is associated with less blood loss and quicker recovery than general anaesthesia. Surgery takes 60–90 minutes. You are encouraged to stand and walk within a few hours with a physiotherapist.

Days 1–2

Pain is managed with regular paracetamol, an anti-inflammatory if suitable, and short-term opioids. You will practise walking with crutches or a frame, climbing stairs, and bending the knee. Most patients are discharged within 1–3 days, some on the same day under modern ERAS protocols.

Before Discharge

You will be given blood-thinning injections or tablets for 2–4 weeks to reduce clot risk, a clear exercise sheet, contact numbers, and a follow-up appointment for around 6 weeks.

Recovery Timeline: Week by Week

Recovery is gradual. The pattern below is typical but individual — your surgical team's advice always takes priority.

Weeks 1–2: Pain & Swelling Control

  • Walk short distances with crutches every 1–2 hours
  • Ice the knee for 15–20 minutes, 4–6 times daily
  • Elevate the leg above heart level when resting
  • Do the prescribed exercises 3–4 times daily — quad sets, ankle pumps, heel slides
  • Aim for knee bend (flexion) of 70–90° by the end of week 2

Weeks 3–6: Building Movement

  • Progress to one crutch, then walking unaided indoors
  • Target flexion of 100–110° and full extension (straight knee)
  • Begin stationary cycling on low resistance once you have 100° of bend
  • 6-week orthopaedic review — surgeon checks wound, range of movement and X-rays
  • Most patients can return to driving once they can do an emergency stop comfortably (typically 6 weeks for a right knee)

Weeks 6–12: Strength & Confidence

  • Return to desk-based work, light shopping, social activities
  • Add resistance training, swimming, and longer walks
  • Swelling around the knee is normal for several more months

Months 3–12: Long-Term Recovery

  • Steady improvement in pain, strength and stamina
  • Return to recommended activities: walking, cycling, swimming, golf, doubles tennis, gentle hiking
  • Avoid high-impact activities — running, contact sport, jumping — which shorten implant life
  • Full recovery is usually reached between 6 and 12 months

Essential Recovery Exercises

These exercises should be done daily from day 1 unless your physiotherapist advises otherwise. See our full exercise hub for more progressions.

  • Quad sets — tighten the thigh muscle and push the back of the knee into the bed for 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Ankle pumps — move feet up and down to reduce clot risk, 20 reps every hour
  • Heel slides — slide the heel towards the buttock to bend the knee, 10 reps
  • Straight-leg raise — with knee locked straight, lift the leg 20 cm, hold 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Seated knee extension — sit on a firm chair, straighten the knee fully, hold 5 seconds, 10 reps
  • Standing knee bends — holding a worktop, bend the operated knee back behind you, 10 reps

Risks and How They Are Managed

Serious complications are uncommon but worth understanding. UK National Joint Registry data show:

  • Deep infection — around 1 in 100. Risk reduced by antibiotics at induction, laminar-flow theatres and good blood sugar control.
  • Blood clots (DVT / PE) — around 1 in 100 symptomatic, reduced by early mobilisation and post-op anticoagulants.
  • Stiffness requiring manipulation under anaesthetic — around 2–3%.
  • Nerve or blood-vessel injury — under 1%.
  • Persistent pain — 15–20% of patients report ongoing discomfort at 1 year; usually mild and manageable.
  • Implant loosening or wear — gradual; most implants last 20–25 years.
  • Death within 90 days — under 0.5%, mostly from cardiovascular events.

Risk is higher in patients who smoke, have a BMI above 40, or have poorly controlled diabetes, heart or kidney disease. Your surgical team will discuss your individual risk before consent.

Public Waiting Lists and Private Options

Knee replacement is a routine UK operation. Under the UK 18-week referral-to-treatment standard you have the right to be treated within 18 weeks of referral. If your local trust cannot meet this, you can ask to be transferred to another public or publicly funded independent provider — this is sometimes called the "right to choose".

Private knee replacement in the UK typically costs £12,000–£16,000 all-inclusive. Patients often choose private care to shorten waits or to select a specific consultant. Outcomes are similar to public care when the same surgeon and implant are used. See our guide on managing the UK waiting list for practical steps while you wait.

Alternatives and Delaying Surgery

Many patients can delay or avoid surgery with a structured non-surgical plan. NICE recommends offering all patients with knee osteoarthritis a combined approach before considering surgery:

  • Weight management — losing 5–10% of body weight reduces knee pain as much as some surgical interventions
  • Structured exercise — supervised physiotherapy for 6–12 weeks; ESCAPE-pain is a UK programme proven to reduce pain by 30–50%
  • Topical NSAID gels (ibuprofen or diclofenac) — first-line analgesia under NICE NG226
  • Oral analgesia — paracetamol, short courses of oral NSAIDs with gastric protection
  • Intra-articular steroid injections — short-term pain relief lasting 4–12 weeks
  • Walking aids — a stick used in the opposite hand can reduce knee load by 25%
  • An anti-inflammatory Mediterranean diet to reduce systemic inflammation and aid weight loss

Newer treatments — PRP (platelet-rich plasma), hyaluronic acid injections and stem-cell therapy — have limited or inconsistent evidence and are not routinely funded by the UK health service.

The Emotional Side of Surgery

Major surgery can be daunting. Anxiety, low mood and sleep disturbance are common before and after the operation. Patients often describe a "third-week dip" when the initial momentum fades and progress feels slow. This is normal. Recovery is rarely linear. Things that help:

  • Setting small weekly goals — bending 5° more, walking 5 minutes longer
  • Keeping a brief daily diary of pain, swelling and movement
  • Staying socially connected — visitors, video calls, the Living With Arthritis community
  • Speaking to your GP early if low mood persists beyond 2–3 weeks

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide draws on NICE guideline NG226 (Osteoarthritis in over 16s: diagnosis and management), the UK National Joint Registry 20th Annual Report (2023), Royal College of Surgeons of England commissioning guidance for knee replacement, British Orthopaedic Association enhanced recovery standards, and Cochrane reviews of prehabilitation and post-operative physiotherapy. It is for general education and does not replace personalised advice from your GP, surgeon or physiotherapist.

How do Mediterranean diet and 'Anti-inflammatory' diet compare?

'Anti-inflammatory' has become a marketing word attached to almost every food trend. The Mediterranean diet is one of the few eating patterns with genuinely strong evidence for reducing arthritis pain and cardiovascular risk. This guide compares the two, for UK readers who want to eat in a way that actually helps their joints — without buying £40 supplements.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

'Anti-inflammatory' has become a marketing word attached to almost every food trend. The Mediterranean diet is one of the few eating patterns with genuinely strong evidence for reducing arthritis pain and cardiovascular risk. This guide compares the two, for UK readers who want to eat in a way that actually helps their joints — without buying £40 supplements.

Mediterranean diet

  • How it works: A defined dietary pattern rich in vegetables, fruit, wholegrains, legumes, olive oil, nuts and oily fish, with modest dairy and low red meat.
  • Best for: Anyone with arthritis (particularly RA and OA), and anyone reducing cardiovascular risk alongside joint health.
  • Common side-effects: None; may cost slightly more if extra virgin olive oil and oily fish are new to your weekly shop.
  • UK healthcare availability: Explicitly recommended by UK healthcare Eatwell and by NICE for cardiovascular prevention.
  • Typical UK cost: £40–£70 per person per week; overlaps with normal UK shopping.

'Anti-inflammatory' diet

  • How it works: Not a single defined pattern — usually a set of principles emphasising oily fish, turmeric, ginger, berries, leafy greens, while cutting sugar, ultra-processed food and, sometimes, gluten or nightshades.
  • Best for: People who want a framework beyond Mediterranean, or who tolerate elimination approaches.
  • Common side-effects: Risk of over-restriction, especially if nightshades or wheat are cut without clinical need.
  • UK healthcare availability: Not a formal UK healthcare pattern; individual foods align with Mediterranean advice.
  • Typical UK cost: Can be expensive if it relies on speciality supplements and superfoods.

How much overlap is there?

In practice, most versions of 'anti-inflammatory eating' are 90% Mediterranean plus a few extras — turmeric, ginger, green tea, sometimes limiting nightshades, wheat or dairy. Both patterns emphasise vegetables, fruit, nuts, seeds, oily fish, olive oil and legumes, and both discourage ultra-processed food, sugary drinks and excess red or processed meat.

The real difference is that the Mediterranean diet is defined by decades of research — including large randomised trials like PREDIMED — whereas 'anti-inflammatory' as a label is looser and often driven by supplement marketing.

What the arthritis evidence actually shows

For rheumatoid arthritis, several trials of Mediterranean-style eating show modest but real reductions in joint pain, tender joint count and CRP. Effects are smaller than DMARDs but real, and improve cardiovascular risk — important because RA itself raises heart-attack risk.

For osteoarthritis, evidence is weaker but consistent: people eating a Mediterranean-style diet report less pain and better function, largely mediated by weight loss and reduced systemic inflammation.

Individual 'anti-inflammatory' foods (turmeric/curcumin, omega-3, ginger, green tea) each have trials of variable quality, generally showing small pain-relief effects. Nothing comes close to the effect size of Mediterranean eating as a whole pattern.

Where they genuinely differ

Some anti-inflammatory approaches recommend cutting nightshades (tomatoes, aubergine, peppers, potatoes), gluten or dairy. There is no consistent evidence these help arthritis in general — although a small subset of people with coeliac disease or genuine intolerances do improve. Blanket elimination risks nutritional gaps and lower quality of life.

Some approaches lean heavily on supplements — turmeric capsules, high-dose fish oil, MSM, glucosamine. The evidence for these is patchy: high-dose omega-3 has modest RA benefit; curcumin has some knee osteoarthritis trials; glucosamine's effect is small and inconsistent.

Building it in real UK life

You don't need to buy anything exotic. A Mediterranean-style shopping list in the UK looks like: bags of frozen berries, tinned tomatoes and beans, oats, rye or wholewheat bread, extra virgin olive oil, mixed nuts, plain yoghurt, two portions of oily fish a week (tinned sardines and mackerel are cheap), plenty of vegetables and occasional lean chicken or eggs. Red meat and processed meat move to the edge of the plate.

If you want to add 'anti-inflammatory' extras, safe additions are turmeric with black pepper in cooking, fresh or powdered ginger, and green tea. Skip the £30 pill bottles unless a rheumatologist or dietitian specifically recommends them.

What to prioritise if you can only change one thing

For arthritis, the highest-yield change is usually: eat oily fish twice a week, swap sunflower/vegetable oil for olive oil, and eat vegetables at every meal. Do just that and you're already Mediterranean, already anti-inflammatory, and likely to feel a difference over 8–12 weeks.

Weight loss, where relevant, amplifies everything: each kilogram off reduces load on the knee joint by roughly 4 kg per step, and losing 10% of body weight can rival the pain relief of common medication in obese OA patients.

At a glance

Mediterranean diet'Anti-inflammatory' diet
Evidence in arthritisStrong (RA and OA)Mixed, mostly single-food studies
Defined pattern?YesLoose set of principles
CostEveryday supermarketHigher if supplement-heavy
Elimination-based?NoSometimes (nightshades, gluten)
NHS-endorsed?Yes (via Eatwell + NICE)Not formally

Key takeaways

  • Mediterranean eating has the strongest evidence for arthritis.
  • Most 'anti-inflammatory' diets are Mediterranean plus optional extras.
  • Skip elimination diets unless clinically indicated.
  • Two portions of oily fish and olive oil are the biggest single wins.
  • Weight loss magnifies the benefit of any dietary change.

What is musculoskeletal health?

Musculoskeletal (MSK) health means healthy bones, joints, muscles, tendons and ligaments. MSK conditions affect 20 million people in the UK. Movement, strength, sleep and weight management are the four proven levers to protect it.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

What is musculoskeletal health and why does it matter?

Musculoskeletal (MSK) health covers the bones, joints, muscles, tendons and ligaments that allow you to move. MSK conditions — back pain, neck pain, repetitive strain and joint disorders — are the single biggest cause of years lived with disability in the UK. Most MSK problems split into acute (under 12 weeks, often injury-related) and chronic (longer-term, needing graded rehabilitation). Physiotherapy, workplace ergonomics, targeted exercise and supportive home tools are the highest-value interventions. Early assessment, graded movement and posture variety prevent most acute problems from becoming chronic.

Medically reviewed by Maxwell

First Contact Practitioner • HCPC PH128483 • Last updated June 2026

Reviewer details and the site's clinical review process are documented in our editorial standards.

1. What MSK dysfunction is and why it matters

Musculoskeletal disorders include back and neck pain, repetitive strain injuries (RSI), tendinopathies, joint conditions and post-injury rehabilitation. They affect around 1 in 5 UK adults at any one time and account for over 30 million working days lost each year.

MSK health overlaps heavily with arthritis — many of the same exercise, weight and posture principles apply across both fields.

2. Common symptoms and causes

MSK symptoms vary by site but commonly include:

  • Pain — aching, sharp, or a dull background ache that changes with movement or time of day
  • Stiffness — particularly first thing in the morning or after sitting still
  • Swelling or warmth around a joint, which can suggest inflammation
  • Reduced range of movement — difficulty reaching, bending or turning fully
  • Weakness in the surrounding muscles, often from disuse during a painful episode
  • Clicking, catching or grinding sensations within a joint

Causes range from a one-off injury or overuse (repetitive strain from typing, lifting or sport), through mechanical wear (osteoarthritis), to inflammatory disease (rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis), poor load management, deconditioning, or simply the accumulated effect of prolonged static posture at a desk.

Certain symptoms need same-day medical attention rather than self-management: sudden severe swelling, redness and heat over a joint, fever alongside joint pain, numbness or weakness spreading down a limb, or loss of bladder/bowel control alongside back pain. If any of these apply to you, contact 999 or 112 or your GP promptly rather than waiting.

3. Acute vs. chronic MSK conditions

  • Acute (under 12 weeks): short-term, often follows a strain, sprain or flare. Relative rest, gradual return to movement and pain modulation are the priority.
  • Chronic (over 12 weeks): needs a structured rehabilitation plan — graded strength, mobility, pacing, sleep and stress strategies.

4. Diagnosis and assessment

Most MSK conditions are diagnosed through a clinical history and physical examination rather than imaging. A physiotherapist or GP will typically ask about the pattern of pain, what aggravates or eases it, any red-flag symptoms, and your work or activity demands, before testing movement, strength and specific joint signs.

Validated screening tools — such as the STarT Back Screening Tool for lower back pain — help clinicians judge whether simple advice, physiotherapy, or a more specialist pathway is the right next step. Our free self-assessment tool can help you organise your symptoms and history ahead of an appointment, though it is educational and does not replace a clinical diagnosis.

Imaging (X-ray, ultrasound or MRI) is reserved for suspected fractures, red-flag symptoms, or when the result would change treatment — for example before considering injections or surgery.

5. Physiotherapy, chiropractic care and sports massage

Physiotherapy is the first-line, evidence-backed treatment for most MSK conditions. Chiropractic and osteopathic care may help in selected cases. Sports and remedial massage support recovery from soft-tissue injuries and tightness, but should sit alongside — not replace — active rehabilitation.

A good clinician will combine hands-on treatment with a progressive home exercise programme. Many UK healthcare areas now offer MSK physiotherapy self-referral — meaning you can book directly without a GP appointment first. Check your GP practice website or search "physiotherapy self-referral" plus your area on NHS.uk to see what's available locally.

6. Exercise and diet for MSK health

Movement — not rest — is the foundation of most MSK recovery plans. Graded strength training around the affected area, combined with general aerobic activity (walking, swimming or cycling), reduces pain and rebuilds capacity over time. Our exercise hub has condition-specific routines to start from.

There's no single "MSK diet", but maintaining a healthy weight measurably reduces load on weight-bearing joints (hips, knees, lower back), and a Mediterranean-style eating pattern — vegetables, oily fish, whole grains, olive oil and legumes — is generally associated with lower systemic inflammation. See our diet & nutrition hub for practical guidance.

7. Workplace ergonomics and occupational assessment

  • Monitor at eye level, screen an arm's length away
  • Elbows at ~90°, wrists neutral, feet flat or supported
  • Chair providing lumbar support and seat depth that allows two fingers behind the knees
  • Move position every 30–45 minutes — sit, stand, walk
  • Document camera, headset and split keyboard for those with neck or wrist symptoms

8. Home solutions: insoles, taping and posture support

Off-the-shelf insoles, kinesiology tape, posture-reminder devices and lumbar cushions can help symptom control while you rehabilitate. They work best as part of a wider strength and movement programme — never as a standalone fix. For anything beyond simple, general supports, an occupational therapist or physiotherapist can match equipment to your specific needs — self-selecting specialist equipment without assessment can sometimes do more harm than good.

9. MSK health in later life: frailty, sarcopenia and falls

Muscle mass and bone density naturally decline with age, and joint tissue becomes less resilient to load — which is why musculoskeletal health overlaps so closely with frailty, sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) and falls risk in later life. Strength and balance work that supports MSK recovery earlier in life is the same foundation that protects independence later on.

If MSK symptoms are appearing alongside general slowing down, reduced grip strength, or a fall or near-fall, it's worth looking at these related guides:

  • Frailty management hub — recognising and managing frailty
  • Sarcopenia & muscle loss — age-related muscle decline and how to counter it
  • Bone density & osteoporosis — protecting skeletal strength
  • Falls prevention for older adults — reducing fall risk at home
  • Preventative MSK health — staying ahead of problems before they start

MSK solutions patients commonly look for

  • Private physiotherapy for faster assessment and treatment
  • Diagnostic imaging — ultrasound, MRI — when red flags or persistent symptoms warrant it
  • Workplace ergonomic evaluations for office, hybrid and manual roles
  • Custom insoles and orthotics for foot, ankle or knee mechanics
  • Ergonomic office furniture — adjustable chairs, sit-stand desks, monitor arms
  • Sports and remedial massage alongside active rehabilitation
