Frequently asked questions

What does musculoskeletal mean?

Musculoskeletal (MSK) refers to the bones, joints, muscles, tendons, ligaments and nerves that allow you to move. MSK conditions are the leading cause of disability worldwide.

What is the difference between acute and chronic MSK pain?

Acute pain lasts under 12 weeks and usually follows an injury or flare. Chronic pain persists beyond 12 weeks and often needs a graded rehabilitation programme rather than rest alone.

When should I see a physiotherapist?

Book an assessment if MSK pain limits work, sleep or daily activity for more than two weeks, or if you have weakness, numbness or pain that wakes you at night.

Can workplace ergonomics really prevent MSK problems?

Yes. Evidence shows correct desk setup, regular movement breaks and supported posture reduce neck, shoulder and lower-back pain in office workers.

Do I need a scan for back or joint pain?

Most MSK conditions do not require imaging — a clinical assessment is usually enough. Scans are reserved for red-flag symptoms, suspected fractures or when surgery is being considered.

What home strategies help most?

Movement, graded strength training, sleep, stress management, postural variety and targeted supports such as insoles or lumbar cushions are the highest-value home interventions.

What are the common symptoms of an MSK condition?

Pain, stiffness, swelling, reduced range of movement, weakness and a catching or grinding sensation in a joint are the most common signs. Symptoms that worsen with rest rather than movement, or that wake you at night, warrant a clinical assessment.

Can I refer myself to physiotherapy on the UK healthcare system?

Many UK healthcare areas in the UK now offer MSK self-referral, meaning you can book a physiotherapy assessment directly without seeing your GP first. Availability varies by local Integrated Care Board, so check your GP practice website or NHS.uk for the self-referral option in your area.

What does a good MSK diet look like?

There is no single "MSK diet", but a Mediterranean-style pattern — vegetables, oily fish, whole grains, olive oil and legumes — combined with maintaining a healthy weight reduces load on weight-bearing joints and supports general tissue health. See our diet hub for specifics.

How does musculoskeletal health change with age?

Muscle mass and bone density naturally decline with age, and joint tissue becomes less resilient. This is why MSK health overlaps closely with frailty, sarcopenia and falls prevention in later life — see our dedicated guides on each below.

Is there a self-assessment score for MSK problems?

Clinicians often use validated tools such as the STarT Back Screening Tool for lower back pain, or region-specific outcome measures, to gauge severity and guide treatment. Our free self-assessment tool can help you organise your symptoms before a clinical appointment.

What mobility aids or equipment might help?

Depending on the condition, options range from simple insoles and lumbar cushions to walking aids, splints or orthotics. An occupational therapist or physiotherapist can recommend equipment matched to your specific needs — self-selecting equipment without assessment can sometimes do more harm than good.

How do UK healthcare rheumatology and Private rheumatology compare?

Getting rheumatology care in the UK usually means the UK healthcare system, but private appointments can shorten waits and give you more choice over your consultant. This guide compares both routes honestly, so you can decide whether — and when — private is worth it.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Getting rheumatology care in the UK usually means the UK healthcare system, but private appointments can shorten waits and give you more choice over your consultant. This guide compares both routes honestly, so you can decide whether — and when — private is worth it.

UK healthcare rheumatology

  • How it works: GP refers you; you're triaged; a rheumatologist assesses, orders tests, starts treatment on NICE-approved pathways. Fully funded.
  • Best for: The overwhelming majority of patients — care is high-quality and complete, if slower than private.
  • Common side-effects: Long waits (often 12–30+ weeks for first appointment), less continuity of consultant, limited appointment times.
  • UK healthcare availability: Universal, free at the point of use for UK residents.
  • Typical UK cost: £0 to the patient (prescription charges may apply in England).

Private rheumatology

  • How it works: Self-referral or GP letter to a private consultant, seen within days to weeks. Any prescribed medicines usually shift back to UK healthcare for long-term supply.
  • Best for: Getting a diagnosis faster, second opinions, more flexible appointment times, complex cases.
  • Common side-effects: Cost; not always straightforward to move biologics from private to NHS; less integration with your UK healthcare record.
  • UK healthcare availability: Runs alongside UK healthcare — most rheumatologists work in both.
  • Typical UK cost: £200–£350 first appointment, £150–£250 follow-ups, plus tests and imaging (often £150–£500).

What you actually get in each

In the UK healthcare system, care follows NICE pathways: bloods, imaging, DMARDs, biologics if criteria are met. Consultants change over time in some clinics; nurse-led follow-up is common. The clinical care is generally excellent, but access is rationed by waiting lists.

Privately, you get a longer first appointment (typically 45–60 minutes), quick access to ultrasound or MRI, and the same consultant every time. The clinical decisions look very similar — most private rheumatologists work in the UK healthcare system too and follow the same guidelines.

Waiting times — the real reason people go private

In parts of the UK the wait for an UK healthcare first rheumatology appointment can be 20+ weeks, and longer for follow-up scans. When early inflammatory arthritis is suspected, that delay matters — every extra month before starting DMARDs adds a small but measurable risk of joint damage.

A private first appointment is often available within 5–10 working days. If bloods and ultrasound confirm inflammation, a private consultant can start DMARDs immediately (usually on private prescription initially).

The medication transfer question

For most patients this is where private care gets complicated. Methotrexate and other conventional DMARDs can usually be transferred back to your UK healthcare GP as a 'shared care' arrangement, saving hundreds of pounds a year. Not all GP surgeries accept shared care immediately — it depends on local guidelines.

Biologics are much harder to transfer. UK healthcare access requires NICE eligibility criteria met by UK healthcare records, which private records don't always satisfy directly. Many patients start biologics privately, then re-enter the UK healthcare system via a formal transfer that essentially repeats the eligibility assessment.

Cost — being realistic

A first private consultation is typically £200–£350; follow-ups £150–£250. Add £50–£150 for bloods, £150–£400 for MRI or ultrasound. So a full private diagnostic workup often costs £500–£1,000 before treatment starts.

Some private health insurance policies cover this; some specifically exclude chronic conditions once diagnosed. Read the policy wording carefully — you cannot 'insure yourself' for arthritis after you're already diagnosed.

When private is worth it — and when it isn't

Private is often worth it if: you have new, potentially inflammatory joint symptoms and the UK healthcare system wait is over 3 months; you want a second opinion on a complex diagnosis; you need faster access to imaging; or you're symptomatic between UK healthcare appointments and want a bridging opinion.

Private is usually not worth it if: you already have a diagnosis and an UK healthcare team; your treatment is stable; you only want private for 'comfort' rather than clinical urgency. The clinical decisions won't differ — you'd just be paying for the same guideline-based care faster.

A common hybrid approach

Many UK patients use a hybrid: one private appointment to get a rapid diagnosis and start treatment, then transfer conventional DMARDs to their GP under shared care, and re-enter the UK healthcare system system for long-term follow-up. This can dramatically shorten the diagnostic delay without long-term cost.

At a glance

UK healthcare rheumatologyPrivate rheumatology
First appointment wait12–30+ weeksWithin 1–2 weeks
First appointment cost£0£200–£350
Consultant continuityVariableSame consultant
Imaging accessWeeks–monthsDays
Biologic accessNICE-eligibility pathwayFaster start; UK healthcare transfer complex
Long-term follow-upExcellent (once in system)Often moved back to NHS

Key takeaways

  • Private mostly buys speed, not different medicines.
  • For suspected early inflammatory arthritis, speed matters clinically.
  • Shared care lets you move DMARDs back to UK healthcare to control costs.
  • Biologics are hardest to transfer privately â†’ NHS; plan accordingly.
  • A one-off private consult can be a smart bridge into the UK healthcare system pathway.

Talk to your clinician

How do Osteoarthritis (OA) and Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) compare?

Osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are the two most common forms of arthritis in the UK, but they are very different diseases. Confusing them delays the right treatment — particularly for rheumatoid arthritis, where early diagnosis genuinely changes outcomes. This guide compares them side-by-side, using UK healthcare and NICE frameworks, so you can recognise which pattern fits and what to ask your GP.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are the two most common forms of arthritis in the UK, but they are very different diseases. Confusing them delays the right treatment — particularly for rheumatoid arthritis, where early diagnosis genuinely changes outcomes. This guide compares them side-by-side, using UK healthcare and NICE frameworks, so you can recognise which pattern fits and what to ask your GP.

Osteoarthritis (OA)

  • How it works: A wear-and-repair disorder of the joint — the cartilage thins, the bone underneath remodels and small bony spurs (osteophytes) form.
  • Best for: 'Best for' doesn't apply — this describes people typically affected: over 45, often after injury, obesity or years of joint load.
  • Common side-effects: Deep aching pain that's worse with use, short (<30 min) morning stiffness, joint enlargement and crepitus.
  • UK healthcare availability: Managed largely in primary care with exercise, weight loss, topical/oral NSAIDs and, if severe, joint replacement.
  • Typical UK cost: Most treatment is NHS-funded; steroid injections, physio and joint replacements are all available on the UK healthcare system.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)

  • How it works: An autoimmune disease — the immune system attacks the joint lining (synovium), causing chronic inflammation and, if untreated, joint erosion.
  • Best for: Typically develops between 40–60 (though possible at any age), three times more common in women, often with a family history.
  • Common side-effects: Symmetrical joint swelling (both hands, both feet), morning stiffness lasting >1 hour, fatigue and sometimes flu-like symptoms.
  • UK healthcare availability: Rapid referral to rheumatology, DMARDs (methotrexate first), progressing to biologics if needed under NICE thresholds.
  • Typical UK cost: All standard treatment is NHS-funded, including biologics for people who meet NICE criteria.

Different causes, different pattern

Osteoarthritis is a disorder of the joint itself. Cartilage — the smooth cap on bone ends — gradually thins and cracks, and the underlying bone tries to compensate by thickening and growing osteophytes. It's driven by mechanical load, past injury, genetics and body weight, and typically affects weight-bearing joints (knees, hips, spine) and the small joints of the hand.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease. The immune system attacks the synovium — the thin lining of every movable joint — creating persistent inflammation that erodes cartilage and bone if left uncontrolled. It usually starts symmetrically in small joints (knuckles, wrists, base of toes) and can affect the whole body: fatigue, weight loss, lung and eye involvement.

Symptoms clues that point one way or the other

Timing of stiffness is one of the most useful clues. OA stiffness is short — usually under 30 minutes on waking and after inactivity — and joints feel better with gentle movement then worse with heavy use. RA stiffness lasts more than an hour, sometimes most of the morning, and improves with movement.

Distribution matters too. OA tends to be asymmetric: one bad knee, one thumb base. RA is classically symmetrical: both wrists, all the knuckles of both hands, or the balls of both feet.

Swelling in OA is bony and hard (Heberden's and Bouchard's nodes on finger joints). In RA it is soft and boggy — the inflamed synovium — with visible warmth.

How UK doctors tell them apart

GPs diagnose osteoarthritis clinically in adults over 45 with typical activity-related joint pain and short morning stiffness — no imaging or blood tests are needed unless the picture is unusual.

For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE recommends urgent referral to rheumatology if small joints of the hands or feet are swollen, if more than one joint is involved, or if there has been a delay of more than three months between symptom onset and being seen. Bloods (CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP) and ultrasound or MRI look for synovitis; anti-CCP in particular is highly specific for RA.

Treatment is genuinely different

OA treatment aims to protect the joint and control symptoms. That means muscle-strengthening and aerobic exercise, weight management if relevant, topical NSAID gel, oral NSAIDs (short courses), and — for advanced cases — joint replacement, which is one of the most successful operations the UK healthcare system performs.

RA treatment aims to switch the disease off. DMARDs — usually methotrexate — are started as soon as possible, with a 'treat-to-target' approach: measure activity every few months and step treatment up (adding hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine, then biologics) until inflammation is under control. Early, aggressive treatment often prevents lasting joint damage.

Long-term outlook

OA is progressive but not systemic. Most people manage well with self-help and pharmacy medicines; a proportion eventually need joint replacement, particularly for the hip or knee.

RA today, treated early, often reaches low disease activity or remission. Untreated, it can cause visible joint deformity, disability and shortens life expectancy through cardiovascular and lung complications. That's why speed of diagnosis matters so much.

At a glance

Osteoarthritis (OA)Rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
CauseWear and joint remodellingAutoimmune synovial inflammation
Typical ageUsually 45+Any age, often 40–60
PatternAsymmetric, weight-bearing jointsSymmetric, small joints of hands/feet
Morning stiffness<30 minutes>1 hour
Blood tests useful?RarelyCRP, ESR, RF, anti-CCP
Main treatmentExercise, weight loss, NSAIDsDMARDs / biologics
Systemic symptomsNoYes — fatigue, sometimes lung, eye

Key takeaways

  • OA is a joint disease; RA is a whole-body autoimmune disease.
  • Long morning stiffness and symmetric small-joint swelling point to RA — see your GP quickly.
  • OA is diagnosed clinically; RA usually needs bloods and rheumatology review.
  • Early DMARDs dramatically change the long-term outlook for RA.
  • Exercise helps both — but never replaces DMARDs in inflammatory arthritis.

Talk to your clinician

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Osteoarthritis (OA) and Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

/guides/painkillers-and-nsaids:
Pillar Guide

Topical gels, oral NSAIDs, paracetamol and opioids — what works, what to avoid, and how to use them safely.

Painkillers and NSAIDs are among the most used arthritis treatments in the UK. This guide explains topical gels, oral NSAIDs, paracetamol and weak opioids — what NICE recommends, what to avoid long-term, and when to ask for a review. Educational information only; check with your GP or pharmacist before changing medicines.

What is the best painkiller for arthritis?

There is no single "best" painkiller — it depends on which joints are affected and your other health conditions. NICE now recommends topical NSAID gels (diclofenac or ibuprofen) as first-line for knee and hand osteoarthritis, with oral NSAIDs added at the lowest effective dose if that isn't enough. Paracetamol and short-course opioids are reserved for specific situations, not routine daily use.

Painkillers and NSAIDs for arthritis: an overview

Painkillers are the most widely used treatments for arthritis in the UK — and the most widely misunderstood. The right medication, at the right dose, for the right length of time can transform daily life. The wrong one, used for too long, can cause stomach bleeding, kidney damage and avoidable cardiovascular events.

This guide covers the four main groups: topical NSAIDs, oral NSAIDs, paracetamol, and weak opioids. It follows NICE guidance (NG226 for osteoarthritis) and the British National Formulary recommendations used in UK clinical practice.

First-line: topical NSAID gels

For knee and hand osteoarthritis, NICE now recommends a topical NSAID gel as the first painkiller to try. Diclofenac (Voltarol) and ibuprofen (Nurofen) gels deliver the anti-inflammatory effect directly to the joint, with only about 5% of the drug absorbed into the bloodstream.

This means most of the benefit with much less of the risk: very low rates of stomach ulcers, kidney problems and cardiovascular events compared with oral tablets. They are well-suited for older adults and anyone with high blood pressure, kidney disease or stomach problems.

To get the most from a topical NSAID:

  • Follow the product leaflet for how much gel to apply and how often
  • Massage in as directed; wash hands after applying
  • Give topical treatment a fair trial (often around two weeks) unless your clinician advises otherwise
  • Do not apply to broken skin

Oral NSAIDs: ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac

If topical NSAIDs and exercise have not controlled symptoms, your GP or rheumatology team may discuss an oral NSAID. Common UK options (see current BNF / SmPC — do not self-dose from this page) include:

  • Ibuprofen — short-acting; often used for short flares when a clinician or pharmacist confirms it is suitable.
  • Naproxen — longer-acting; sometimes preferred for ongoing arthritis pain when cardiovascular and stomach risks are acceptable.
  • Diclofenac — potent but higher cardiovascular risk in tablet form, so often used as a topical gel rather than oral tablets.

All oral NSAIDs share risks: stomach ulcers and bleeding, kidney injury, raised blood pressure, fluid retention, and a small increase in heart attack and stroke risk. Risks rise with dose, age and duration. Exact dose and duration must come from your clinician or the product label — not from educational websites.

People who need an oral NSAID for more than a few weeks are often also prescribed a proton-pump inhibitor to protect the stomach — especially if over 65, with ulcer history, or on blood-thinners. Ask your GP or pharmacist what applies to you.

Naproxen for arthritis: uses and safety

Naproxen is an NSAID that can ease pain and inflammation in conditions including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis and gout. Whether it is suitable depends on your health and other medicines.

Follow your prescription or the product leaflet. Take it with or after food, using the lowest effective dose for the shortest time needed. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber about stomach protection.

Do not combine naproxen with ibuprofen or another NSAID. If you take prescribed aspirin, blood thinners or other regular medicines, ask your pharmacist before taking naproxen; do not stop prescribed medicines yourself.

Check first if you have had a stomach ulcer, have kidney, heart or liver problems, have reacted to NSAIDs, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. Seek urgent advice for suspected serious side effects, including black, tar-like stools or vomiting blood. Call 999 for difficulty breathing or swelling of the tongue or throat.

Read the NHS naproxen information and ask a pharmacist about your own circumstances.

Paracetamol: useful but limited

Paracetamol used to be the standard first-line painkiller for osteoarthritis. NICE downgraded it in 2022 after evidence reviews showed only modest benefit at best. It remains useful for:

  • Short-term, mild pain
  • Topping up an NSAID at flare-ups
  • People who can't take NSAIDs (kidney disease, ulcer history, certain heart conditions)

Adult labelled maximums are on the pack and in the BNF (commonly discussed as up to 4 g in 24 hours for healthy adults, with gaps between doses). Older adults, lower body weight and liver disease often need lower limits — follow the label and ask a pharmacist or GP; do not exceed labelled maximums.

Codeine, tramadol and stronger opioids

NICE no longer recommends routine opioid use for osteoarthritis. The benefits are small, and the risks — constipation, drowsiness, falls in older adults, dependence — are significant. Weak opioids (codeine, dihydrocodeine, tramadol) are reserved for short courses when:

  • Other treatments have genuinely been tried and failed
  • A specific event (e.g. waiting for joint replacement) requires temporary cover
  • A clear plan to stop within weeks is agreed

Strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl patches) have no routine place in arthritis care. If you have been on opioids for joint pain for more than a few months, a structured review with your GP or pain clinic is the right next step.

Who should avoid which painkiller

  • Kidney disease — avoid oral NSAIDs; topical NSAIDs and paracetamol are usually safer.
  • Heart failure or recent heart attack — avoid oral NSAIDs (especially diclofenac).
  • Stomach ulcer or bleeding history — avoid oral NSAIDs unless essential, always with a stomach-protector.
  • Asthma triggered by aspirin or NSAIDs — avoid all NSAIDs.
  • Liver disease — paracetamol dosing may need to be reduced; check with your prescriber or pharmacist before use.
  • Pregnancy — avoid NSAIDs (especially after 20 weeks); paracetamol is usually preferred.
  • Anticoagulants (warfarin, DOACs) — combining with NSAIDs significantly raises bleeding risk.

Combining painkillers safely

Combinations clinicians sometimes discuss (always check suitability for you):

  • Topical NSAID + paracetamol — often lower systemic risk than two oral NSAIDs
  • Oral NSAID + paracetamol — different mechanisms; stay within labelled maxima
  • Short-course weak opioid with a clear stop plan — only when a clinician recommends it

Do not combine two oral NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen and naproxen) unless a clinician explicitly directs it — risks rise without clear extra benefit. Check with a pharmacist before adding any over-the-counter painkiller to prescribed medication.

What works alongside painkillers

Painkillers are most effective when they enable the things that actually change arthritis over the long term:

  • Strengthening and aerobic exercise — the strongest evidence base for reducing arthritis pain
  • Weight management — every 1 kg lost reduces force across the knee by about 4 kg with each step
  • Heat, cold and pacing — simple, cheap and effective for daily flares
  • Steroid injections — strategic short-term relief that enables rehabilitation (see our steroids guide)
  • Disease-modifying drugs — for inflammatory arthritis, the foundation of long-term control

When to ask for a medication review

  • You've been on a daily NSAID for more than 3 months without a recent kidney and blood-pressure check
  • You're on an opioid for arthritis pain and haven't had a structured review
  • Your painkillers aren't working as well as they did
  • You're getting indigestion, black stools, or unusual bruising
  • You're stacking over-the-counter painkillers on top of prescribed ones

Key takeaways

  • Topical NSAID gels are first-line for knee and hand osteoarthritis — most of the benefit, very little of the risk.
  • Oral NSAIDs work but should be used at the lowest dose for the shortest time, almost always with a stomach-protector.
  • Paracetamol is helpful as a top-up or for people who can't take NSAIDs; it is no longer first-line.
  • Opioids have a very limited role in arthritis pain — short courses only, with a stop plan.
  • The right combination depends on your kidneys, your heart, your stomach and the rest of your medication list.
  • Painkillers buy time for the treatments that actually change arthritis: movement, strength, weight management and disease-modifying drugs.

How do Paracetamol and Ibuprofen compare for arthritis?

Paracetamol and ibuprofen are the two most common over-the-counter painkillers used for arthritis in the UK. They look similar on the shelf but work in very different ways, and current NICE guidance treats them very differently. This guide explains what each one does, how well the evidence says it works for osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis, the safety trade-offs, and when it is worth stepping up to a stronger option.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Paracetamol and ibuprofen are the two most common over-the-counter painkillers used for arthritis in the UK. They look similar on the shelf but work in very different ways, and current NICE guidance treats them very differently. This guide explains what each one does, how well the evidence says it works for osteoarthritis and inflammatory arthritis, the safety trade-offs, and when it is worth stepping up to a stronger option.

Paracetamol

  • How it works: Acts mainly in the brain to reduce pain signalling. It is not a strong anti-inflammatory, so it does not reduce joint swelling.
  • Best for: Mild osteoarthritis pain, breakthrough pain on top of other treatment, and people who cannot safely take NSAIDs.
  • Common side-effects: Very safe at recommended doses (up to 4 g/day for adults). Liver damage with overdose or in heavy drinkers.
  • UK healthcare availability: First-choice simple analgesic on UK healthcare repeat prescriptions, though NICE 2022 no longer recommends routine long-term use for osteoarthritis.
  • Typical UK cost: £0.30–£2 for 16 tablets over the counter; free on UK healthcare prescription if exempt (~£9.90 charge otherwise).

Ibuprofen

  • How it works: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that blocks COX enzymes, reducing both pain and inflammation.
  • Best for: Inflammatory flare-ups, morning stiffness, painful osteoarthritis flares — especially in the knee, hand or hip.
  • Common side-effects: Stomach irritation and ulcers, raised blood pressure, kidney strain, heart-attack and stroke risk with high doses or long-term use.
  • UK healthcare availability: Available on UK healthcare prescription, often paired with a stomach-protecting drug (PPI) if used regularly. Topical NSAID gels are preferred for hand and knee OA.
  • Typical UK cost: £0.50–£3 for 16 tablets; topical gel around £4–£8 a tube.

How each one actually works

Paracetamol's mechanism is still debated, but its main effect is in the central nervous system, dampening how pain signals are processed. Crucially, it barely touches inflammation — so it can take the edge off aching joints but doesn't shrink swollen ones.

Ibuprofen works peripherally at the joint. By blocking cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), it stops the production of prostaglandins, the chemicals that drive inflammatory pain, swelling and warmth. That's why it tends to work better on obvious flares with visible swelling.

What the UK evidence says

NICE's 2022 osteoarthritis guideline changed the landscape: it no longer recommends paracetamol as routine treatment for osteoarthritis, because trials show only a small effect, similar to placebo. Instead, it recommends topical NSAIDs (like ibuprofen gel) first, then oral NSAIDs when needed, at the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.

For inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid, psoriatic, ankylosing spondylitis) neither paracetamol nor ibuprofen changes the underlying disease. They only help with symptoms while disease-modifying drugs (DMARDs) or biologics do the real work.

Safety — where the differences really show

Paracetamol is remarkable in that, at the correct dose, most people can take it long-term with minimal issues. The main risk is overdose — deliberate or accidental — which can silently damage the liver.

Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs carry more day-to-day risk. Even short courses can raise blood pressure, worsen heart failure, irritate the stomach or reduce kidney function — particularly in people over 65, on blood pressure or diuretic medication, or with kidney disease. Regular users are often prescribed a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) like omeprazole to protect the stomach lining.

Ibuprofen gel applied to the joint gives similar pain relief to tablets for hand and knee osteoarthritis with far less systemic absorption, which is why UK guidance now leads with it.

Cost and access on the UK healthcare system

Both are cheap. A pack of 16 tablets of either is under £3 in most UK supermarkets and pharmacies. On UK healthcare prescription in England a single item costs £9.90 (2024/25), so buying either over the counter is usually cheaper unless you have an exemption or a Prescription Prepayment Certificate.

Topical ibuprofen gel is available both over the counter and on prescription, and is often stocked cheaply in supermarket own-brand tubes.

Which should you choose?

For a flare with obvious swelling, warmth and stiffness, ibuprofen (topical first, oral if needed) is usually the more effective option — provided you can tolerate it. For general aching without much swelling, or if NSAIDs are risky for you, paracetamol is still a sensible option, even if the strength of evidence for osteoarthritis is modest.

Many people end up using both: paracetamol as a background painkiller, with topical or short-course oral ibuprofen when a flare hits. Talk to your pharmacist or GP before combining them regularly, especially if you're over 65 or on other medications.

At a glance

ParacetamolIbuprofen
Reduces inflammation?No — mostly a painkillerYes — anti-inflammatory
Best forMild aches, when NSAIDs are unsafeFlares with swelling and stiffness
Main riskLiver damage in overdoseStomach, kidney, heart, blood pressure
NICE OA guidanceNo longer routineTopical first, then oral, lowest dose
OTC cost (16 tablets)£0.30–£2£0.50–£3
UK healthcare prescription (England)£9.90 per item£9.90 per item

Key takeaways

  • For osteoarthritis with visible swelling, topical ibuprofen is now the NICE first-line choice.
  • Paracetamol is safer day-to-day but works less well than NSAIDs on inflamed joints.
  • Never exceed 4 g paracetamol or the ibuprofen pack dose without medical advice.
  • Ask your pharmacist about stomach protection if you take ibuprofen regularly.
  • Neither drug slows arthritis — inflammatory arthritis needs DMARDs or biologics.

Talk to your clinician

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Paracetamol and Ibuprofen with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

/guides/preventative-msk-health:
How do I keep my muscles and joints healthy?

The three pillars are: 150 minutes moderate aerobic activity per week, 2 strength sessions per week, and 7-9 hours of sleep. Add Mediterranean-style diet, don't smoke, and keep BMI under 27 for lowest lifetime arthritis risk.

Medically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 Updated 11 September 2026

Can early intervention prevent arthritis getting worse?

Yes. Early intervention — within weeks, not years — significantly reduces joint damage. Building strength, managing weight, treating injuries promptly, and adjusting daily load preserves cartilage and slows progression. Most adults aged 40–60 have a 5–10 year window to change their arthritis trajectory.

Medically reviewed by Maxwell

First Contact Practitioner • HCPC PH128483 • Last updated June 2026

Reviewer details and the site's clinical review process are documented in our editorial standards.

1. Recognising early arthritis signs

Early arthritis often whispers before it shouts. Watch for morning stiffness that eases within 30 minutes, brief joint clicking with discomfort, mild swelling after activity, and reduced range of motion. Many people dismiss these as "getting older" — but they are opportunities for intervention.

2. Prevention vs management: what's the difference?

Prevention aims to delay or reduce the severity of a condition before it develops or worsens. Management addresses a condition that already exists. In practice the two overlap heavily — the same strength training, weight management, movement variety and diet principles that prevent MSK problems are also the backbone of managing them once they've started. This is why our guides on exercise and diet apply whether you're trying to stay ahead of a problem or already living with one.

3. The role of posture and movement patterns

There is no single "perfect" posture. The body needs variety. Long hours in one position — at a desk, on a sofa, behind the wheel — overload specific tissues. Aim to change position every 30–45 minutes and strengthen muscles that support your daily postures. See our musculoskeletal health guide for a full workplace ergonomics checklist.

4. Load management during daily activities

  • Carry shopping in two balanced bags rather than one heavy one
  • Use both hands to lift, keeping objects close to the body
  • Break long gardening sessions into 20-minute blocks
  • Wear supportive footwear with good shock absorption
  • Add 10% volume per week when building exercise — not more

5. Preventative exercise: which joints to target first

Prioritise the joints most likely to develop arthritis: knees, hips, hands and lower back. Quadriceps strength predicts knee arthritis outcomes. Hip abductor strength protects the hip and lower back. Grip strength is a marker of whole-body health.

Visit the exercise hub for programmes.

6. When to see a physio, GP or specialist

  • Physio: any joint pain over 2 weeks, post-injury stiffness, recurring symptoms
  • GP: swelling, redness, hot joint, prolonged morning stiffness over an hour, fatigue with joint pain
  • Specialist: suspected inflammatory arthritis, family history, multiple small joints affected

7. Prevention across the life course

The strength, balance and mineral-intake habits that prevent arthritis progression in your 40s and 50s are the same foundation that prevents frailty, falls and muscle loss decades later. Preventative MSK health isn't a one-off fix — it's a life-course strategy that pays off at every age, including your 70s and 80s.

Frequently asked questions

Can arthritis be prevented?

You cannot fully prevent age-related joint changes, but you can significantly delay onset and reduce severity by managing weight, building strength, treating injuries early, and addressing posture and load.

What are the earliest signs of arthritis?

Morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes, joint clicking with mild discomfort, brief swelling after activity, and reduced range of motion — often dismissed as "just getting older".

Does running cause arthritis?

Recreational running does not increase osteoarthritis risk and may protect joints. High-volume competitive running, repeated injury and poor recovery do raise risk.

When should I see a physio?

Any joint pain lasting more than 2 weeks, swelling that does not settle, or a fall or twist that changes how you move warrants a physiotherapy assessment — sooner is better.

Does posture really matter?

Posture matters less than variety and strength. Static positions held for hours load tissues unevenly. Move often, build strength in mid-range, and avoid prolonged extremes.

What supplements help prevent arthritis?

Vitamin D, omega-3 and a Mediterranean-style diet have the best preventative evidence. Glucosamine and chondroitin have mixed evidence and are unlikely to prevent disease.

Is prevention still worth it later in life?

Yes. While the biggest gains come from acting in your 40s and 50s, strength training, weight-bearing activity and mineral intake continue to protect joints, bones and muscle at any age — including your 70s and 80s.

What is the difference between prevention and management?

Prevention aims to delay or reduce the severity of MSK conditions before they develop or worsen. Management addresses a condition that already exists. The two overlap heavily — most preventative strategies (strength, movement, weight, diet) also form the backbone of good management.

How does preventative MSK health connect to frailty in later life?

The strength, balance and bone-density work that prevents arthritis progression in your 40s and 50s is the same foundation that prevents frailty, falls and muscle loss in your 70s and beyond. Preventative MSK health is really a life-course strategy, not a one-off fix.

/guides/shoulder-pain-relief:
Clinical Guide

What is causing it, what settles it fastest, and a staged mobility-then-strength routine you can start at home today.

Most shoulder pain comes from the rotator cuff, a stiffening joint capsule, or osteoarthritis — and in nearly every case, gentle movement relieves it faster than rest. This guide explains how to tell the causes apart, what settles a painful week quickly, and gives you a staged routine of mobility and strengthening exercises aligned with UK physiotherapy practice.

What is actually causing your shoulder pain

The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body, and that mobility comes at the cost of stability. Four small rotator cuff muscles hold the ball of the upper arm bone into a shallow socket while the larger muscles do the lifting. Nearly all non-traumatic shoulder pain traces back to one of four sources:

  • Rotator cuff related shoulder pain (roughly 70% of cases) — pain on the outer upper arm, worst when reaching overhead, out to the side, or behind your back to fasten a seatbelt.
  • Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) — the joint capsule thickens and tightens. The hallmark is loss of movement in every direction, including when someone else lifts your arm for you. More common between 40 and 60, and in people with diabetes or thyroid disease.
  • Shoulder osteoarthritis — deep, grinding pain, morning stiffness that eases within about 30 minutes, and sometimes an audible crunch on movement. It affects the main ball-and-socket joint or the smaller acromioclavicular joint on top of the shoulder.
  • Inflammatory arthritis — rheumatoid arthritis and polymyalgia rheumatica both commonly involve the shoulders, typically with stiffness lasting well over an hour in the morning and often affecting both sides.

Distinguishing between these matters, because the routine below is deliberately staged: mobility first, then strength. Pushing strengthening work into a genuinely frozen or acutely inflamed shoulder makes things worse.

Immediate relief in a painful week

When the shoulder is at its most painful, four measures give the fastest change:

  • Topical NSAID gel. UK NICE guidance recommends topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatories ahead of oral tablets for a single painful joint. Applied three to four times daily, they reach the tissue directly with far less risk to the stomach and kidneys.
  • Keep moving within a pain-free range. Slings and total rest are the single biggest cause of a shoulder that stiffens and stays painful. Move the arm gently every hour you are awake.
  • Fix your sleeping position. Lie on the unaffected side with a pillow hugged in front of you to support the sore arm, or sleep on your back with a folded towel under the elbow. Night pain is the symptom people find hardest, and positioning helps more than anything else.
  • Heat before movement. Ten minutes of a warm shower or a heat pack before your exercises makes the range-of-motion work considerably easier.

Stage one: the daily mobility routine

Do these every day, including flare days. They take about eight minutes. Move slowly; you are not stretching to the point of pain.

  • Pendulum swings. Lean forward, supporting yourself with the good arm on a table. Let the sore arm hang and swing it gently in small circles, 30 seconds each direction. This uses gravity rather than muscle to open the joint space.
  • Table slides. Sit at a table with your forearm resting on a cloth. Slide the arm forward as far as comfortable, then back. 10 repetitions.
  • Wall walks. Face a wall, walk your fingers up it as high as is comfortable, hold five seconds, walk back down. 8 repetitions.
  • Assisted external rotation. Hold a walking stick or broom handle with both hands, elbows tucked at your sides. Use the good arm to push the sore forearm outwards. Hold 10 seconds, 8 repetitions.
  • Cross-body reach. Bring the sore arm across your chest, supporting it at the elbow with the other hand. Hold 20 seconds, 3 repetitions.

Stage two: strengthening, two to three times a week

Add these once daily mobility work is comfortable — usually after one to two weeks. Use a light resistance band or a tin of beans; the rotator cuff responds to control, not heavy load.

  • Isometric holds. Stand beside a wall and press the outside of your elbow into it, holding gently at about 30% effort for 10 seconds. 5 repetitions. These are the safest starting point because the shoulder does not move.
  • Band external rotation. Elbow tucked at your side at 90 degrees, band anchored at waist height, rotate the forearm outwards away from your body. 2–3 sets of 10.
  • Band internal rotation. The same setup, rotating inwards across your stomach. 2–3 sets of 10.
  • Scapular squeezes. Draw both shoulder blades down and together, hold five seconds. 10 repetitions. Shoulder blade control is routinely the missing link in stubborn shoulder pain.
  • Scaption raises. With a light weight, raise the arm to shoulder height at about 30 degrees in front of your body (not straight out to the side). 2 sets of 8.
  • Wall press-ups. Hands on the wall at chest height, slow press-ups. 2 sets of 10. Builds tolerance to loading through the whole shoulder girdle.

A realistic weekly plan

  • Every day — the eight-minute mobility routine, ideally after a warm shower.
  • Monday, Wednesday, Friday — add the strengthening set (about 15 minutes).
  • Most days — 20–30 minutes of walking. General activity reduces pain sensitivity across all joints, shoulders included, and counts toward the UK Chief Medical Officer target of 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly.

Three short sessions a week sustained for three months beat an intensive fortnight followed by abandonment. Track how the shoulder feels the morning after each session rather than during it — the next-morning response is the honest signal.

Everyday adjustments that reduce shoulder load

  • Move frequently used items in cupboards down to waist height so you are not repeatedly reaching overhead.
  • Carry bags in the unaffected hand, or use a rucksack across both shoulders.
  • Raise your work surface or screen so you are not shrugging or reaching forward all day.
  • Swap a heavy handbag for a cross-body bag worn on the opposite side.
  • Use a long-handled sponge or a hair-washing rinse jug during the painful phase.

When self-management is not enough

If six to eight weeks of consistent exercise has not shifted the pain, options in the UK include a referral to musculoskeletal physiotherapy (self-referral is available in most areas), a corticosteroid injection — most useful for frozen shoulder and acutely inflamed cuff pain, and best combined with continued exercise rather than used alone — and imaging or a specialist opinion if a full-thickness cuff tear or advanced osteoarthritis is suspected. Surgery is a late option and, for most rotator cuff pain, no better than a well-delivered exercise programme in trial comparisons.

Red flags — seek medical advice promptly

Contact a GP or urgent care if you have: shoulder pain after a fall or a sudden wrench with an inability to lift the arm, a visibly deformed shoulder, numbness or weakness spreading down the arm, fever or feeling systemically unwell alongside the pain, unexplained weight loss, a history of cancer, or new severe pain in both shoulders with prolonged morning stiffness in someone over 50 (which can indicate polymyalgia rheumatica and needs prompt assessment).

Your next step

Start today with the pendulum swings and cross-body reach — two minutes total. Build to the full mobility routine over the coming week, then add strengthening. Most people with rotator cuff pain see a clear improvement within six weeks of doing this consistently.

Sources & disclaimer

Based on NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries on shoulder pain and rotator cuff disorders, NICE guideline NG226 (Osteoarthritis in over 16s, 2022), UK Chief Medical Officer Physical Activity Guidelines (2019) and Chartered Society of Physiotherapy shoulder rehabilitation guidance. For educational use only and not a substitute for personalised advice from a physiotherapist or GP.

/guides/steroids-for-arthritis:
Pillar Guide

A plain-English guide to corticosteroid injections and tablets — how they work, what to expect, side effects and how to access them in the UK.

Steroid injections and short courses of oral steroids are among the most widely used treatments for arthritis pain in the UK. They don't cure arthritis, but used strategically they can break a flare-up, reduce inflammation quickly and create a window for exercise and rehabilitation to work. This guide explains exactly what they do, what to expect, and how to access them on the public health service.

Steroids for arthritis: an overview

Corticosteroids — often shortened to "steroids" — are one of the most widely used treatments for inflammatory joint pain. They are synthetic versions of cortisol, a hormone the body produces naturally, and they work by switching off the chemical signals that cause inflammation, swelling and pain.

In arthritis care, steroids are used in three main ways: as injections into a joint (intra-articular), as short courses of tablets (oral), and occasionally as an intramuscular injection for a body-wide effect. Each route has a different role, and choosing the right one depends on the type of arthritis, which joints are affected, and how long-lasting the relief needs to be.

Steroids do not slow the underlying disease in osteoarthritis, and they are not a long-term solution. What they offer is a window of relief — often enough to get someone moving, sleeping, exercising or completing physiotherapy that would otherwise be impossible because of pain.

How steroids work in an inflamed joint

In a healthy joint, the synovial lining produces a small amount of lubricating fluid. In inflammatory arthritis (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, gout) and during osteoarthritis flares, this lining becomes thickened and produces excess fluid loaded with inflammatory chemicals — prostaglandins, cytokines and white blood cells.

A steroid injection delivers a concentrated dose directly into this inflamed tissue. Within hours it begins to:

  • Block the production of inflammatory prostaglandins
  • Reduce the number of immune cells in the joint
  • Shrink the swollen synovial lining
  • Lower the volume of excess joint fluid

The result is less pressure inside the joint capsule, less mechanical pain, and often a noticeable improvement in range of movement.

Types of steroid injection

The three corticosteroids most commonly used in UK arthritis clinics are:

  • Methylprednisolone (Depo-Medrone) — medium-acting, widely used for knees, shoulders and hips
  • Triamcinolone (Kenalog) — longer-acting, often used for larger joints and tendon sheaths
  • Hydrocortisone — shorter-acting, sometimes used in smaller joints like fingers

The injection is usually mixed with a small dose of local anaesthetic (lidocaine), which gives almost immediate but brief pain relief while the steroid begins to work over the following 24–72 hours.

What to expect during a joint injection

A joint injection takes about 10–15 minutes from start to finish. You can drive yourself home afterwards. Here is what typically happens:

  • The clinician examines the joint and marks the injection site
  • The skin is cleaned with antiseptic
  • A fine needle is inserted into the joint space (sometimes guided by ultrasound)
  • If excess fluid is present, it may be drawn off first (aspiration)
  • The steroid and local anaesthetic mixture is injected
  • A small plaster is applied; you rest the joint for 24–48 hours

It is common to feel a brief sharp pressure as the needle enters the joint. Most people describe it as uncomfortable rather than painful.

Side effects and risks

Steroid injections are generally safe when given correctly and not used too often. The most common side effects are mild and short-lived:

  • Post-injection flare — a temporary increase in pain for 24–48 hours, experienced by 1 in 20 people
  • Facial flushing — warmth and redness lasting a day or two
  • Raised blood sugar — important if you have diabetes; monitor closely for 3–5 days
  • Skin changes — thinning or loss of pigment at the injection site (more visible in darker skin)
  • Mood or sleep disturbance — brief and self-limiting

Rare but more serious risks include joint infection (less than 1 in 10,000), tendon weakening if injected too close to a tendon, and accelerated cartilage loss with repeated injections. This is why most clinicians limit injections to a maximum of 3–4 per joint per year.

Oral steroids and inflammatory arthritis

For people with rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, lupus or vasculitis, short courses of oral steroids — usually prednisolone — are a standard part of treatment. They are used as a "bridge" to control inflammation rapidly while slower disease-modifying drugs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine, biologics) take effect over 6–12 weeks.

Typical regimens range from a short tapering course over a few weeks to longer maintenance doses in conditions like polymyalgia rheumatica, which may need treatment for 1–2 years.

Long-term oral steroids carry meaningful risks — weight gain, raised blood pressure, osteoporosis, increased infection risk and changes to blood sugar control. Anyone taking prednisolone for more than 3 months should be assessed for bone protection (calcium, vitamin D and often a bisphosphonate) under NICE guidance.

Steroids for osteoarthritis: what the evidence says

NICE guidance (NG226, 2022) lists intra-articular steroid injections as an option for osteoarthritis when other measures have not controlled symptoms. Cochrane reviews show short-term pain relief of 4–8 weeks for knee osteoarthritis, with less convincing evidence for hip and hand osteoarthritis.

Steroids do not slow cartilage loss in osteoarthritis, and there is some evidence that frequent repeat injections (more than 4 per year in the same joint) may accelerate it. For this reason they are best used strategically — to break a flare-up cycle, to enable physiotherapy, or to bridge the wait for joint replacement surgery — rather than as a routine treatment.

Alternatives to steroid injections

Steroids are one option among several. Depending on your joint, your diagnosis and your goals, your clinician may discuss:

  • Hyaluronic acid injections — sometimes offered for knee osteoarthritis, though NICE no longer routinely recommends them on the public health service
  • Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) — privately available; evidence is mixed and improving
  • Topical NSAIDs — diclofenac or ibuprofen gels are first-line for hand and knee osteoarthritis
  • Oral pain relief — paracetamol, short courses of oral NSAIDs with stomach protection
  • Strengthening exercise and weight management — the strongest evidence base for long-term improvement in osteoarthritis
  • Disease-modifying drugs (DMARDs) — for inflammatory arthritis, the foundation of long-term control

How to access steroid treatment in the UK

Steroid injections and short courses of oral steroids are available free through the public health service. The most common routes are:

  • Your GP — many GPs are trained to inject knees, shoulders and the base of the thumb
  • First Contact Physiotherapists — increasingly trained as independent prescribers and joint injectors; bookable without a GP referral
  • Rheumatology clinics — for inflammatory arthritis and complex small-joint injections
  • Orthopaedic outpatients — when injections are part of a surgical pathway
  • Musculoskeletal interface services — local triage clinics that can inject larger joints quickly

Private steroid injections typically cost £150–£300 per joint and are available through physiotherapy clinics, MSK specialists and private rheumatologists if you need faster access.

Questions to ask your clinician

  • How long is this injection likely to last for me?
  • What is the realistic chance it will help?
  • How many injections have I had in this joint, and is another safe?
  • What should I do — and avoid — in the 48 hours after the injection?
  • How will this affect my diabetes / blood pressure / other medication?
  • Are there alternatives I should consider first?
  • What is the plan if this injection doesn't work?

Key takeaways

  • Steroids reduce inflammation; they don't cure arthritis or repair cartilage.
  • Injections work best when used strategically — to break a flare or enable rehabilitation — not as a long-term routine.
  • Limit injections to 3–4 per joint per year to protect cartilage.
  • Oral steroids are essential in inflammatory arthritis but need bone-protection planning if used long-term.
  • Available free through GPs, First Contact Physios and rheumatology on the public health service.
  • Always pair steroid treatment with exercise, weight management and disease-modifying therapy where appropriate.

How do Swimming (and water-based exercise) and Walking compare?

Regular movement is one of the most powerful treatments for arthritis — the closest thing to a wonder drug. But when joints hurt, choosing the right kind of movement matters. This guide compares swimming and walking side-by-side for UK arthritis patients, drawing on UK healthcare and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) guidance.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Regular movement is one of the most powerful treatments for arthritis — the closest thing to a wonder drug. But when joints hurt, choosing the right kind of movement matters. This guide compares swimming and walking side-by-side for UK arthritis patients, drawing on UK healthcare and Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) guidance.

Swimming (and water-based exercise)

  • How it works: Water supports up to 90% of body weight, taking load off painful joints while still building strength, aerobic fitness and range of motion.
  • Best for: Hip, knee and back osteoarthritis, flare recovery, people carrying extra weight, or those very deconditioned.
  • Common side-effects: Chlorine may irritate skin; access can be limited by cost and pool availability; getting in and out can be tricky with hip/knee pain.
  • UK healthcare availability: Some areas offer NHS-referred hydrotherapy or subsidised 'aquatic exercise on prescription' schemes.
  • Typical UK cost: £4–£7 a public swim; £30–£50 monthly gym membership; UK healthcare hydrotherapy free but usually short courses.

Walking

  • How it works: Low-impact aerobic exercise that strengthens leg muscles, improves cardiovascular health and maintains bone density.
  • Best for: Most mild-to-moderate arthritis, people who prefer outdoor exercise, and anyone building daily activity habits.
  • Common side-effects: Weight-bearing means more knee and hip load than swimming; can flare pain if pace, terrain or footwear are wrong.
  • UK healthcare availability: Actively recommended by UK healthcare 'Better Health' campaigns; UK healthcare Couch to 5K and walking groups are widely available.
  • Typical UK cost: Essentially free — you already have shoes.

The joint-load question

The single biggest difference between swimming and walking is joint load. Chest-deep water reduces effective body weight by around 75%, and neck-deep water by around 90%. That's why hydrotherapy pools are heated and used specifically for people whose joints can't tolerate normal exercise — after a knee replacement, during a rheumatoid flare, or when hip osteoarthritis makes even a short walk painful.

Walking, by contrast, loads each knee with about 1.5 times body weight per step. That's usually fine for mild osteoarthritis and actually helps cartilage stay healthy through 'load and unload' cycles — but it can be too much during a flare or with badly deconditioned muscles.

What each does for your fitness

Both count towards the UK's recommended 150 minutes per week of moderate activity. Swimming works upper body, core and legs simultaneously, so it builds more overall muscular endurance than walking. Walking, however, is more specific to the daily task of walking, which matters if your goal is getting to the shops without pain.

Cardiovascular benefits are comparable at equivalent intensity. Where the two really diverge is bone density: walking preserves bone through mechanical loading, while swimming — pleasant as it is — does not. Post-menopausal women and anyone at risk of osteoporosis should ideally include some weight-bearing exercise even if they primarily swim.

What UK guidelines say

NICE recommends any exercise that a person will actually do, tailored to their condition and preference. Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and the UK healthcare system emphasise the same message: something is better than nothing, and the 'best' exercise is the one you enjoy enough to keep going.

For inflammatory arthritis flares and after joint surgery, hydrotherapy (physiotherapist-led exercise in a warm pool) is often prescribed short-term to rebuild strength without triggering pain. Once pain settles, most people are gradually moved onto walking, cycling or land-based physiotherapy.

Practical realities

Swimming has real barriers: getting to a pool, changing rooms, hair care, cost and — for some — anxiety about being in a swimming costume. Walking removes almost all of those. On the other hand, walking in a British winter with icy pavements is riskier for anyone unsteady on their feet.

A good compromise for many patients: walking as everyday movement (aiming for a modest step target), plus one or two pool sessions per week for range of motion and non-weight-bearing strength.

Choosing based on your joint

Hip and knee osteoarthritis often favour swimming as the primary exercise, particularly during flares. Back arthritis and mild lower-limb OA usually do very well with walking. Hand and wrist arthritis? Neither is particularly targeted, but both help general fitness — pair with specific hand exercises from a physiotherapist.

If your pain rises by more than two points on a 0–10 scale during exercise, or is still worse the next morning, reduce intensity rather than stop entirely. That's not a sign to give up; it's a sign to adjust.

At a glance

Swimming (and water-based exercise)Walking
Joint loadVery low (up to 90% offloaded)Full body weight per step
Cardiovascular fitnessExcellentExcellent
Bone densityMinimal effectPreserves it
Best during a flareYesUsually no
AccessRequires poolAnywhere, anytime
Typical cost£4–£7 per sessionFree

Key takeaways

  • Swimming is gentler on joints; walking is better for bones.
  • During a flare, water-based exercise usually wins.
  • Walking counts towards your weekly 150 minutes and is free.
  • Combining both — pool weekly, walk daily — suits many arthritis patients.
  • Speak to a physio about NHS-referred hydrotherapy if pain limits walking.

Talk to your clinician

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Swimming (and water-based exercise) and Walking with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

/guides/uk-arthritis:
Pillar Guide

Everything you need to know about arthritis — types, symptoms, treatments and support available across the United Kingdom.

Arthritis is an umbrella term for more than 100 conditions that cause joint pain, swelling and stiffness. In the UK, around 10 million people live with arthritis — roughly 1 in 6 adults. The most common type is osteoarthritis, followed by rheumatoid arthritis and gout. This guide covers the main types, how they are diagnosed and treated, and the UK services and benefits available to you.

What Is Arthritis?

Arthritis is not one disease. It is an umbrella term for more than 100 conditions. They all cause pain, swelling and stiffness in or around the joints.

In the UK, about 10 million people live with arthritis (Versus Arthritis, now Arthritis UK, 2024). It is one of the most common long-term health conditions in the country. It affects people of all ages and backgrounds. It is more common in women and in people over 45.

The Main Types at a Glance

  • Osteoarthritis (OA) — the "wear and tear" type. Cartilage in the joints thins over time.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) — an autoimmune type. The immune system attacks the joint lining.
  • Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) — linked to the skin condition psoriasis.
  • Gout — caused by uric acid crystals in the joints.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — mainly affects the spine.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis — the main type in children.

How Common Is Arthritis in the UK?

Arthritis affects about 1 in 6 adults in the UK. That is roughly 10 million people. It is the top cause of pain and disability in the country.

Around 8.75 million people aged 45 and over in the UK have sought treatment for osteoarthritis (Arthritis Research UK, now Arthritis UK, 2013; cited by NICE CKS). Rheumatoid arthritis affects around 400,000 people. Psoriatic arthritis affects around 146,000.

The Cost to the UK

The numbers are huge. Arthritis and bone or joint problems make up 30% of all GP visits in England. They are the biggest cause of time off work.

The total cost to the UK is about £12.6 billion a year in lost work, sick days and care (Versus Arthritis, now Arthritis UK, 2024). Even so, arthritis gets far less research funding than cancer or heart disease.

Cases are rising. The UK is ageing. More people are living with obesity and sitting more. By 2030, over 12 million people in the UK are expected to have arthritis.

Types of Arthritis Explained

Osteoarthritis (OA)

Osteoarthritis is the most common type. Around 8.75 million people aged 45 and over in the UK have sought treatment for it (Arthritis Research UK, now Arthritis UK, 2013; cited by NICE CKS). It is often called the "wear and tear" type. The cartilage cushioning the joints breaks down over time.

As cartilage thins, bones start to rub. This causes pain, swelling and stiffness. The joints hit hardest are the knees, hips, hands, spine and feet.

Who is at risk

  • Being over 45
  • Being female
  • Carrying extra weight
  • Past joint injury
  • Repeat strain at work
  • Family history

Common symptoms

  • Morning stiffness that eases within 30 minutes
  • Pain that gets worse with activity
  • A grating or crackling feeling (crepitus)
  • Swelling around the joint
  • Slow loss of flexibility

There is no cure for OA. But symptoms can be managed well. Useful steps include weight loss, gentle exercise, physiotherapy and pain relief. In severe cases, joint replacement surgery can help.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

RA is an autoimmune disease. It affects about 400,000 people in the UK. The immune system attacks the joint lining. This causes long-term inflammation that can damage cartilage and bone.

RA often affects joints on both sides of the body. For example, both wrists or both knees. It can also affect the lungs, heart and eyes.

Symptoms to watch for

  • Morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Pain and swelling in the hands, wrists or feet
  • Tiredness and feeling unwell

Early diagnosis matters a lot. NICE guidelines say a GP should refer you to a rheumatologist within 3 working days if RA is suspected. Early treatment with drugs like methotrexate can stop lasting joint damage.

Psoriatic Arthritis (PsA)

PsA affects up to 30% of people with psoriasis. That is about 146,000 people in the UK. It causes joint pain, stiffness and swelling alongside skin patches.

PsA often hits the fingers and toes. This can cause swollen "sausage digits". It can also affect the spine and the spots where tendons join bone.

Other Types

  • Gout — affects about 1.6 million people. Caused by uric acid crystals, often in the big toe.
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — mainly the spine. Can cause inflammatory back pain and stiffening over time.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) — the main type in children. Around 15,000 under-16s in the UK.
  • Reactive arthritis — starts after an infection.
  • Fibromyalgia — not arthritis, but a related chronic pain condition. Affects an estimated 2.9 million UK adults.

Symptoms and Diagnosis

Most types of arthritis share a core set of symptoms:

  • Joint pain — from a dull ache to sharp pain
  • Stiffness — often after rest or in the morning
  • Swelling — from inflammation or fluid
  • Redness and warmth — around the joint
  • Less movement — harder to bend, grip or walk
  • Fatigue — common in RA and other inflammatory types
  • Crepitus — grinding, clicking or popping

How diagnosis works

Most people start with a GP visit. The GP may ask for blood tests. These can include CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies. X-rays are common too. MRI or ultrasound may be used in some cases.

Your GP can refer you to a rheumatologist. Many practices also let you see a physiotherapist first, without a GP referral, under the First Contact Practitioner scheme.

Treatment Options in the UK

Treatment depends on the type and how severe the arthritis is. Most plans mix three things: self-care, medication and (sometimes) surgery.

Conservative Management

  • Exercise — the most effective non-drug treatment. Try walking, swimming or cycling.
  • Weight management — losing just 5% of body weight can cut knee pain in OA.
  • Physiotherapy — guided exercises, hands-on therapy and electrotherapy.
  • Occupational therapy — joint protection, aids and home changes.
  • Diet — a Mediterranean-style diet can lower inflammation.

Medications

  • Paracetamol — first choice for mild OA pain
  • NSAIDs — such as ibuprofen or naproxen
  • Steroid injections — short-term relief for badly inflamed joints
  • DMARDs — such as methotrexate for RA and PsA
  • Biologics — such as adalimumab or etanercept for severe cases
  • JAK inhibitors — newer targeted drugs for RA

Surgical Options

  • Joint replacement — knee and hip replacements are very successful. Over 160,000 are done each year in the UK.
  • Arthroscopy — keyhole surgery for diagnosis or minor repairs.
  • Joint fusion — used for badly damaged small joints.

Living Well With Arthritis

Managing arthritis is about more than medicine. The best results come from a whole-person plan. This means activity, food, mental health support and community.

Seven habits that help

  • Stay active — aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week.
  • Eat well — a Mediterranean-style diet rich in oily fish, fruit, veg and whole grains.
  • Manage stress — try mindfulness, meditation or CBT.
  • Sleep well — aim for 7–9 hours. Poor sleep makes pain feel worse.
  • Pace yourself — mix activity with rest to avoid flare-ups.
  • Use aids — jar openers, long-handled reachers and walking aids can help a lot.
  • Connect with others — peer groups reduce isolation and improve coping.

Mental Health and Arthritis

Chronic pain wears people down. People with arthritis are 2–3 times more likely to have depression or anxiety (Arthritis Research UK). The link works both ways. Pain lowers mood, and low mood makes pain feel worse.

Where to get help

  • UK healthcare Talking Therapies (IAPT) — free talking therapy and CBT. Self-referral is available.
  • Pain management programmes — group programmes mixing physio, psychology and OT.
  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) helpline — 0800 5200 520 (free, weekdays).
  • Mind — 0300 123 3393 for general mental health support.

Arthritis in Younger People

Many people think arthritis only affects older adults. That is a myth.

About 15,000 children in the UK have juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Many adults in their 20s and 30s also develop types like RA, PsA or ankylosing spondylitis.

Young people with arthritis face extra challenges. These can include study, work, relationships and family planning. Charities like Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and NRAS offer tailored support.

Research and Future Treatments

UK arthritis research is moving fast. Key areas include:

  • Regenerative medicine — stem cell therapy to regrow cartilage
  • Precision medicine — using DNA to pick the best drug for each person
  • Digital health — apps, wearables and remote monitoring
  • New biologics — drugs that target inflammation more precisely
  • The gut microbiome — how gut bacteria affect autoimmune arthritis

Main UK funders include Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) (over £9 million a year), the NIHR and the Medical Research Council. Clinical trials are open via the NIHR Clinical Research Network.

Key UK Resources

  • Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) — arthritis-uk.org — helpline: 0800 5200 520
  • NRAS — nras.org.uk — helpline: 0800 298 7650
  • Health and social care (UK Government) — NHS services
  • Arthritis Action — arthritisaction.org.uk
  • Citizens Advice — help with benefits and PIP
  • Living With Arthritis — free virtual physio, diet plans and community support

Sources & Disclaimer

This guide draws on public data from the UK health service, NICE guidelines (NG100, NG226, CG79), Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis) and NRAS. It also uses peer-reviewed research from The Lancet, Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases and the BMJ. Figures are the most recent available as of 2024.

This page is for information only. It is not medical advice. Always speak to your GP or rheumatologist about your own care.
