/guides/understanding-pain:
Pain is the nervous system’s alarm. It can warn that tissue is injured or under threat, or it can keep sounding after the original problem has settled. It may feel sharp, dull, burning, tingling, stabbing or deep and hard to place. It can sit in one joint or spread across the body — and two people with the same condition can rate the same day completely differently.

Unrelieved pain does more than hurt. It can shrink social life, disturb sleep, sap mood and make work or caring feel impossible. Surveys of adults with ongoing pain often find the back, hips, knees and feet are common sites, with knock-on limits on daily tasks and more days off work than peers without chronic pain.

Chronic pain is especially common later in life and has been linked with higher health risks, but it is not only an older person’s problem — a sizeable share of younger adults also live with long-term pain. Speaking to your GP matters: for many people, pain is a daily companion, and a clear description of yours is one of the best diagnostic clues you can give.

Types of Pain

Clinicians often treat pain as a warning signal first — then ask what is driving it. Sorting the source helps you know when to protect a joint and when carefully graded movement is safer than complete rest.

Pain can be grouped by site, by inflammatory versus mechanical drivers, by whether it is focal or whole-body, by whether both sides are involved, by how severe or long-lasting it is (acute versus chronic), by fibromyalgia-type widespread sensitivity, or by nerve (neuropathic) damage. Whatever label fits best, naming the pattern is the first step toward the right treatment plan.

Inflammatory vs. Mechanical Pain

Inflammatory pain can mean heightened sensitivity after tissue injury, or pain from a disease process — often autoimmune — in which the immune system targets healthy tissue. Typical features include lasting longer than three months, heat and swelling, stiffness after rest, flare–remission cycles, and a deep gnawing or throbbing quality.

Conditions that can drive inflammatory patterns include:

  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Gout
  • Inflammatory bowel disease–related arthritis
  • Lyme disease
  • Lupus
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica
  • Psoriatic arthritis
  • Rheumatoid arthritis

Inflammatory flares can intensify without a clear lifestyle trigger — for example a sudden spike of heat, redness and swelling in gout, or an unexplained step-up in psoriatic arthritis pain.

Mechanical pain is often felt in the spine or weight-bearing joints and reflects stress on discs, ligaments, muscle or nerve. It tends to be acute or clearly linked to injury, load or degenerative change, may start suddenly, and does not always ease simply by keeping moving.

Examples linked with mechanical patterns include:

  • Degenerative disc disease
  • Spinal stenosis
  • Herniated disc
  • Fracture
  • Severe scoliosis
  • Osteoarthritis

Questions that help separate the two include how long pain has been present, family history of inflammatory arthritis, how it began, and whether mornings are worst.

Mechanical problems are often managed with relative rest (not total stillness), NSAIDs if suitable, heat or ice, and physiotherapy — you still need modified movement so joints do not seize and muscles do not waste. Inflammatory disease usually needs medicines that calm the underlying process (from NSAIDs and steroids to DMARDs, biologics or JAK inhibitors, as advised by your team). Even after inflammation settles, some people still feel chronic pain, so ongoing symptom plans still matter.

Focal vs. Systemic Pain

Focal pain is local — you can often point to it with one finger — and commonly follows trauma or a single injured structure. Systemic muscle or joint pain is widespread and may follow illness, infection or a medicine reaction. Most inflammatory rheumatic diseases sit in the systemic group, as do infections such as Lyme disease, COVID-19 or hepatitis.

A practical contrast: waking so stiff that the whole body takes two or three hours to loosen suggests a systemic pattern; waking with stiffness mainly in one knee sounds more focal.

Bilateral Pain

Bilateral means both sides of the body. Feeling pain left and right together can intensify symptoms and limit mobility; swelling and stiffness often travel with it. Bilateral patterns lean toward inflammatory illness more than a single-site mechanical injury — though osteoarthritis can sometimes affect matching joints on both sides.

Apart from osteoarthritis, many bilateral inflammatory conditions are autoimmune. Examples (with typical sites) include:

  • Fibromyalgia — tender points in many regions
  • Osteoarthritis — less often strictly bilateral; knees, hips, hands, feet
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica — shoulders, upper arms, neck, pelvis
  • Psoriatic arthritis — knees, ankles, hands, feet
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — hands, wrists, knees or hips

Finding the cause matters: untreated psoriatic arthritis, osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis can permanently damage joints.

Fibromyalgia Pain

Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition of widespread pain and heightened sensitivity. There is no cure yet, but medicines and non-drug approaches can ease symptoms. It can affect anyone and is more often diagnosed in women and people over 40. It frequently coexists with rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, osteoarthritis or ankylosing spondylitis.

Widespread aching, burning, throbbing or stabbing pain — often in the limbs, trunk, head and buttocks — is central. Other features can include fatigue, poor sleep, stiffness, tenderness, limb tingling, concentration problems, sensory sensitivity, and gut symptoms such as bloating or constipation.

Tender points (small, often symmetrical areas away from the joints that hurt with light pressure) are a classic feature. Common sites include the front of the lower neck, upper chest edge, near the elbow, the knee, the skull base, the hip bone, the upper outer buttock, and the back of the neck and shoulders.

Without support, symptoms can worsen and weigh heavily on mood. If you recognise widespread tender points, discuss them with your GP so you can get a clear diagnosis and a plan.

Acute vs. Chronic Pain

Acute pain arrives suddenly and usually settles within days to weeks — generally under three months. It can feel sharp, throb, tingle, burn or numb, is often intense, and usually has a clear trigger such as illness, injury or surgery. That protectiveness is useful: it flags that an area needs care.

Examples include fractures, muscle sprains or tears, post-operative pain, burns and cuts.

Chronic pain builds or persists over months or years. Intensity can wax and wane. People describe ache, burn or shooting sensations. It touches every part of daily life and is linked with higher rates of anxiety and depression.

Examples of how chronic disease pain may feel (everyone differs):

  • Ankylosing spondylitis — ongoing deep, dull back pain
  • Fibromyalgia — whole-body ache, muscle discomfort, twitching feelings
  • Inflammatory bowel disease — abdominal cramping, burning, stabbing or aching
  • Lower back pain — tingling, burning, dull, sharp or radiating
  • Osteoarthritis — swelling, tenderness, stiffness, grating sensations
  • Psoriatic arthritis — morning-worse, tender, throbbing joints
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — hand and foot tingling, joint stiffness and swelling

Pain lasting beyond three months should be reported — early treatment of some diseases can prevent irreversible joint damage.

Neuropathic Pain

Neuropathic pain comes from disease or damage in the nerves that carry touch, pressure and temperature. Roughly a quarter of people with chronic pain have a neuropathic component. Messages to the brain become distorted; the feeling is often less of a clean “cut” and more burning, tingling or electric.

Frequent drivers include:

  • Diabetes — high glucose injures nerves; burning or tingling often starts in the feet and can climb the legs, sometimes with later loss of feeling
  • Chemotherapy — some cancer treatments cause tingling, numbness or weakness in hands and feet that may ease after treatment ends
  • HIV — advanced disease can bring burning, stiffness or prickling in the toes or soles
  • Multiple sclerosis — from mild irritation to intense burning or sharp pain

Neuropathic pain from diabetes or HIV may not fully reverse, but treating the underlying condition can slow worsening. Ask your clinical team about options suited to your diagnosis.

Questions to Ask Your Doctor About Pain

How you describe pain shapes what your clinician hears and which treatments they consider. It is reasonable to ask how they decided you have joint, muscle or nerve pain — for example, “How can you tell which structure is involved?”

Other useful questions:

  • If the pain shoots or burns, could it be nerve-related?
  • When joints feel stiff or tender, which arthritis patterns should we consider?
  • What might a deep, throbbing ache point to?
  • Why has this lasted more than three months?
  • Why is morning pain worse?
  • What does pain that spreads from my back into my thighs or buttocks suggest?

Clear communication is often the shortest route to the right next test or treatment.

How do Yoga and Pilates compare?

Both yoga and Pilates can help arthritis, and for most people the better choice is simply the one you will keep doing. As a rough guide, yoga suits you if stiffness, balance and stress are your main problems, while Pilates suits you if you want to build core and hip strength for back, hip or knee pain. Either works best as a gentle, adapted class taught by someone who understands arthritis, and both can be done on a chair. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and yoga and Pilates are two good ways of doing it.

Updated 11 July 2026

Frequently asked questions

Last reviewed 11 July 2026

Both yoga and Pilates can help arthritis, and for most people the better choice is simply the one you will keep doing. As a rough guide, yoga suits you if stiffness, balance and stress are your main problems, while Pilates suits you if you want to build core and hip strength for back, hip or knee pain. Either works best as a gentle, adapted class taught by someone who understands arthritis, and both can be done on a chair. NICE recommends exercise as a core treatment for osteoarthritis, and yoga and Pilates are two good ways of doing it.

Yoga

  • How it works: Combines held postures, slow movement between positions, breathing and relaxation. It mainly improves flexibility, balance and body awareness, with some strengthening from holding positions.
  • Best for: Stiffness, reduced range of movement, balance worries, stress and poor sleep linked to pain. Gentle, chair or 'yoga for arthritis' classes suit beginners.
  • Common side-effects: Deep twists, deep knee bends, inversions and pushing into end-of-range stretches can irritate sore joints. People with a hip replacement, osteoporosis or rheumatoid arthritis affecting the neck need specific adaptations.
  • UK healthcare availability: Not usually prescribed directly, but some NHS physiotherapy, falls and social prescribing services link to local gentle yoga or chair yoga classes.
  • Typical UK cost: Community and leisure-centre classes are often cheaper than private studios; free online chair yoga sessions are widely available.

Pilates

  • How it works: Slow, controlled exercises focused on deep abdominal and back muscles, hip control, posture and breathing. Mat Pilates uses body weight; studio Pilates adds spring-based equipment.
  • Best for: Low back pain, hip and knee osteoarthritis where muscle control is weak, posture concerns and rebuilding confidence in movement. Clinical Pilates is often run by physiotherapists.
  • Common side-effects: Some classic mat exercises involve lying flat, rolling or repeated forward bending, which may not suit osteoporosis, a recent hip replacement or a painful back. Getting up and down from the floor can be a barrier.
  • UK healthcare availability: Some NHS and community physiotherapy services run Pilates-based exercise classes, especially for back pain. Private clinical Pilates is common.
  • Typical UK cost: Mat classes cost similar to yoga; one-to-one or equipment-based studio sessions cost considerably more.

The short answer

There is no strong evidence that one is better than the other for arthritis. Both are low-impact, can be scaled to your ability, and combine strength, flexibility and control. Research reviews suggest both can modestly improve pain and function in osteoarthritis and back pain, and that the benefit depends far more on doing it regularly than on which method you pick.

If you have never done either, try a beginners' class of each and ask yourself afterwards: did my joints feel better or worse the next day, did I enjoy it, and could I get to this class every week? Those three answers matter more than the label on the class.

How they differ in practice

Yoga tends to move you through a wider range of positions and spends more time on stretching, balance and relaxation. A typical gentle class includes standing balance work, seated or lying stretches and a calm ending. That makes it a good fit if you feel stiff and tense, or if worry about falling is creeping in.

Pilates tends to stay in smaller, more controlled movements and focuses on switching on the deep muscles around the trunk and hips before you move. That makes it a good fit if your back or hips feel unstable or weak, or if you have been told your knee pain is linked to weak hip and thigh muscles.

Many modern classes blend the two, and a good teacher of either will adapt the session to you.

By joint and condition

Knee osteoarthritis: both help, but avoid deep kneeling and deep squats. Use a cushion under the knees and keep bends within a comfortable range. Pilates-style hip and thigh strengthening is particularly useful.

Hip osteoarthritis or hip replacement: after a hip replacement, follow your surgical team's movement precautions, which often mean avoiding deep bending, crossing the legs and twisting on the operated leg for a period. Tell the teacher before the class. Pilates side-lying hip work is often a good fit once you are cleared.

Back pain and spinal arthritis: Pilates has the most research behind it for long-term low back pain, though yoga also helps. Avoid forcing deep forward bends or twists.

Rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis: gentle movement helps stiffness. If rheumatoid arthritis affects your neck, avoid putting weight through the head and neck, such as in headstands, shoulder stands or 'plough'. For ankylosing spondylitis, yoga and Pilates that work on posture and spinal extension are often encouraged by rheumatology physiotherapists.

Osteoporosis: avoid repeated or loaded forward bending and deep twisting of the spine, as in roll-ups and toe-touches. Ask for back-extension and balance work instead.

Making either one safe

Choose a beginners', gentle or arthritis-specific class, or chair-based yoga or Pilates if getting to the floor is hard. Tell the teacher about your arthritis, any joint replacements, osteoporosis and any recent flare. Move within a comfortable range: mild aching that settles within a day is normal, but sharp pain or pain that is worse the next day means you did too much, so do less next time rather than stop altogether.

During a flare, rest the inflamed joint from loaded exercise but keep the rest of your body gently moving. Return to classes gradually as the flare settles.

Check the teacher's training. Clinical Pilates and many yoga for health classes are run by physiotherapists or teachers with extra training in long-term conditions. You can also ask your GP or physiotherapist whether a local NHS, leisure-centre or charity class is available.

When to stop and get help

Stop and seek medical advice if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen, if you get new numbness or weakness, or if pain is severe and does not ease with rest. Call 999 for chest pain, sudden breathlessness or signs of a stroke. For a single hot, swollen joint with fever, get same-day help, as this can be a joint infection: call NHS 111 or go to A&E. For other worries, NHS 111 can advise.

At a glance

YogaPilates
Main focusFlexibility, balance, relaxationCore and hip strength, control, posture
Best forStiffness, balance, stressBack pain, weak hips and thighs
Chair-based optionYes, widely availableYes, less common
Watch out forDeep twists, inversions, kneelingRoll-ups and loaded forward bending
Evidence for arthritisModest benefit for pain and functionModest benefit, strongest for back pain
Typical costLow to moderate; free online sessionsModerate; one-to-one studio sessions cost more

Key takeaways

  • Both yoga and Pilates are safe, low-impact options for most people with arthritis.
  • Yoga leans towards flexibility and balance; Pilates leans towards core and hip strength.
  • The best choice is the one you enjoy and will do every week.
  • Tell the teacher about joint replacements, osteoporosis or neck involvement in rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Mild aching that settles within a day is normal; pain worse the next day means ease off, not give up.

Talk to your clinician

This is general information, not medical advice. Discuss Yoga and Pilates with your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist before starting, stopping or switching treatment.

/library/achilles-tendonitis:
Condition

Inflammation of the tendon connecting calf to heel

What is Achilles Tendonitis?

Achilles tendonitis (or tendinopathy) is inflammation or degeneration of the Achilles tendon — the large tendon at the back of the ankle that connects the calf muscles to the heel bone. It is one of the most common overuse injuries, particularly in runners and people who participate in sports involving jumping or sudden changes in direction.

Causes and Risk Factors

  • Overuse — a sudden increase in training intensity or volume
  • Tight or weak calf muscles
  • Flat feet or high arches
  • Running on hard or uneven surfaces
  • Inappropriate or worn-out footwear
  • Age — tendons become less flexible with age
  • Certain medications (fluoroquinolone antibiotics) can weaken tendons

Symptoms

  • Pain and stiffness along the Achilles tendon, especially in the morning
  • Pain that worsens with activity
  • Tenderness when touching the tendon
  • Swelling or thickening of the tendon
  • A crunching sensation when moving the ankle

Treatment

  • Rest from aggravating activity
  • Ice application
  • Eccentric heel drop exercises — the most evidence-based treatment
  • NSAIDs for pain and inflammation
  • Heel lifts in shoes to reduce tendon stress
  • Physiotherapy
  • Shockwave therapy for stubborn cases

Medical Disclaimer: If you suspect an Achilles tendon rupture (a sudden pop and inability to push off), seek emergency care immediately.

/library/adalimumab:
Medication

A biologic treatment for inflammatory conditions

What is Adalimumab?

Adalimumab (brand name Humira, and several biosimilars) is a biologic medication — a type of treatment made from biological sources. It belongs to a class of drugs called TNF (tumour necrosis factor) inhibitors, or anti-TNF agents. TNF is a protein produced by the immune system that promotes inflammation. In conditions like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and Crohn's disease, TNF is overproduced, driving harmful inflammation. Adalimumab works by blocking TNF, reducing inflammation and preventing joint and tissue damage.

What is it Used For?

  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Psoriatic arthritis
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Psoriasis
  • Crohn's disease
  • Ulcerative colitis
  • Uveitis (eye inflammation)
  • Hidradenitis suppurativa

How is it Given?

Adalimumab is given as a subcutaneous injection (under the skin), usually every two weeks. It comes as a pre-filled syringe or auto-injector pen for self-injection at home. Patients are trained by healthcare professionals on how to administer the injection safely.

Side Effects

  • Injection site reactions — redness, pain, or swelling
  • Increased risk of infections — particularly respiratory infections
  • Reactivation of latent tuberculosis (TB) — TB screening is required before starting
  • Rare: serious infections, certain cancers (especially lymphoma), heart failure

Monitoring

Regular blood tests and monitoring for signs of infection are essential. Live vaccinations should be avoided while on adalimumab. It should not be used in people with active infection, severe heart failure, or a history of certain cancers.

Medical Disclaimer: Adalimumab is a powerful medication requiring specialist oversight and regular monitoring.

/library/aps:
Condition

An autoimmune clotting disorder

What is APS?

Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), also known as Hughes syndrome, is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system produces antibodies (antiphospholipid antibodies) that attack normal proteins in the blood, making it prone to clotting. This can lead to blood clots in arteries and veins and is a significant cause of strokes, deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism, and pregnancy complications. APS affects women more than men and is often associated with lupus.

Symptoms and Complications

  • Blood clots — in the legs (DVT), lungs (pulmonary embolism), brain (stroke or TIA)
  • Recurrent miscarriages — APS is a leading treatable cause of recurrent pregnancy loss
  • Livedo reticularis — a mottled, net-like discolouration of the skin
  • Low platelet count (thrombocytopenia)
  • Headaches and migraines
  • Memory problems and cognitive difficulties
  • Heart valve problems

Diagnosis

APS is diagnosed when someone has had a clot or pregnancy complication AND tests positive for antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, or anti-beta2 glycoprotein-I antibodies) on at least two separate occasions, 12 weeks apart.

Treatment

  • Anticoagulation (blood thinning) — warfarin or newer anticoagulants (DOACs) to prevent clots
  • Low-dose aspirin — particularly for pregnancy-related APS
  • Hydroxychloroquine — to reduce antibody levels
  • Heparin injections during pregnancy to prevent miscarriage

Medical Disclaimer: APS requires specialist management. Blood-thinning medications need regular monitoring.

/library/aspirin:
Medication

A versatile medicine with many uses

What is Aspirin?

Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is one of the oldest and most widely used medications in the world. It belongs to the NSAID class and has three main effects: it relieves mild to moderate pain, reduces fever, and reduces inflammation. At low doses (75mg), it also has blood-thinning (antiplatelet) properties, which is why it is widely used to prevent heart attacks and strokes in people at risk.

Uses of Aspirin

  • Pain relief — headaches, toothache, period pain, muscle pain (300–900mg doses)
  • Fever reduction
  • Prevention of heart attacks and strokes — low-dose aspirin (75mg) prevents platelets from clumping together and forming clots
  • Treatment of acute heart attack — 300mg chewed immediately as first aid
  • Antiphospholipid syndrome
  • Kawasaki disease
  • Pre-eclampsia prevention in pregnancy (under medical supervision)

Who Should Not Take Aspirin?

  • Children under 16 (risk of Reye's syndrome)
  • People with stomach ulcers or bleeding disorders
  • Those with aspirin allergy or asthma triggered by NSAIDs
  • Pregnant women (except low-dose under medical supervision)

Side Effects

  • Stomach irritation and indigestion
  • Increased bleeding risk
  • Stomach ulcers with long-term use
  • Tinnitus at high doses

Medical Disclaimer: Do not give aspirin to children. Consult your doctor before taking aspirin regularly for heart disease prevention.

/library/bursitis:
Condition

Inflammation of the fluid-filled sacs around joints

What is Bursitis?

Bursitis is inflammation of the bursae — small, fluid-filled sacs that cushion bones, tendons, and muscles near the joints. Bursae reduce friction and allow smooth movement between tissues. When a bursa becomes inflamed, it causes pain and swelling near the affected joint. Bursitis most commonly occurs in the shoulder, elbow, hip, and knee.

Causes

  • Repetitive movements or prolonged pressure on a joint
  • Sudden injury or trauma
  • Rheumatoid arthritis or gout
  • Infection (septic bursitis)
  • Certain occupations (e.g. carpet laying, gardening)

Symptoms

  • Aching or stiffness in the affected joint
  • Swelling and redness
  • Pain that worsens with movement or pressure
  • Limited range of motion

Treatment

Most cases of bursitis improve within a few weeks with proper rest and treatment. Avoiding the activities that caused it helps prevent recurrence.

  • Rest the affected joint
  • Apply ice for 20 minutes several times a day
  • Anti-inflammatory medications (NSAIDs)
  • Physiotherapy exercises
  • Corticosteroid injections
  • Draining the bursa (aspiration) if severely swollen
  • Antibiotics for infected bursitis

Medical Disclaimer: See a doctor if you have severe pain, fever, or redness around a joint, as these may indicate infected bursitis.

/library/colchicine:
Medication

Fast-acting treatment for acute gout

What is Colchicine?

Colchicine is a medication derived from the autumn crocus plant (Colchicum autumnale). It has been used for centuries to treat gout. Today, it is one of the most effective and recommended treatments for acute gout attacks and is also used to prevent recurrent gout. It is sometimes also used for other conditions including familial Mediterranean fever and pericarditis (inflammation around the heart).

How Does it Work?

Colchicine works by reducing the inflammation caused by uric acid crystals in the joint. It interferes with the migration of white blood cells (neutrophils) to the inflamed joint, thereby reducing the inflammatory response and the pain and swelling of a gout attack.

How to Take it

For an acute gout attack, colchicine is most effective when taken within the first 12–24 hours of an attack starting. The usual dose is 500 micrograms 2–3 times daily. For prevention of recurrent attacks, a low dose is taken daily (usually 500 micrograms once or twice daily).

Side Effects

  • Diarrhoea — the most common side effect, often dose-related
  • Nausea and stomach cramps
  • Vomiting
  • In overdose, colchicine can be very dangerous — store safely away from children

Interactions

Colchicine can interact with several medications, including statins, clarithromycin, and ciclosporin, potentially increasing the risk of serious side effects. Always inform your doctor and pharmacist of all medications you take.

Medical Disclaimer: Take colchicine exactly as prescribed. Do not exceed the recommended dose. Seek urgent help if you have signs of toxicity.

/library/ginger:
Supplement

A natural remedy with anti-inflammatory properties

What is Ginger?

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) is a flowering plant whose root has been used for thousands of years as both a culinary spice and a medicinal herb. It is native to Southeast Asia and is widely used in traditional medicine systems including Ayurveda and Chinese medicine. Its main bioactive compound, gingerol, is responsible for most of its health benefits.

Health Benefits of Ginger

  • Anti-inflammatory — gingerol and shogaol have potent anti-inflammatory properties, which may benefit arthritis and other inflammatory conditions
  • Anti-nausea — very effective for nausea and vomiting, including morning sickness, motion sickness, and chemotherapy-induced nausea
  • Digestive aid — helps with indigestion, bloating, and stomach discomfort
  • Pain relief — some research suggests ginger may reduce muscle soreness and joint pain
  • Blood sugar control — may improve insulin sensitivity
  • Immune support — has antimicrobial and antioxidant properties

How to Use Ginger

  • Fresh ginger in cooking and smoothies
  • Ginger tea — steep fresh slices in hot water
  • Ginger supplements (capsules or extracts)
  • Dried ground ginger in recipes
  • Ginger ale (with real ginger content)

Is it Safe?

Ginger is generally safe when consumed in food amounts. High doses of ginger supplements may cause heartburn, diarrhoea, or stomach discomfort. People taking blood-thinning medications should consult their doctor before using ginger supplements, as it may increase bleeding risk.

Medical Disclaimer: Ginger is a food supplement, not a medicine. Do not stop prescribed treatments in favour of ginger.

/library/hip-pain:
Symptom

Causes, assessment, and management

Overview

Hip pain is a very common complaint that can affect people of all ages. The hip is one of the largest and most important weight-bearing joints in the body. Hip pain can originate from structures within the joint itself (intra-articular) or from surrounding muscles, tendons, and bursae (extra-articular). It can also be referred from the lower back or, less commonly, from the knee.

Common Causes

  • Osteoarthritis — the most common cause, especially in older adults
  • Hip bursitis — inflammation of the trochanteric bursa (outer hip)
  • Tendonitis — inflammation of hip tendons
  • Hip labral tear — damage to the cartilage lining the hip socket
  • Hip fracture — particularly in older adults with osteoporosis
  • Avascular necrosis — loss of blood supply to the femoral head
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Referred pain from the lower back (sciatica)
  • IT band syndrome

Symptoms Indicating the Source

  • Groin pain — usually from inside the joint itself
  • Outer hip pain — often bursitis or tendonitis
  • Buttock pain — may be from the sacroiliac joint or referred from the back
  • Pain worse on stairs, getting up from a chair, or walking — suggests hip arthritis

Treatment

  • Rest and activity modification
  • NSAIDs for pain and inflammation
  • Physiotherapy — strengthening hip and gluteal muscles
  • Weight loss — reduces load on the hip joint
  • Corticosteroid or local anaesthetic injections
  • Hip replacement surgery — for severe osteoarthritis

Medical Disclaimer: Sudden severe hip pain after a fall in an older person may indicate a fracture and requires emergency assessment.

/library/hypermobility:
Condition

When joints move beyond their normal range

What is Hypermobility?

Hypermobility means that joints can move beyond the normal range of motion. Many people have hypermobile joints ("being double-jointed") without any problems, and some sports people and dancers even benefit from it. However, for others, hypermobility is associated with pain, joint instability, and a range of other symptoms — a condition known as hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) or hypermobility spectrum disorder (HSD).

Why Does Hypermobility Cause Problems?

In people with symptomatic hypermobility, the connective tissue (which gives joints their stability) is more stretchy and lax than normal. This can lead to joints that are unstable, prone to sprains and dislocations, and surrounded by muscles that work harder to compensate — causing pain and fatigue.

Symptoms of Symptomatic Hypermobility

  • Widespread joint and muscle pain
  • Joint instability and frequent sprains or dislocations
  • Fatigue
  • Soft, stretchy skin
  • Digestive problems (IBS, acid reflux)
  • Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) — dizziness on standing
  • Anxiety and autonomic nervous system symptoms

Management

  • Physiotherapy — the most important treatment, focusing on strengthening muscles around unstable joints
  • Pain management — pacing, rest, and appropriate pain relief
  • Occupational therapy
  • Braces and supports for unstable joints
  • Proprioception training — to improve joint position sense

Medical Disclaimer: If you think you may have a hypermobility syndrome, seek assessment from a specialist.

/library/hypermobility-and:
Condition

Flexible joints and systemic symptoms

The Hypermobility Spectrum

Hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) and hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) are a continuum of conditions characterised by joint hypermobility (excessive range of movement), pain, and systemic symptoms. They are more common than previously recognised and are thought to affect 1 in 500 people, though many remain undiagnosed. The conditions predominantly affect women and often run in families.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (hEDS)

hEDS is the most common type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of inherited connective tissue disorders. In hEDS, the connective tissue that gives joints their structure is more elastic than normal, leading to widespread hypermobility, joint instability, and a range of systemic features. Diagnosis requires meeting specific clinical criteria including evidence of generalised hypermobility, symptoms of joint instability and pain, and systemic features.

Associated Conditions

HSD and hEDS are frequently associated with:

  • Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) — dizziness and rapid heart rate on standing
  • Mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS) — allergic-type reactions
  • Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and gut dysmotility
  • Anxiety and depression
  • Fatigue — often severe
  • Chronic pain

Management

There is no cure but symptoms can be managed effectively. Key approaches include physiotherapy (the most important treatment), pain management, cardiovascular support for POTS, pacing strategies for fatigue, occupational therapy, and psychological support. Referral to a specialist centre with experience in hypermobility disorders is beneficial for complex cases.

Medical Disclaimer: HSD and hEDS require specialist multidisciplinary management. Self-diagnosis should be confirmed by a medical professional.

/library/knee-support:
Treatment

Braces and supports for knee pain and instability

Types of Knee Supports

Knee supports range from simple elasticated sleeves to custom-made rigid braces. The right type depends on your condition and the level of support needed:

  • Compression sleeves — provide mild support and warmth; suitable for mild osteoarthritis, general knee aching, and swelling
  • Hinged knee braces — provide stability and limit range of motion; used after ligament injuries or surgery
  • Patellar tracking braces — help keep the kneecap in proper alignment; used for patellofemoral syndrome
  • Unloader (offloading) braces — shift weight away from the affected compartment; used for unicompartmental osteoarthritis
  • Custom orthopaedic braces — prescribed by a specialist and fitted individually for maximum support

Benefits of Knee Supports

  • Reduce pain during activity
  • Provide proprioceptive feedback (sense of joint position)
  • Reduce swelling through compression
  • Improve confidence and reduce fear of joint "giving way"
  • Allow continued activity during rehabilitation

Using a Knee Support Safely

  • Do not rely solely on a support — strengthening exercises remain essential
  • Ensure a proper fit — a poorly fitted support can worsen symptoms
  • Remove during sleep unless specifically advised otherwise
  • Check skin regularly for irritation or pressure sores

Where to Get a Knee Support

Knee supports are available from pharmacies, sports shops, and online. For complex knee conditions, ask for a physiotherapy referral for professional advice on the most appropriate support. Custom braces are available through UK healthcare orthotics departments or private providers.

Medical Disclaimer: Knee supports complement, not replace, treatment. Get a diagnosis first to ensure you choose the right type.

/library/lower-back-back:
Symptom

The most common cause of disability worldwide

Overview

Lower back pain affects up to 80% of people at some point in their lives and is the leading cause of disability worldwide. In most cases, it is not caused by a serious condition and improves with time and self-management. However, for some people it becomes chronic and significantly impacts quality of life.

Types of Lower Back Pain

  • Acute back pain — lasts less than 6 weeks, usually improves on its own
  • Subacute back pain — lasts 6–12 weeks
  • Chronic back pain — lasts more than 12 weeks
  • Specific back pain — caused by an identifiable condition (herniated disc, spinal stenosis, fracture)
  • Non-specific back pain — no clear structural cause (the most common type)

Common Causes

  • Muscle or ligament strain
  • Poor posture and sedentary behaviour
  • Herniated (slipped) disc
  • Spinal stenosis
  • Osteoarthritis of the spine
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Kidney problems (referred pain)

Treatment

  • Stay active — rest is not recommended; gentle movement helps
  • Pain relief — paracetamol, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants
  • Hot or cold packs
  • Physiotherapy and exercise
  • Psychological support — CBT for chronic pain
  • Epidural steroid injections for nerve pain
  • Surgery — rarely needed (only for specific structural causes)

Red Flags

See a doctor urgently if back pain is accompanied by bladder or bowel problems, weakness or numbness in the legs, unexplained weight loss, fever, or follows a significant injury.

Medical Disclaimer: Always seek medical advice if back pain is severe, persistent, or associated with red flag symptoms.

/library/musculoskeletal:
Condition

Looking after your bones, muscles, and joints

What is the Musculoskeletal System?

The musculoskeletal system includes all the bones, muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints in the body. Together, these structures support the body, enable movement, and protect organs. Musculoskeletal conditions are the leading cause of disability worldwide and include conditions such as arthritis, back pain, osteoporosis, fibromyalgia, and sports injuries.

Common Musculoskeletal Conditions

  • Arthritis (osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis)
  • Back pain and neck pain
  • Osteoporosis
  • Fibromyalgia
  • Tendonitis and bursitis
  • Sports injuries (sprains, strains, fractures)
  • Hypermobility disorders
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome

Protecting Musculoskeletal Health

  • Stay active — regular weight-bearing and strength exercise maintains bone density and muscle strength
  • Maintain a healthy weight — reduces stress on joints
  • Eat well — a diet rich in calcium, vitamin D, and protein supports bone and muscle health
  • Protect your joints — use correct technique during exercise and at work
  • Posture — good posture reduces strain on the spine and joints
  • Don't smoke — smoking weakens bones and reduces blood supply to tissues
  • Warm up and cool down — before and after exercise

When to See a Doctor

See your GP if you have persistent joint or muscle pain that interferes with daily activities, pain that is worsening, swelling, redness, or warmth around a joint, or if you have had a fall or injury. Early assessment and treatment can prevent long-term damage.

Medical Disclaimer: This is general guidance. See a healthcare professional for assessment of musculoskeletal symptoms.

/library/naproxen-500mg:
Medication

Prescription-strength anti-inflammatory dosage

What is Naproxen 500mg?

Naproxen 500mg is a prescription-strength dose of the NSAID naproxen. While lower doses (220–250mg) are available over the counter for mild pain and fever, the 500mg dose is typically prescribed by a doctor for more significant inflammatory conditions such as arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout, and moderate to severe musculoskeletal pain.

When is it Prescribed?

  • Rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis
  • Gout attacks
  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Bursitis and tendonitis
  • Post-surgical pain and inflammation
  • Severe menstrual pain
  • Acute musculoskeletal injuries

Dosage

The usual starting dose is 500mg twice daily (morning and evening), giving a total of 1,000mg per day. Some conditions may be treated with 500mg three times daily. The maximum daily dose on prescription is 1,500mg. Always take it with food or milk to reduce the risk of stomach upset.

Stomach Protection

Because naproxen 500mg is a higher dose taken regularly, your doctor will often prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) such as omeprazole alongside it to protect the stomach lining and reduce the risk of stomach ulcers.

Important Considerations

  • Do not combine with other NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin for pain)
  • Monitor blood pressure — NSAIDs can raise it
  • Use with caution in older adults and those with kidney or heart problems
  • Not suitable for people with active stomach ulcers

Medical Disclaimer: Naproxen 500mg is a prescription medicine. Only take as directed by your doctor.

/library/naproxen-side-effects:
Medication

What to watch for when taking naproxen

Overview

Naproxen is well-tolerated by many people, but like all NSAIDs, it can cause side effects. The risk of side effects increases with higher doses and longer duration of use. This guide covers the most important side effects to be aware of.

Common Side Effects (affect more than 1 in 100 people)

  • Indigestion and heartburn
  • Stomach pain or discomfort
  • Nausea
  • Constipation or diarrhoea
  • Headache
  • Dizziness
  • Drowsiness

Serious Side Effects (seek medical advice promptly)

  • Stomach ulcer — symptoms include persistent stomach pain, indigestion that doesn't improve, and loss of appetite
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding — dark, tarry, or bloody stools; vomiting blood (coffee-ground appearance) — seek emergency help immediately
  • Allergic reaction — rash, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, difficulty breathing — seek emergency help
  • Kidney problems — reduced urine output, swollen ankles, unusual tiredness
  • Liver problems — yellowing of skin or eyes (jaundice)
  • Heart attack or stroke symptoms — chest pain, sudden severe headache, facial drooping, arm weakness — call 999

How to Reduce Side Effect Risk

  • Always take with food or milk
  • Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time
  • Take a stomach-protecting medicine (PPI) if prescribed
  • Avoid alcohol
  • Stay hydrated
  • Inform your doctor of all other medications

Medical Disclaimer: Stop naproxen immediately and seek medical help if you experience serious side effects as described above.

/library/neck-pain:
Symptom

Understanding and managing cervical pain

Overview

Neck pain is one of the most common musculoskeletal problems and affects most people at some point in their lives. The neck (cervical spine) is made up of seven vertebrae (C1–C7) and is responsible for supporting the head and allowing a wide range of movement. This combination of mobility and the weight of the head makes the neck particularly susceptible to pain and injury.

Common Causes

  • Muscle strain — from poor posture, sleeping awkwardly, or prolonged sitting
  • Whiplash — from car accidents or sudden jerking movements
  • Cervical spondylosis — age-related wear and tear of the cervical discs and vertebrae
  • Herniated disc — a damaged disc pressing on a nerve
  • Cervical radiculopathy — nerve compression causing pain, numbness, or weakness radiating down the arm
  • Rheumatoid arthritis affecting the neck
  • Meningitis (rare but serious — stiff neck with fever requires urgent care)

Treatment

  • Pain relief — paracetamol or NSAIDs
  • Gentle movement — staying active and avoiding prolonged rest
  • Heat or ice therapy
  • Physiotherapy — exercises and manual therapy
  • Posture correction and ergonomic adjustments
  • TENS machine
  • Corticosteroid injections for nerve pain
  • Surgery — rarely needed

Prevention

  • Maintain good posture — especially when working at a computer
  • Take regular breaks from screens
  • Use a supportive pillow
  • Strengthen neck and upper back muscles
  • Avoid holding the phone between your shoulder and ear

Medical Disclaimer: Neck pain with fever, stiff neck, severe headache, or neurological symptoms (weakness, numbness) requires urgent medical assessment.

/library/pins-needles:
Symptom

Understanding paraesthesia in the hands

What Are Pins and Needles?

Pins and needles — medically known as paraesthesia — is a sensation of tingling, prickling, or numbness in the hands (or other body parts). Most people are familiar with the temporary "pins and needles" feeling after sitting in an awkward position that briefly cuts off blood supply or presses on a nerve. However, persistent or recurring pins and needles in the hands can indicate an underlying condition that needs assessment.

Common Causes

  • Carpal tunnel syndrome — the most common cause of pins and needles in the hands
  • Cervical radiculopathy — a pinched nerve in the neck
  • Cubital tunnel syndrome — ulnar nerve compression at the elbow
  • Peripheral neuropathy — nerve damage, often from diabetes
  • Raynaud's phenomenon
  • Vitamin B12 deficiency
  • Thoracic outlet syndrome
  • Multiple sclerosis (rarely)

Which Fingers Are Affected?

The pattern of pins and needles can help identify the cause:

  • Thumb, index, middle, and half of ring finger — carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve)
  • Ring and little finger — cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve)
  • Whole hand — cervical radiculopathy or peripheral neuropathy

When to See a Doctor

See your GP if pins and needles in the hands are persistent, progressive, associated with weakness or loss of grip, or accompanied by other symptoms such as neck pain, visual changes, or balance problems.

Medical Disclaimer: Sudden onset of pins and needles with weakness on one side of the body may indicate a stroke — call 999 immediately.

/library/psoriatic-arthritis:
Condition

Arthritis linked to the skin condition psoriasis

What is Psoriatic Arthritis?

Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) is a type of inflammatory arthritis that affects some people who have psoriasis — a chronic skin condition causing red, scaly patches. PsA causes joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, and can affect any joint in the body. It can also affect the spine (psoriatic spondylitis), fingernails and toenails (nail psoriasis), and cause a sausage-like swelling of entire fingers or toes (dactylitis).

About 20–30% of people with psoriasis develop psoriatic arthritis. It affects men and women equally and most commonly develops between the ages of 30 and 50.

Symptoms

  • Joint pain and swelling
  • Morning stiffness
  • Dactylitis — swollen, sausage-shaped fingers or toes
  • Nail changes — pitting, thickening, or separation from the nail bed
  • Enthesitis — pain at tendon and ligament attachment sites
  • Back pain and stiffness (in spinal involvement)
  • Fatigue

Treatment

  • NSAIDs — for mild symptoms
  • DMARDs — methotrexate, sulfasalazine, leflunomide
  • Biologics — TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept), IL-12/23, IL-17 inhibitors
  • JAK inhibitors — newer targeted treatments
  • Physiotherapy and exercise
  • Skin treatments for psoriasis

Medical Disclaimer: PsA requires specialist care. Early treatment can prevent joint damage.

/library/scleroderma:
Condition

A rare autoimmune condition affecting the skin and organs

What is Scleroderma?

Scleroderma (also known as systemic sclerosis) is a rare, chronic autoimmune condition in which the immune system triggers an overproduction of collagen, causing skin and connective tissues to harden and tighten. The name comes from the Greek words for hard (sclero) and skin (derma). Scleroderma can range from a mild condition affecting only the skin to a severe systemic disease involving the lungs, kidneys, heart, and digestive system.

Types

  • Limited cutaneous scleroderma (lcSSc) — skin thickening limited to the hands, face, and lower arms; associated with CREST syndrome (Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia)
  • Diffuse cutaneous scleroderma (dcSSc) — more widespread skin involvement and higher risk of organ involvement
  • Localised scleroderma (morphoea) — affects only the skin, not internal organs

Symptoms

  • Skin thickening, hardening, and tightening
  • Raynaud's phenomenon — almost universal in scleroderma
  • Puffy or swollen hands and fingers
  • Difficulty swallowing (oesophageal involvement)
  • Heartburn and reflux
  • Joint pain and stiffness
  • Lung fibrosis or pulmonary hypertension
  • Telangiectasia — small red spots from dilated blood vessels

Treatment

There is no cure for scleroderma. Treatment focuses on managing specific symptoms and preventing organ damage. This may include medications for Raynaud's, immunosuppressants for skin and lung disease, proton pump inhibitors for reflux, and specialist management for pulmonary hypertension or kidney crisis.

Medical Disclaimer: Scleroderma requires specialist care from a rheumatologist with experience in connective tissue diseases.

/library/selenium:
Supplement

An essential trace mineral for immune and thyroid health

What is Selenium?

Selenium is an essential trace mineral that the body needs in small amounts to function properly. It is found naturally in soil and enters the food chain through plants and animals. Selenium plays a critical role in antioxidant defence, thyroid hormone metabolism, immune function, and DNA synthesis.

Health Benefits

  • Antioxidant protection — selenium is a component of glutathione peroxidase, one of the body's most powerful antioxidant enzymes
  • Thyroid health — essential for thyroid hormone production and metabolism; deficiency can contribute to thyroid problems
  • Immune function — supports the immune response and may help protect against certain infections
  • Anti-inflammatory — some research suggests selenium may help reduce inflammation in conditions like rheumatoid arthritis
  • Cancer prevention — population studies suggest adequate selenium levels may lower cancer risk
  • Reproductive health — important for male fertility

Dietary Sources

  • Brazil nuts — the richest source (just 1–2 per day provides the daily requirement)
  • Fish and shellfish (tuna, sardines, oysters)
  • Meat and poultry
  • Eggs
  • Dairy products
  • Wholegrains (selenium content depends on soil levels)

Deficiency and Toxicity

Selenium deficiency is rare in the UK but can occur in people with malabsorption conditions. Symptoms include fatigue, hair loss, and weakened immunity. Too much selenium (selenium toxicity or selenosis) from high-dose supplements can cause nausea, hair loss, nail brittleness, and neurological problems. Do not exceed the recommended daily intake from supplements (400 micrograms/day for adults).

Medical Disclaimer: More selenium is not always better. Stick to recommended doses and consult your doctor before supplementing.

/library/shoulder-exercises:
Treatment

Strengthening and rehabilitating the shoulder

Why Exercise the Shoulder?

Exercise is one of the most important treatments for shoulder problems including rotator cuff injuries, frozen shoulder, impingement syndrome, bursitis, and shoulder arthritis. Strengthening the muscles around the shoulder joint improves stability, reduces pain, and helps restore normal movement. Physiotherapy-guided exercises are the cornerstone of shoulder rehabilitation.

Key Muscle Groups to Target

  • Rotator cuff muscles — supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis
  • Deltoid — the main shoulder muscle
  • Trapezius and rhomboids — upper back muscles that support shoulder blade movement
  • Serratus anterior — stabilises the shoulder blade

Effective Shoulder Exercises

  • Pendulum exercises — let the arm hang and make small circular movements; helps in frozen shoulder
  • External rotation — with an elastic band, rotate the arm outwards; strengthens the rotator cuff
  • Shoulder press — using light weights, press overhead; builds deltoid strength
  • Rows — pull a resistance band or cable towards you; strengthens upper back and rear shoulder
  • Wall slides — slide arms up a wall while maintaining contact; improves shoulder blade mechanics
  • Doorway stretch — stretches the chest and anterior shoulder to improve posture

Safety Tips

  • Always warm up before exercising
  • Start gently and progress gradually
  • Stop any exercise that causes significant pain
  • Seek guidance from a physiotherapist for personalised advice

Medical Disclaimer: Always get a proper diagnosis before starting a shoulder exercise programme. A physiotherapist can tailor exercises to your specific condition.

/library/sore-bottom-back:
Symptom

Pain in the lower lumbar and sacral region

Overview

Pain at the very bottom of the back — in the lower lumbar and sacral region — is extremely common and can have a wide range of causes. The area includes the lowest vertebrae (L4, L5), the sacrum (the triangular bone at the base of the spine), and the sacroiliac joints (where the spine meets the pelvis). Pain here can radiate to the buttocks, hips, and down the legs.

Common Causes

  • Sacroiliac joint dysfunction — a common and often overlooked cause of low back and buttock pain
  • Lumbar disc herniation — a slipped disc pressing on the sciatic nerve (sciatica)
  • Lumbar spondylosis — age-related wear and tear of the lower spine
  • Piriformis syndrome — the piriformis muscle irritating the sciatic nerve in the buttock
  • Coccydynia — pain in the tailbone (coccyx), often after injury or prolonged sitting
  • Ankylosing spondylitis — inflammatory arthritis affecting the sacroiliac joints
  • Gluteal muscle tightness or strain

Treatment

  • Physiotherapy — targeted exercises for the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joint
  • Massage therapy
  • Anti-inflammatory medications
  • Heat and ice therapy
  • Posture and ergonomic advice
  • Sacroiliac joint injections if conservative measures fail

Posture Tips

Sitting for prolonged periods is a major aggravating factor. Take regular breaks from sitting, use a lumbar support cushion, and try to maintain a neutral spine position. Strengthening the core and gluteal muscles reduces strain on the lower back.

Medical Disclaimer: Pain in the lower back with bladder or bowel changes, or weakness in the legs, requires urgent medical evaluation.

/library/tens-machine:
Treatment

Electrical pain relief at home

What is a TENS Machine?

TENS stands for Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation. A TENS machine is a small, battery-operated device that delivers low-voltage electrical impulses through electrodes (sticky pads) placed on the skin near the area of pain. It is a non-invasive, drug-free method of pain relief that can be used at home.

How Does it Work?

There are two main theories about how TENS works:

  • Gate control theory — the electrical impulses interfere with pain signals travelling to the brain, effectively "closing the gate" on pain perception
  • Endorphin release — the electrical stimulation triggers the release of the body's natural painkillers (endorphins and enkephalins)

What is it Used For?

  • Arthritis pain
  • Back pain
  • Knee pain
  • Sports injuries
  • Period pain
  • Labour pain during childbirth
  • Fibromyalgia
  • Endometriosis

How to Use a TENS Machine

Place the electrodes on clean, dry skin near the area of pain (not on broken skin, over the spine, or near the heart). Start at a low intensity and gradually increase until you feel a strong but comfortable tingling sensation. Sessions typically last 20–40 minutes. The device can be used multiple times a day.

Is it Safe?

TENS is generally safe for most people. However, it should not be used by people with pacemakers, epilepsy, or during pregnancy (except under medical supervision for labour pain). Always follow the manufacturer's instructions.

Medical Disclaimer: Consult your doctor before using a TENS machine, especially if you have any underlying medical conditions.

Arthritis affects 10 million people in the UK. Experiences vary by condition and person, but many people continue meaningful activities with the right treatment, movement, pacing and practical support. This evidence-based guide covers what arthritis is, how symptoms may affect daily life, and questions to discuss with a healthcare professional.

What is arthritis?

Arthritis is inflammation of one or more joints. It affects the cartilage (the smooth tissue that covers the ends of bones), causing pain, stiffness and reduced mobility. More than 100 types exist, but osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis are the most common.

Key facts:

  • 10 million people in the UK have arthritis
  • It can affect people at any age, not just older adults
  • Early management can slow progression and reduce symptoms
  • Many people live well with arthritis using the right strategies
  • Arthritis is not a single disease but a group of conditions

Types of arthritis

Osteoarthritis (OA)

The most common type, affecting around 8 million people in the UK. Osteoarthritis is caused by wear and tear of cartilage over time. It typically affects the knees, hips, hands and spine. Symptoms develop gradually and worsen with activity. Read our osteoarthritis guide.

Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA)

An autoimmune condition where the body's own immune system mistakenly attacks the joints. This causes swelling, pain and often fatigue. RA can develop rapidly and may affect your whole body, not just the joints. Read our rheumatoid arthritis guide.

Juvenile Arthritis (JA)

Arthritis affecting children under 16. Despite the name, juvenile arthritis can persist into adulthood. Early diagnosis and treatment are crucial. Read our juvenile arthritis guide.

Other types

Psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, gout, lupus, and many others. Each type requires tailored management. If you think you have arthritis, see your GP for diagnosis.

Symptoms & diagnosis

Arthritis symptoms vary depending on the type and which joints are affected. However, some symptoms are common across most types:

  • Joint pain and stiffness (especially in the morning)
  • Swelling, redness and warmth around affected joints
  • Reduced range of motion and difficulty moving
  • Fatigue and general tiredness
  • Low mood and anxiety (often from chronic pain)
  • Sleep disturbance

When to see your GP: If you have joint pain, stiffness or swelling lasting more than 2 weeks, contact your GP. Early diagnosis is crucial for effective management and preventing joint damage.

Management strategies

Living well with arthritis requires a multi-pronged approach. No single strategy works for everyone, so it's about finding what works for you.

Medical management

  • Medications (painkillers, anti-inflammatories, DMARDs)
  • Injections (corticosteroids, biologics)
  • Regular monitoring with your GP or rheumatologist

Exercise & movement

  • Gentle range-of-motion exercises to maintain flexibility
  • Strengthening routines to support joints
  • Walking and low-impact activities like swimming
  • Physiotherapy guidance tailored to your needs

Lifestyle changes

  • Weight management (reduces joint stress)
  • Heat and cold therapy for pain relief
  • Sleep optimisation (good sleep helps inflammation)
  • Stress reduction techniques

Exercise & movement

Exercise is one of the most powerful tools for managing arthritis. Regular movement reduces pain, improves mobility, strengthens muscles around joints and boosts mood.

Read our complete guide to arthritis exercises →

Key principles:

  • Start gently and progress gradually
  • Warm up before exercise (5 minutes of gentle movement)
  • Do low-impact activities (walking, swimming, cycling)
  • Include strength training 2-3 times per week
  • Include flexibility and stretching work daily
  • Rest when needed (rest is part of good management)
  • Stop if you have sharp pain (mild discomfort is OK)

Diet & nutrition

What you eat can influence arthritis symptoms. Some foods reduce inflammation; others may trigger flares. While diet alone can't cure arthritis, it plays an important role in managing symptoms.

Read our Mediterranean diet guide →

Foods to include:

  • Fatty fish (omega-3s: salmon, mackerel, sardines, herring)
  • Olive oil (contains anti-inflammatory compounds)
  • Colourful vegetables (antioxidants reduce inflammation)
  • Fruits, especially berries (high in antioxidants)
  • Nuts, seeds and legumes
  • Whole grains (fibre reduces inflammation)

Mental health & emotional wellbeing

Living with chronic arthritis affects not just the body but also mental health. Persistent pain, fatigue and lifestyle limitations can lead to depression, anxiety and isolation. These feelings are normal and treatable.

Read our mental health FAQ →

  • Talk to your GP about mood changes
  • Consider counselling or CBT (proven effective for chronic pain)
  • Join support groups
  • Practise stress-reduction techniques (meditation, mindfulness)
  • Maintain social connections
  • Set realistic goals and celebrate small wins

Work & employment rights

Many people with arthritis continue to work and have fulfilling careers. The Equality Act 2010 protects disabled workers in the UK, including those with arthritis.

Read our employment rights FAQ →

Your legal rights:

  • Right to reasonable adjustments (flexible hours, ergonomic equipment)
  • Protection from discrimination
  • Right to request flexible working (if eligible)
  • Access to occupational health support

Benefits & financial support

If arthritis affects your ability to work or care for yourself, you may be eligible for government benefits.

Read our PIP & benefits guide →

  • Personal Independence Payment (PIP) — ages 16-64
  • Employment Support Allowance (ESA) — if unable to work
  • Attendance Allowance — for those 65+
  • Disability Living Allowance (DLA) — under 16

Living Well with Arthritis: Practical Strategies for Independence

Living well with arthritis is about working with your joints rather than against them. The strategies that make the biggest day-to-day difference combine gentle, consistent movement, joint-protection techniques, an anti-inflammatory eating pattern, good sleep, and the right supportive equipment. Many people find that small adaptations — a kettle tipper, a long-handled shoehorn, a raised toilet seat — make the difference between struggling and staying independent.

An occupational therapy assessment is often the single most valuable step: a clinician will review your home, your routines and your goals, then recommend specific equipment, adaptations and pacing strategies tailored to your needs.

Essential Adaptive Equipment

  • Kitchen tools: ergonomic utensils, jar openers, kettle tippers, reachers and lightweight pans
  • Clothing aids: magnetic buttons, Velcro closures, long-handled shoehorns, dressing sticks
  • Home safety: grab rails, shower seats, raised toilet seats, stairlifts and walk-in showers
  • Fitness: chair yoga and aquatic therapy classes — see our exercise hub
  • Furniture: lift-assist recliners, supportive mattresses and ergonomic seating

For nutrition strategy see our diet hub and foods to avoid with arthritis.

Educational information only — we don't endorse specific brands or products. An occupational therapy assessment is the best starting point.

Frequently asked questions

Can arthritis be cured?

Most types of arthritis cannot be cured, but symptoms can be effectively managed with the right combination of treatment and lifestyle changes.

Is arthritis only for older people?

No. Arthritis can affect people of any age, including children with juvenile arthritis.

Can exercise make arthritis worse?

Suitable activity often helps maintain strength and function, but the type and amount should match your condition and general health. Start gradually and ask a physiotherapist or other qualified professional for individual advice.

Can I have a normal life with arthritis?

Yes. Many people with arthritis work, exercise, travel and pursue hobbies.

/myths/does-cracking-knuckles-cause-arth:
Myth-busting · Evidence-based · UK

Short answer: no. A plain-English look at what the research actually shows — for knuckles, toes, backs and necks — plus what to do if you crack out of habit.

What causes arthritis

The short answer

Cracking your knuckles or toes does not cause arthritis. Multiple studies — including X-ray comparisons of crackers and non-crackers — have looked for a link and found none. The pop you hear is a small gas bubble forming inside the joint's lubricating fluid, not anything tearing or wearing down.

The myth has stuck around for almost a century, but the research is now consistent and clear.

What's that pop?

What's actually happening when a joint cracks

Every joint in your body is wrapped in a capsule filled with a thick, slippery liquid called synovial fluid. The fluid contains dissolved gases — mostly carbon dioxide, oxygen and nitrogen — kept in solution by the pressure inside the joint.

When you stretch the joint (by pulling on a finger or curling your toes), the capsule expands and pressure inside it drops sharply. The dissolved gas can no longer stay dissolved, so a small bubble suddenly forms. That's the pop. The process is called tribonucleation, and it was filmed for the first time in a 2015 real-time MRI study by Kawchuk and colleagues.

The bubble takes around 20 minutes to dissolve back into the fluid — which is why you usually can't crack the same knuckle twice in quick succession. No cartilage, ligament or bone is being damaged in the process.

The evidence

What the research actually shows

Four studies, three decades, one consistent finding.

Castellanos & Axelrod, 1990

300 adults aged 45+ surveyed in a Los Angeles outpatient clinic. Habitual knuckle crackers were no more likely to have hand osteoarthritis than non-crackers — but they were more likely to report hand swelling and reduced grip strength.

Deweber, Olszewski & Ortolano, 2011

215 people aged 50–89 had hand X-rays compared with their cracking history. Rates of arthritis were almost identical: 18.1% in crackers vs 21.5% in non-crackers. No association.

Kawchuk et al., 2015 (PLOS ONE)

Real-time MRI captured the actual 'pop' for the first time. The sound is a gas cavity rapidly forming inside synovial fluid — a process called tribonucleation. No tissue is being damaged.

Boutin et al., 2017 (radiology cohort)

40 adults imaged with ultrasound before and after knuckle cracking. No acute joint damage detected and no link to long-term arthritis risk.

Even Dr Donald Unger — who cracked the knuckles of one hand only for 60 years and published his self-experiment in Arthritis & Rheumatism in 1998 — found no difference in arthritis between his two hands. The work earned him a 2009 Ig Nobel Prize in Medicine.

What about cracking your toes?

Toe cracking has been studied much less than knuckle cracking, but the joint anatomy and the gas-bubble mechanism are identical. There is no evidence that cracking your toes causes arthritis, and no plausible biological reason it would.

One nuance worth flagging: if your big toe feels stiff or sore when it cracks, that can be an early sign of hallux rigidus — a form of osteoarthritis at the base of the big toe — or a developing bunion. The cracking didn't cause it; the underlying joint change is what makes the toe more likely to click. If pain or stiffness is involved, it's worth seeing a GP or podiatrist.

What cracking can — and cannot — cause

The honest version, with no scaremongering and no false reassurance.

What it can (mildly) cause

  • A small reduction in grip strength in lifelong, very frequent crackers (one older study only)
  • Mild soft-tissue swelling around the knuckles in heavy habitual crackers
  • Occasional, brief discomfort if you crack a joint already inflamed by injury or arthritis

What it does not cause

  • Osteoarthritis of the hands or fingers
  • Rheumatoid arthritis or any other autoimmune arthritis
  • Permanently enlarged knuckles or 'big knuckles'
  • Bunions, hallux rigidus or any structural foot deformity

When cracking is a red flag

The cracking sound itself is harmless. But if it is paired with any of the following, see a GP — these are signs of a joint problem that existed before the cracking and that needs proper assessment:

  • Pain when the joint cracks (not just the sound)
  • Visible swelling, warmth or redness around the joint
  • A joint that locks, gives way or won't fully straighten
  • Morning joint stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes
  • Cracking that is new, asymmetrical, or paired with weight loss or fever

Read more in our guide to osteoarthritis symptoms and our page on arthritis flare-ups.

What actually causes arthritis

The real risk factors — none of which are joint cracking.

Age

Cartilage gradually thins after about 50. The single biggest risk factor for osteoarthritis.

Genetics

Family history strongly predicts hand and knee osteoarthritis, and most autoimmune arthritis.

Previous joint injury

A serious knee, hip or wrist injury raises later osteoarthritis risk in that joint by 3–6×.

Excess body weight

Every extra kilogram adds roughly 4 kg of load through the knees and increases low-grade inflammation.

Repetitive occupational load

Decades of heavy lifting, kneeling or vibration tools raise risk in the loaded joints.

Autoimmune drivers

Rheumatoid, psoriatic and other inflammatory arthritis are immune-system conditions, not wear-and-tear.

Healthier alternatives

What to do instead if you crack out of habit

You don't have to stop. But if you want to, these four work better than willpower.

Gentle hand mobility (60 seconds)

Make a loose fist, then fan the fingers wide. Repeat 10 times. Roll the wrists slowly in both directions. Most of the 'need to crack' urge fades after one round.

Squeeze and release

A soft stress ball or a rolled-up sock works. Squeeze for 3 seconds, release for 3 seconds, 10 times. Builds grip strength — the one thing chronic cracking may slightly reduce.

Warm water soak

If joints feel stiff in the morning, a 5-minute warm hand soak loosens them more effectively (and more safely) than cracking.

Treat the underlying habit

Cracking is often a stress or boredom tic. A fidget ring, worry beads or a 30-second breathing pause replaces the loop without harming the joint.

Common questions

Does cracking your knuckles give you big knuckles?

No. The 1990 Castellanos study found a small association with mild soft-tissue swelling in lifelong heavy crackers, but no change in the underlying bone or cartilage. Knuckle size is set by your bone structure, not your habits.

Why do my joints crack more as I get older?

Cartilage naturally thins with age and tendons lose a little elasticity, so joint surfaces glide with slightly more friction. The clicks and pops you notice are usually harmless. Only see a GP if the cracking comes with pain, swelling or stiffness.

Is it bad to crack your back or neck?

The same gas-bubble mechanism applies. Self-cracking now and then is generally fine. Repeated, forceful neck twisting is best avoided because of the (very small) risk to the vertebral arteries — see a physio or chiropractor if your back or neck regularly feels like it 'needs' cracking.

Can children safely crack their knuckles?

Yes. There is no evidence that knuckle cracking damages a child's joints or causes arthritis later in life. If a child cracks knuckles compulsively, treat it as a habit to redirect rather than a medical concern.

Does cracking your toes cause bunions?

No. Bunions and hallux rigidus are caused by genetics, foot mechanics and footwear — not by cracking. If toe cracking is paired with stiffness in the big toe, that points to early hallux rigidus, which existed before you started cracking.

Should I stop cracking my knuckles anyway?

Only if you want to. The arthritis fear is unfounded. The one mild downside found in older research — slightly reduced grip strength in chronic crackers — is easily offset by the gentle hand mobility and squeeze-release routine in this guide.

/pets/arthritis-in-cats:
All pet guidesCats

Up to 90% of cats over 12 have arthritic changes on X-ray, yet most are never diagnosed — cats mask pain superbly. Here's how to spot it and what genuinely helps.

Cats rarely limp — they simply stop doing things that hurt.

Important: Never give your cat human painkillers. Paracetamol is extremely toxic to cats — a single tablet can be fatal. Only use medication prescribed by your vet.

Why cat arthritis goes unnoticed

Cats don't limp the way dogs do — they modify behaviour instead. A cat with sore joints jumps less, climbs less, grooms less (look for a scurfy or matted coat over the back and hips), sleeps more, and may start missing the litter tray because climbing in hurts. Owners often put this down to 'just ageing'. It's usually pain, and it's treatable.

Hesitating before jumps is one of the clearest arthritis signs in cats.

The five-question home check

Ask yourself monthly: Does my cat still jump to its favourite high spot? Use stairs freely? Groom its whole body? Play, even briefly? Get in and out of the litter tray easily? Two or more 'no' answers deserve a vet visit.

Grooming changes and grumpiness when touched can signal joint pain.

Treatment options for cats

Weight management matters just as much as in dogs. Vet options include cat-licensed NSAIDs (meloxicam oral suspension is widely used long-term at low dose with monitoring) and Solensia — the feline equivalent of Librela, a monthly antibody injection licensed in the UK. Joint supplements formulated for cats can help as part of the plan.

Make your home arthritis-friendly

Provide steps or a ramp to favourite perches, a low-sided litter tray (a large storage box with a cut-down entrance works), soft warm bedding away from draughts, food and water at floor level in easy reach, and gentle daily grooming help for areas your cat can no longer reach.

All pet guidesDogs

Around 80% of dogs over 8 show signs of arthritis. Learn the early warning signs, what your vet can offer (from supplements to Librela), and simple home changes that make a big difference.

Long-backed and large breeds are at higher risk of joint problems.

Important: Never give your dog human painkillers. Paracetamol and ibuprofen are toxic to dogs and can be fatal. Only use medication prescribed by your vet.

Early signs owners miss

Dogs hide pain well. Look for: slowing on walks, hesitating at stairs or the car boot, stiffness after rest that eases with movement, licking one joint, reluctance to jump on the sofa, and irritability when touched. Limping is a late sign — by the time a dog visibly limps, arthritis is usually well established.

Little-and-often walks beat one long weekend hike for arthritic joints.

Weight is treatment number one

Every excess kilogram multiplies load through your dog's joints. In overweight arthritic dogs, weight loss alone can reduce lameness as much as medication. Ask your vet for your dog's body condition score (BCS) and a target weight; feed to that target, not the bowl.

Your vet can grade arthritis and build a stepped treatment plan.

What your vet can offer

A stepped plan usually starts with weight and exercise adjustment plus a quality joint supplement (glucosamine, chondroitin, green-lipped mussel, omega-3). If signs persist, prescription options include dog-specific NSAIDs (meloxicam, carprofen) and Librela — a monthly antibody injection licensed in the UK that many owners report transforms mobility. Physiotherapy and hydrotherapy are increasingly available for dogs too.

Home adaptations that help today

Non-slip runners on hard floors, a ramp for the car or sofa, a warm orthopaedic bed away from draughts, raised food and water bowls for large breeds, and keeping nails short all reduce daily joint strain. Little-and-often exercise (three 15-minute walks beats one 45-minute hike) keeps joints moving without overload.

/pets/arthritis-in-horses:
All pet guidesHorses

Degenerative joint disease is the leading cause of early retirement in UK horses. Early management — footcare, surfaces, warm-up and vet support — keeps horses comfortable for years longer.

Consistent turnout keeps joints moving — box rest stiffens arthritic horses.

Important: Always work with your vet and farrier as a team. Never medicate a horse with drugs prescribed for another animal, and be aware of competition withdrawal times for anti-inflammatories.

Spotting it early

Early equine arthritis shows as stiffness that improves with work ('warming out of it'), shortened stride, reluctance on one rein, bunny-hopping into canter, fidgeting for the farrier, or heat and mild filling around a joint after work. Hocks, coffin joints and fetlocks are most commonly affected.

A long, progressive walk warm-up is the cheapest joint treatment there is.

Management fundamentals

Maximise turnout — movement is medicine and standing in a stable stiffens arthritic joints. Keep weight down (obesity is as damaging in horses as in dogs). Warm up in walk for at least 10-15 minutes before any work. Work on consistent, well-maintained surfaces and avoid repetitive small circles on the affected rein. Keep a regular farriery cycle: balanced feet directly reduce joint strain.

Balanced, regular farriery directly reduces abnormal joint loading.

Veterinary options

Your vet may suggest oral joint supplements, prescription anti-inflammatories (phenylbutazone 'bute' remains widely used), intra-articular injections (corticosteroid, hyaluronic acid, or biologics like IRAP/arthramid), and in some cases Cartrophen courses. Many arthritic horses stay in ridden work for years with a well-managed programme.

Know when to adjust the job

Arthritis is progressive but manageable. Stepping down from jumping to flatwork, or from competition to hacking, often gives a horse many more happy, comfortable years. Retirement to good pasture with a companion is a kind option when ridden work is no longer comfortable.

/pets/arthritis-in-llamas-and-alpacas:
All pet guidesLlamas & Alpacas

Camelids are stoic animals that hide lameness until it's advanced. Learn the subtle signs of joint disease in llamas and alpacas and the husbandry changes that keep them comfortable.

Camelids mask pain — watch for lying down more and lagging behind the herd.

Important: Camelids metabolise drugs differently from other livestock. Never dose a llama or alpaca with medication prescribed for sheep, horses or dogs — always get camelid-specific veterinary advice.

Signs in a stoic species

Llamas and alpacas rarely show obvious lameness until joint disease is advanced. Earlier clues: spending more time cushed (lying down), rising slowly or awkwardly, lagging behind the herd, reduced range while grazing, weight shifting at the standing rest, and reluctance on slopes or rough ground. Older animals and those with previous limb injuries are most at risk.

Arthritic camelids often separate slightly from the herd and graze less widely.

Husbandry adjustments

Keep body condition lean — overweight camelids load their joints heavily. Provide well-drained, even paddocks and avoid deep mud, which strains joints with every step. Ensure shelter with deep, dry bedding so animals can cush comfortably. Keep toenails trimmed on schedule: overgrown nails alter limb alignment and accelerate joint wear. Position hay and water so arthritic animals don't have to travel far or compete.

Working with your vet

A camelid-experienced vet can confirm arthritis by examination and X-ray. Treatment typically combines NSAIDs dosed for camelids, joint supplements, and management changes. Because llamas and alpacas are herd animals, keep an arthritic animal with at least one calm companion — isolation causes stress that worsens everything.
