All pet guidesAll pets

Ramps, rugs, raised bowls and warm beds — small changes around the home dramatically reduce daily joint strain for arthritic dogs and cats.

A supportive orthopaedic bed in a draught-free spot pays for itself in comfort.

Important: If your pet suddenly can't manage stairs, cries when handled, or drags a limb, that's beyond home adaptation — see your vet promptly.

Flooring and traction

Slipping on laminate or tile is both painful and dangerous for arthritic pets. Lay non-slip runners along main routes, add a mat where your pet eats and drinks, and keep claws and foot fur trimmed for grip. Toe grips (small rubber rings for dog claws) help dogs that still slip.

Steps or a ramp let cats keep their favourite high spots without painful jumps.

Beds, warmth and rest

An orthopaedic memory-foam bed with a low entry lip, placed away from draughts and off cold floors, reduces morning stiffness noticeably. For cats, a warm igloo bed at floor level plus a heated pad (thermostatically controlled, pet-safe) is often the most-used gift you'll ever buy.

Access without jumping

A car ramp saves a large dog's elbows and shoulders many times a day. Pet steps beside the sofa or bed let dogs and cats keep their favourite spots. For cats, cut a low entrance into a high-sided litter tray, and add a tray on every floor of the house.

Food, water and routine

Raise bowls for large dogs so they don't load sore necks and elbows. Keep water on every floor. Feed puzzle feeders at ground level for gentle mental and physical activity. Keep routines predictable — arthritic pets manage best when they can pace themselves.

Excess weight is the most powerful — and most fixable — driver of arthritis pain in pets. A practical guide to body condition scoring and safe weight loss for dogs, cats, horses and camelids.

You should feel ribs easily under a light fat cover and see a waist from above.

Important: Never starve or crash-diet a pet — rapid weight loss is dangerous, especially in cats. Ask your vet practice for a supervised weight clinic; most UK practices run them free with a vet nurse.

Why weight matters more than any supplement

In dogs, studies show weight loss of 6-9% of body weight measurably reduces lameness — an effect comparable to starting an NSAID. The mechanics are simple: less load per stride, thousands of strides per day. The same principle holds for cats, horses and camelids.

Cats lose weight safely at no more than 1-2% of body weight per week.

Score, don't guess

Use body condition scoring (BCS): for dogs and cats, you should feel ribs easily under a thin fat layer and see a waist from above. Your vet or vet nurse will score your pet free at most practices and set a target weight. Weigh monthly on the same scales.

Safe rate of loss

Dogs: 1-2% of body weight per week. Cats: no more than 1-2% weekly — rapid feline weight loss risks serious liver disease (hepatic lipidosis), so never crash-diet a cat. Horses: aim for gradual loss over a season with soaked hay, grazing muzzles and increased work as comfort allows. Always cut treats first; they're usually 20-30% of calories.

All pet guidesAll pets

The single most common mistake owners make is weekend-warrior exercise. Here's how to build a joint-friendly movement routine for dogs, cats and horses alike.

Consistency beats intensity: the same gentle route daily is ideal.

Important: If your pet shows increased lameness, night restlessness or pain lasting more than 48 hours after exercise, contact your vet before continuing the routine.

The golden rule

Consistent, moderate, frequent movement — never boom and bust. For dogs: three short walks daily beats one long weekend hike. For cats: several short play sessions with a wand toy at ground level. For horses: daily turnout plus regular gentle ridden or in-hand work. Two days of soreness after activity means it was too much; scale back and rebuild gradually.

Avoid high-speed chase games that twist and jar arthritic joints.

Warm up, especially in winter

Cold, stiff joints injure easily. Start every walk slowly for the first five minutes; for horses, walk 10-15 minutes before trot work. In cold weather, a coat for short-haired or elderly dogs and a quarter sheet for clipped horses keeps joint-supporting muscles warm.

Surfaces matter

Grass and woodland paths are kinder than pavement for dogs. For horses, consistent arena surfaces beat rutted frozen ground. Swimming and hydrotherapy (widely available for dogs in the UK, increasingly for horses) build strength with near-zero joint load.

Most pet arthritis can be managed at a routine appointment — but some signs need urgent attention. Know the difference.

Book a routine appointment for gradual stiffness; go urgently for sudden non-weight-bearing lameness.

Important: Never give any pet human painkillers while waiting for an appointment. Paracetamol and ibuprofen are toxic to dogs and cats — paracetamol can kill a cat in a single dose.

Book a routine appointment when...

Your pet is gradually stiffer after rest, slower on walks, jumping less, grooming less (cats), or you've noticed two or more changes on the home checks in our species guides. Gradual-onset signs suit a planned consultation where your vet can examine properly and build a stepped plan.

Many UK practices run free nurse-led mobility and weight clinics.

See a vet urgently when...

Your pet suddenly cannot bear weight on a limb, a joint is hot and swollen, there's a possible injury, your pet cries when touched or moved, stops eating, or a previously managed animal deteriorates rapidly. Sudden severe signs can mean fracture, ligament rupture or joint infection — all need same-day attention.

What to bring to the appointment

A short phone video of the stiffness or lameness at home is genuinely useful — many pets move differently (or perfectly!) in the consult room. Note when signs are worst (mornings? after exercise? cold weather?), what helps, and any products you already give, including doses.

Money worries shouldn't delay care

Ask about nurse-led mobility clinics (often free), payment plans, and whether your insurance covers physiotherapy or hydrotherapy on referral. UK charities including PDSA and Blue Cross provide subsidised veterinary care for owners on qualifying benefits.

1. Who We Are

Living With Arthritis ("we", "us", "our") is committed to protecting your personal data. This policy explains how we collect, use and safeguard information when you use our website and services. We operate in accordance with the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018.

2. Information We Collect

We may collect the following types of personal information:

  • Contact details: Your name, email address and phone number when you email us (many site forms currently open your email client via mailto) or contact us by phone.
  • Health-related information: Details you voluntarily share about your arthritis condition when using our self-help tools or chatbot.
  • Usage data: Information about how you navigate our website, including pages visited, time spent and device information, collected through cookies and similar technologies.
  • Donation data: Payment information processed securely through our payment provider when you make a donation. We do not store full card details.
  • Communication records: Content of messages you send us by email, phone, or (if enabled) chat feedback tools. We do not currently operate a server-side form database on this website.

3. How We Use Your Information

We use your personal data to:

  • Provide our services, including virtual physiotherapy guidance, self-help tools and online assistance.
  • Respond to enquiries you send us.
  • Process and acknowledge donations. Gift Aid reclaim will only apply after HMRC Gift Aid registration is live; we will update this policy when that happens.
  • Improve our website, services and user experience through anonymised analytics.
  • Comply with legal obligations and protect against fraud.

4. Legal Basis for Processing

We process your data based on one or more of the following grounds:

  • Consent: Where you have given clear consent for us to process your personal data for a specific purpose.
  • Contract: Where processing is necessary to fulfil a service you have requested (e.g. responding to a donation or enquiry).
  • Legitimate interests: Where we have a genuine reason to use your data and this does not override your rights (e.g. improving our services).
  • Legal obligation: Where we are required to process data by law.

5. Sharing Your Information

We do not sell your personal information to third parties. We may share data with:

  • Service providers who help us deliver our website and services (e.g. hosting, payment processing, email delivery), under strict data protection agreements.
  • Regulatory or law enforcement bodies where required by law.
  • HMRC for Gift Aid processing only once Gift Aid registration is live and a valid declaration exists.

6. Data Retention

We retain personal data only for as long as necessary to fulfil the purposes for which it was collected. Donation records are kept for up to 7 years for financial compliance. Contact enquiries are kept for up to 2 years unless ongoing communication is required.

7. Your Rights

Under UK GDPR, you have the right to:

  • Access the personal data we hold about you.
  • Request correction of inaccurate or incomplete data.
  • Request deletion of your data (right to be forgotten).
  • Restrict or object to certain processing activities.
  • Data portability — receive your data in a structured, machine-readable format.
  • Withdraw consent at any time where processing is based on consent.

To exercise any of these rights, please contact us at info@livingwitharthritis.org.uk.

8. Security

We implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect your personal data against unauthorised access, alteration, disclosure or destruction. All data transmitted through our website is encrypted using industry-standard TLS/SSL protocols.

9. Children's Privacy

Our services are not directed at children under 13. We do not knowingly collect personal data from children under 13. If you believe a child has provided us with personal data, please contact us and we will take steps to delete it.

10. Changes to This Policy

We may update this Privacy Policy from time to time. Any changes will be posted on this page with an updated revision date. We encourage you to review this policy periodically.

11. Current website processing model

As of September 2026 this website is primarily a static educational site. Many forms hand off to email (mailto) rather than posting personal data to our servers. Analytics (for example Google Analytics) load only with cookie consent where required. Donation card details, if you use a payment link, are handled by the payment provider — we do not store full card numbers. This summary is not a substitute for solicitor-reviewed privacy wording; trustees should commission a formal review as processing expands.

12. Contact Us

You also have the right to lodge a complaint with the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) at ico.org.uk.

/resources/pip-evidence-diary:
Resources · Linkable asset

Quick answer: A PIP evidence diary is a day-by-day record of how arthritis affects everyday tasks and getting around. Keep it for at least 2 to 4 weeks, including bad days. Note what you tried, how long it took, any pain, aids or help you needed, and what happened afterwards. Use it to write your PIP form answers.

Clinically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 · 23 October 2026

Educational information for people in the UK living with arthritis — not a diagnosis or personal medical advice. Check medicines and exercises with your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111. See our medical disclaimer, editorial standards and claims policy.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Personal Independence Payment and the DWP PIP assessment guide. This diary is not a DWP form. It is a tool to help you remember and explain how arthritis affects you.

When you fill in the PIP form, it is easy to forget the bad mornings, the extra time things take, the help you quietly rely on and how you feel the day after a busy one. A diary solves this. It gives you real, specific examples in your own words, and shows how often difficulties happen, which is exactly what the assessment looks at. The templates below can be printed (use the print button above) or copied into a notebook or notes app.

Why a diary helps a PIP claim

PIP is not awarded for a diagnosis. It is based on how your condition affects 12 everyday activities. Three rules make a diary especially useful for arthritis:

  • "Most of the time". GOV.UK says you must have difficulty with tasks on more than half of the days over a 12-month period. A diary shows how many days are affected, not just how bad the worst day is.
  • The "reliably" test. The DWP assessment guide says you should only count as able to do something if you can do it safely, to an acceptable standard, repeatedly and in a reasonable time (no more than twice as long as someone without your condition would take). A diary captures the time, pain, rests and near misses that show this.
  • Fluctuation. PIP regulations look at which descriptor applies on more than 50% of days. A diary covering several weeks shows the real pattern of good and bad days and flares.

How to use the templates

  1. Keep it for at least 2 to 4 weeks, ideally including a flare. If your claim form has already arrived, start straight away; GOV.UK says you should usually return it within 1 month, and you can ask the PIP enquiry line for more time.
  2. Fill it in at the end of each day, or ask someone to help if writing is painful. Voice notes on a phone are fine too.
  3. Be honest and specific. Record good days as well as bad. A diary that only shows bad days is less believable.
  4. Record what happens, not just what you do. Note time taken, pain before and after, rests, help needed, aids used, accidents and how you felt later or the next day.
  5. Use the weekly grid below for a quick overview, and the daily page for detail.
  6. Keep a copy and send a summary (not necessarily every page) with your form, along with clinic letters and prescription lists.

Template 1: weekly overview grid

Put a short note or code in each box. For example: OK (managed without difficulty), S (slow, more than twice as long), P (painful), A (used an aid), H (needed help or prompting), X (could not do it). Use the pain row for a 0 to 10 score.

ActivityMonTueWedThuFriSatSun
Pain / stiffness (0–10)
Preparing food
Eating and drinking
Medicines / injections
Washing and bathing
Using the toilet
Dressing / undressing
Moving around (distance, aid, rests)
Going out / journeys
Help needed from someone else
Falls, near misses, dropped items

Template 2: daily diary page

Copy this page for each day. Short notes are enough.

QuestionYour notes
Date, and was today a good, average or bad day?
Morning stiffness: how long until you could move more easily?
Pain score on waking, midday and evening (0 to 10)
Washing and bathing: what you did, how long it took, aids or help used
Using the toilet: any difficulty getting on or off, or managing clothing
Dressing and undressing: fastenings, socks, shoes, time taken, help needed
Preparing food: what you made, whether you sat down, used a microwave or needed help
Eating and drinking: cutting food, lifting cups, any difficulty
Medicines and treatments: opening packs, injections, reminders, help from others
Moving around: how far you walked, how long it took, rests, aids, how you felt afterwards
Going out and journeys: did you go out, how, and did anyone need to go with you?
Falls, near misses, dropped items, burns or spills
Tiredness and how today affects tomorrow
Anything you could not do or put off because of your arthritis

Template 3: prompts for each PIP activity

The PIP form asks about each activity in turn. These prompts help you notice the details that matter for arthritis.

PIP activityWhat to note in your diary
1. Preparing foodPeeling, chopping, opening jars and packets, lifting pans or a full kettle, standing at the cooker, using a perching stool, relying on ready meals or a microwave
2. Eating and drinkingCutting food, holding cutlery, lifting a cup, needing adapted cutlery
3. Managing treatmentsOpening blister packs and bottles, self-injecting (for example methotrexate or a biologic), remembering doses, needing someone to help
4. Washing and bathingGetting in and out of the bath or shower, washing hair, reaching feet and back, using a shower seat or bath board, someone nearby for safety
5. Managing toilet needsGetting on and off the toilet, wiping, raised seat or rails, managing clothing
6. Dressing and undressingButtons, zips, bras, socks, tights, shoes and laces, dressing aids, sitting to dress, time taken
7. CommunicatingUsually not affected by arthritis alone; note any difficulty if it applies to you
8. ReadingNote any difficulty if it applies (for example holding books or papers with painful hands is not usually scored, but sight problems are)
9. Mixing with other peopleAnxiety, low mood or exhaustion that stops you engaging with others, if relevant
10. BudgetingUsually not affected by arthritis alone; note if another condition affects it
11. Planning and following journeysRelevant if anxiety, confusion or another condition affects journeys
12. Moving aroundDistance you can walk reliably and repeatedly, your pace, rests, aids, pain, and how you feel afterwards and the next day

Template 4: walking and moving around log

Moving around is often the hardest activity to describe accurately. Measure a familiar route once (for example, front door to the end of the road) using a map app, then log each walk.

DateRoute and distanceAid usedTime takenWhen did pain start? When did you stop?How did you feel afterwards and the next day?

Only walk as far as is safe and comfortable for you. Do not push yourself to "prove" a point; you should describe your usual ability, not test your limits.

Template 5: flare log

Flare startedFlare endedJoints affectedWhat you could not do during the flareHelp you neededContact with GP, rheumatology or 111

Add up how many days a month you are in a flare. This helps show whether difficulties happen on more than half of days.

Template 6: statement from someone who helps you

A short statement from a partner, relative, friend or carer can back up your diary. They can copy and complete this:

My name is [name]. I am [relationship, for example partner, daughter, neighbour] and I have known [your name] for [time]. I see them [how often].

Because of their arthritis, I help them with: [for example dressing most mornings, getting in and out of the bath, opening medicines, cooking hot meals].

On a typical day: [what they can and cannot do, how long things take].

On a bad day, which happens about [number] days a week or month: [what changes].

I have seen: [falls, near misses, burns, dropping things, needing to stop and rest].

Signed: [name] Date: [date] Contact number (optional): [number]

An illustrative example of a good entry

This is a made-up example to show the level of detail that helps. It is not a real person.

Tuesday, bad day. Hands and knees very stiff for about 90 minutes after waking. Could not grip the kettle until my tablets started working, so my partner made breakfast. Took about 35 minutes to dress sitting on the bed; partner did my bra and socks. Showered with the seat, but could not wash my hair. Walked to the corner shop with my stick (about 150 metres by map app), had to stop twice, took about 6 minutes and needed to sit down when I got home. Knees throbbing all evening.

Notice it includes time taken, help from another person, aids, distance, rests and the after-effects.

Template 7: one-page summary to attach to your form

At the end of your diary period, fill in this summary. It makes it easy for the person deciding your claim to see the pattern.

ActivityDays with difficulty (out of total days recorded)Aid or help neededTypical time takenBest example from the diary (date)
Preparing food
Washing and bathing
Dressing and undressing
Managing treatments
Moving around
Other activities that apply to you

Common diary mistakes to avoid

  • Only writing "bad day" or "pain 8/10". Say what the pain stopped you doing, and what you did instead.
  • Leaving out help you take for granted. If your partner always opens jars or does up your buttons, write it down, even if it feels minor.
  • Forgetting the after-effects. If a trip to the shops means you spend the afternoon on the sofa, that affects whether you can do it repeatedly.
  • Not mentioning things you avoid. If you no longer cook hot meals or have a bath because it is unsafe, say so and explain why.
  • Exaggerating. An honest, consistent record is far more persuasive than one that does not match your clinic letters.
  • Stopping once the form is sent. Keep going until the decision arrives. You may need it for an assessment or a challenge.

What to keep with your diary

  • Your latest prescription list, including injections and side effects
  • Clinic letters from rheumatology, orthopaedics, pain clinic, physiotherapy or occupational therapy
  • Any care plan, equipment list or occupational therapy report
  • Your supporter statement (Template 6)
  • A copy of the completed PIP form before you send it

Turning your diary into form answers

  1. For each activity, count how many days in the diary you had difficulty, and how many of those you needed an aid, help or much more time.
  2. Write a short summary: "On about 5 days a week I need help to get dressed. It takes me around 30 minutes and I have to sit down."
  3. Add one or two specific examples from the diary.
  4. Explain what happens if you try without help: pain, risk of falling, not being able to repeat it later.
  5. Attach supporting evidence such as clinic letters and your prescription list.

Our complete PIP guide explains the points system, the form and the assessment in full. If you are refused, the diary is also useful evidence for a mandatory reconsideration or appeal.

Using the diary for other claims

The same records can help with Adult Disability Payment in Scotland, Attendance Allowance if you are over State Pension age (see our Attendance Allowance guide), a Blue Badge application, or a Work Capability Assessment for Universal Credit or ESA. In Northern Ireland, PIP is run by the Department for Communities, and the activities assessed are the same.

Getting free help

Citizens Advice (England and Wales), Citizens Advice Scotland, Advice NI, Turn2us, Scope and Disability Rights UK all provide free information or advice about disability benefits. We are not connected to these organisations. Many councils also run a welfare rights service. An adviser can look at your diary and help match your difficulties to the PIP descriptors.

When to talk to your GP or rheumatology team

A diary sometimes shows that things are worse than you realised. Contact your GP or rheumatology advice line if flares are getting more frequent or lasting longer, you are falling, or pain is stopping you looking after yourself. Get urgent help from NHS 111 or your GP the same day if a joint becomes suddenly hot, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel unwell or have a fever.

Frequently asked questions

How long should I keep a PIP diary?

Aim for at least 2 to 4 weeks, ideally including a flare and some better days. If your claim form has already arrived, start straight away and keep going while you fill it in.

Do I have to send my diary to DWP?

No, it is optional. Many people send a summary or a few representative weeks with their form, plus clinic letters and prescription lists. Keep the original and a copy of anything you send.

Is this diary an official DWP form?

No. It is a free template to help you record and explain how arthritis affects you. The official form is called 'How your disability affects you'.

What if writing is painful?

Ask someone to write for you, use voice notes or a notes app, or use short codes in the weekly grid. The detail matters more than the format.

Should I record good days too?

Yes. Recording good and bad days gives an honest picture and shows how often difficulties happen, which is what PIP looks at.

Can I use the diary in Scotland?

Yes. Adult Disability Payment looks at similar daily living and mobility activities, so the same records are useful for an ADP application.

Can someone else fill in the diary for me?

Yes. A partner, relative or carer can write it for you, or add their own notes about the help they give. Make sure it reflects what actually happens and that you agree with it.

What to record each day

  • Pain (0–10)

Contact NHS 111 urgently, or call 999 in an emergency, if a single joint becomes hot, red and swollen and you feel feverish or unwell, if you suddenly cannot bear weight, or if you have new weakness, numbness or loss of bladder or bowel control.

/safeguarding:
Last updated: March 2026

1. Our Commitment

Living With Arthritis is committed to safeguarding and promoting the welfare of all individuals who engage with our services. We recognise our responsibility to take all reasonable steps to promote safe practice and to protect vulnerable adults from harm, abuse and exploitation.

2. Scope

This policy applies to all trustees, staff, volunteers, and anyone working on behalf of Living With Arthritis, including those providing services through our website, community forums, and virtual physiotherapy sessions.

3. Definitions

A vulnerable adult is a person aged 18 or over who may be unable to take care of themselves or protect themselves from harm or exploitation due to mental or physical disability, age, or illness. Abuse includes physical, emotional, financial, sexual abuse, neglect, and discriminatory abuse.

4. Principles

  • The welfare of adults at risk is paramount
  • All adults have the right to be protected from abuse regardless of age, disability, gender, racial heritage, religious belief, sexual orientation, or identity
  • All suspicions and allegations of abuse will be taken seriously and responded to swiftly and appropriately
  • We will work in partnership with other agencies to safeguard adults at risk

5. Online Safety

Our community forums and help chat are moderated. All user-generated content is reviewed for harmful material. Our help chat provides evidence-based health information only and explicitly directs users to 111 helpline or emergency services for urgent concerns. We do not provide medical diagnoses.

6. Reporting Concerns

If someone is in immediate danger, call 999.

For non-emergency safeguarding concerns about our services, please contact:

safeguarding@livingwitharthritis.org.uk 07760 512 084

7. Review

This policy is reviewed annually by the Board of Trustees and updated as necessary to reflect changes in legislation, best practice, or organisational structure.

Medications and supplements for joint health

When exercise, weight management and physiotherapy are not enough on their own, people and their clinicians often turn to medication or supplements to help control joint pain and inflammation. The decision is never trivial — it always involves weighing benefit against risk. UK search behaviour shows steady interest in specific drugs such as allopurinol and corticosteroids, alongside growing curiosity about natural options like turmeric. Understanding what each does, and what it cannot do, helps people make safer, more informed choices alongside their GP or rheumatology team.

Allopurinol is widely used to treat chronic gout, a type of inflammatory arthritis caused by excess uric acid in the blood. The high search volume around “allopurinol side effects” suggests many patients are either monitoring their own treatment or hesitating to start. Allopurinol is effective at lowering uric acid levels and preventing painful flares, but it requires careful education. Common side effects include rash and gastrointestinal upset; rare but serious hypersensitivity reactions are also possible. People taking it should know the warning signs and attend the blood tests their GP requests to monitor kidney and liver function.

Corticosteroids are another commonly searched group. They are powerful anti-inflammatory drugs that can give rapid relief in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, severe osteoarthritis flares and acute back pain. The trade-off is real: long-term systemic steroid use is associated with osteoporosis, weight gain, raised blood sugar and increased infection risk. For that reason, they are typically used either as short courses or as targeted injections into the affected joint, which keeps systemic exposure low.

Alongside these pharmaceutical options, interest in natural alternatives continues to grow — turmeric in particular. The active compound curcumin has been studied for its anti-inflammatory effects, and many people prefer it as a long-term option compared with continuous NSAID or steroid use. Evidence supports a modest benefit for joint pain and inflammation, but “natural” does not automatically mean safe. Turmeric can interact with blood thinners and may cause gastrointestinal upset in high doses. Curcumin also has poor natural bioavailability — it is usually combined with piperine (from black pepper) for meaningful absorption.

Most people do best with a combined approach rather than a single magic bullet: appropriate prescribed medication where it is genuinely needed, supplements used carefully alongside conventional care, and consistent attention to exercise, sleep and diet underneath it all.

This is general information, not medical advice. Speak to a GP, rheumatologist or pharmacist before starting, stopping or combining any medication or supplement.

/supplements/collagen:
Clinically reviewed · Louis Maxwell, HCPC PH128483 · 16 September 2026

Educational information for people in the UK living with arthritis — not a diagnosis or personal medical advice. Check medicines and exercises with your GP, pharmacist or rheumatology team. For emergencies call 999; for urgent advice use NHS 111. See our medical disclaimer, editorial standards and claims policy.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against Arthritis UK's collagen page, NICE NG226 and the published trials listed below. This page is general education, not a recommendation to buy any product.

What collagen is

Collagen is a protein found throughout your body. It gives structure and strength to cartilage, bone, tendons, ligaments and skin. Your body makes its own collagen from the protein you eat, and it needs vitamin C to do this. The NHS lists "maintaining healthy skin, blood vessels, bones and cartilage" among the jobs vitamin C does.

As we get older, the body makes less collagen. That is the main reason researchers, and supplement companies, have looked at whether taking collagen by mouth could help joints.

The types of collagen supplement

Collagen supplements are always made from animal or fish sources. Products vary a lot, and research on one type does not automatically apply to another. The two main forms are:

FormWhat it isUsual source
Hydrolysed collagen (collagen peptides, collagen hydrolysate)Collagen broken down into small pieces so it dissolves in drinks and is easier to digest. Mostly types I and III.Cow hides and bones (bovine), pig skin or fish skin and scales (marine)
Undenatured type II collagen (often sold as UC-II)Collagen kept in its natural structure. Type II is the main collagen in cartilage. It is thought to work by influencing the immune system rather than by supplying building blocks.Chicken breastbone cartilage

You will also see "plant-based collagen" or "vegan collagen". Arthritis UK points out this is not real collagen: it contains ingredients meant to help the body make its own, and there is much less research on it.

What the evidence shows

The honest summary: some trials suggest collagen may slightly improve pain or stiffness for some people with osteoarthritis, but results are inconsistent, products and doses differ, and many studies are small or industry-funded. There is no good evidence that collagen rebuilds damaged cartilage. The NHS does not recommend collagen for arthritis, and NICE does not include it in its osteoarthritis treatments.

Osteoarthritis

  • Arthritis UK says studies suggest collagen may reduce pain or improve movement for some people, particularly with osteoarthritis, but studies have not all found the same results and there is not enough evidence to recommend it as a routine treatment.
  • A 2026 umbrella review (Ravindran and colleagues) pooled 16 systematic reviews covering 113 trials and almost 8,000 participants on skin and musculoskeletal outcomes. It found some evidence of benefit for osteoarthritis symptoms, but the trials used different types and doses of collagen and measured results in different ways, so firm conclusions are difficult.
  • A 2019 meta-analysis (García-Coronado and colleagues, International Orthopaedics) of placebo-controlled trials found collagen reduced overall osteoarthritis symptom scores and pain on a visual scale. However, when the symptom score was split into parts, only stiffness improved significantly; the pain and function sub-scores did not.
  • A 2016 trial of undenatured type II collagen (Lugo and colleagues, Nutrition Journal) gave 191 people with knee osteoarthritis either 40 mg a day of UC-II, glucosamine plus chondroitin, or placebo for 180 days. The UC-II group did better than both other groups. Two of the authors worked for the company that made the supplement, which is important to know when weighing the result.

Rheumatoid arthritis

Arthritis UK says studies of collagen for rheumatoid arthritis have had mixed results. Some found fewer swollen or tender joints and others found little or no benefit. In one trial that compared type II collagen with methotrexate, both groups improved, but the methotrexate group improved most. Overall, the results are not consistent enough to support collagen as a treatment for RA. Collagen should never be used instead of disease-modifying medicines.

What NICE says

NICE's osteoarthritis guideline, NG226, does not recommend collagen. Its core treatments are therapeutic exercise, weight management where appropriate, and information and support. It specifically says not to offer glucosamine, explaining there is "no strong evidence of benefit". For rheumatoid arthritis, NICE NG100 says complementary therapies may give some people short-term symptom relief, but there is little or no evidence of long-term benefit.

Why the evidence is so uncertain

  • Different products. Hydrolysed peptides and undenatured type II collagen are very different, yet they are often grouped together in reviews.
  • Different doses and lengths. Trials have used very different amounts for different lengths of time.
  • Small studies. Many trials have small numbers of people, which makes chance results more likely.
  • Industry funding. Several trials were funded or run by supplement manufacturers. That does not make the results wrong, but independent studies are needed.
  • Osteoarthritis pain naturally varies. Symptoms go up and down, and people in trials often improve on placebo too, so a good placebo-controlled design matters.

Can you get collagen from food?

You do not need to eat collagen to make collagen. Your body builds it from amino acids, which come from any protein in your diet, and it needs vitamin C. Most adults aged 19 to 64 need 40mg of vitamin C a day, and the NHS says you should be able to get all you need from your diet.

Foods that support your body's own collagen production include:

  • Protein foods: fish, eggs, chicken, dairy, beans, lentils, tofu and nuts. Our protein guide explains how much you need and how to spread it through the day.
  • Vitamin C foods: oranges, berries, kiwi fruit, peppers, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and potatoes.
  • Foods containing collagen itself: bone broth, chicken skin, fish skin and gelatine. These contain collagen in unpredictable amounts, so they are not the same as the products used in trials.

A varied, balanced diet based on the NHS Eatwell Guide covers these naturally. Taking large amounts of vitamin C, more than 1,000mg a day, can cause stomach pain, diarrhoea and wind, and will not boost collagen further.

Is collagen safe?

Arthritis UK says studies suggest collagen supplements are safe for most people and serious side effects are uncommon. Reported side effects tend to be mild, such as feeling full or bloated, mild indigestion or an unpleasant taste.

Collagen may not be suitable if:

  • you have a fish or shellfish allergy (marine collagen) or an egg allergy (some products contain eggshell membrane)
  • you are vegetarian or vegan, or avoid certain animal products for religious reasons. Check the source on the label
  • you have been told to limit your protein, for example because of kidney disease. Collagen powders add protein, so ask your kidney team or dietitian first
  • you are pregnant or breastfeeding, as there is little research in these groups

Medicines and interactions

Arthritis UK says there are no well-known interactions between collagen and arthritis medicines. The bigger risk is what else is in the product. Many "joint formula" supplements combine collagen with other ingredients, and some of those do matter:

  • Warfarin and other anticoagulants: combination products may contain turmeric (curcumin) or fish oil, which may increase the risk of bleeding with blood thinners. The NHS also advises telling your doctor about any vitamins or supplements before taking warfarin and not taking vitamin K supplements. See our turmeric evidence guide for more on this.
  • Methotrexate: the NHS says not to take vitamin or mineral supplements that contain folic acid (folate) if you already take folic acid prescribed by your doctor, and not to take folic acid on the same day as methotrexate. Some "joint and skin" collagen blends contain added vitamins, so check the label. Turmeric products have also been linked with liver problems, and methotrexate can affect the liver.
  • NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen: Arthritis UK advises people taking anti-inflammatory painkillers to get medical advice before using fish oil, because it can increase the risk of bleeding. NSAIDs can already cause stomach bleeding on their own.
  • Glucosamine: often added to joint products. NICE does not recommend it for osteoarthritis. Ask a pharmacist before taking it with any blood thinner.

Before you start any supplement, ask your community pharmacist to check the full ingredients list against everything you take, including over-the-counter medicines.

If you decide to try collagen

Collagen is not available on NHS prescription, so any trial is at your own cost. Food supplements are regulated as foods in the UK, not as medicines, which means they are not tested for effectiveness before they go on sale. If you choose to try it:

  1. Talk to your GP, rheumatology team or pharmacist first, especially if you take any regular medicines.
  2. Choose a single-ingredient product so you know what you are taking and can tell whether it helps.
  3. Check the label for the collagen type and source, the amount per serving, other ingredients, and allergy information.
  4. Be wary of big claims. Supplements cannot legally claim to treat, prevent or cure a disease. Words like "rebuilds cartilage" or "cures joint pain" are a red flag.
  5. Start one thing at a time. If you start collagen, a new exercise programme and a new medicine in the same week, you will not know what made the difference.
  6. Set a time limit and keep a record. Arthritis UK notes that most studies followed people for several months. Score your pain, stiffness and function from 0 to 10 each week. If you notice no difference after about 3 months, it is reasonable to stop and spend the money elsewhere.
  7. Keep taking your prescribed treatment. Collagen must not replace medicines, exercise or other treatment.

What has stronger evidence for joint pain

If your aim is less pain and better movement, these have more support from NICE than any supplement:

  • Therapeutic exercise, including muscle strengthening and general aerobic activity, tailored to you. This is a core NICE treatment for osteoarthritis.
  • Weight management if you are living with overweight or obesity. NICE says any amount of weight loss is likely to help.
  • Effective treatment for inflammatory arthritis, such as disease-modifying medicines for rheumatoid arthritis, started early and reviewed regularly.
  • A balanced, Mediterranean-style diet with enough protein, oily fish, fruit and vegetables.

For a wider look at which nutrition claims hold up, see our arthritis diet myths checked, and compare collagen with other options on our glucosamine page.

Questions to ask a pharmacist

  • Is this product safe with all the medicines I take?
  • Does it contain anything else, such as turmeric, fish oil, glucosamine, vitamin K or folic acid?
  • Is it suitable with my allergies or other health conditions?
  • How should I take it, and what side effects should I look out for?
  • When should I stop if I do not notice any benefit?

When to get medical help

Speak to your GP, rheumatology team or call NHS 111 if:

  • you have a hot, red, swollen joint, especially if you feel feverish or unwell. Call 999 or go to A&E if you feel very unwell
  • your joint pain, swelling or stiffness is getting worse despite treatment
  • you get a rash, swelling of the lips or face, or difficulty breathing after taking a supplement. This could be an allergic reaction and needs urgent help: call 999 if breathing is affected
  • you notice yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine or unusual tiredness while taking a combination joint supplement, especially if it contains turmeric
  • you take warfarin or another blood thinner and notice unusual bruising or bleeding
  • you have kidney disease and want to know whether extra protein is safe for you

Take the supplement packaging with you so the clinician can see exactly what you have been taking.

/supplements/collagen-alternatives:
Last reviewed: 1 August 2026

What can I take instead of collagen for joint pain?

There is no such thing as vegan collagen, but you do not need collagen to support your joints. Turmeric/curcumin (~1,000 mg/day) has the strongest anti-inflammatory evidence, glucosamine sulfate (1,500 mg/day) has the most data, MSM (1.5–3 g/day) gives modest knee relief, and omega-3, vitamin C and vitamin D cover the nutritional side. Adequate protein plus vitamin C lets your body build its own collagen. None of these beat strength training and weight management.

Why look for an alternative to collagen?

Every collagen supplement on the shelf comes from an animal. There is no plant source, because plants do not make collagen.

  • Bovine collagen — from cattle hide. Not suitable for vegetarians or vegans, and rarely certified halal or kosher.
  • Marine collagen — from fish skin and scales. Off-limits with a fish allergy.
  • Undenatured type II (UC-II) — from chicken sternum cartilage.

Cost is the other reason people look elsewhere. A 10 g daily dose of hydrolysed collagen gets through a tub quickly, and the evidence behind it is younger and thinner than the marketing suggests.

What are the evidence-based alternatives?

Turmeric and curcumin — the strongest case

Curcumin blocks inflammatory pathways including NF-κB and COX-2. Trials of around 1,000 mg/day report pain and function improvements in knee osteoarthritis in some small trials. Evidence is limited, and curcumin is not an equivalent alternative to NSAIDs. Absorption is poor on its own, so look for piperine (black pepper extract) or a phospholipid formulation. Plant-based, so it fits every restricted diet. Full turmeric guide.

Glucosamine sulfate — the most-studied option

1,500 mg/day of glucosamine sulfate is the form with the best data, though results across trials are inconsistent and NICE does not recommend it. Most glucosamine is made from shellfish shells; vegetarian corn-fermented versions exist. Avoid it if you take warfarin, as it can raise INR. Full glucosamine guide.

MSM — modest but well tolerated

Methylsulfonylmethane at 1.5–3 g/day produced small improvements in pain and physical function in knee osteoarthritis studies. It is a sulfur compound, not animal-derived, and is one of the better-tolerated supplements. Full MSM guide.

Omega-3 — fish oil or algal oil

The evidence is strongest in rheumatoid arthritis, where 2.7 g+ of EPA/DHA a day reduces morning stiffness and tender joint counts. Vegans and anyone with a fish allergy can use algal oil, which supplies the same EPA and DHA grown directly from algae.

Vitamin C and adequate protein — the collagen builders

Your body synthesises its own collagen from amino acids, and the enzymes that do it require vitamin C. Older adults typically need 1.0–1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight a day to hold on to muscle, which is what stabilises an arthritic joint. Fruit and vegetables cover the vitamin C. This is what "vegan collagen" products are actually selling you — usually at a markup.

Vitamin D — correct a deficiency, do not megadose

Low vitamin D is common in the UK, particularly October to March, and is linked with muscle weakness and more pain. The standard advice is 10 µg (400 IU) daily through autumn and winter. Correcting a deficiency helps; taking more than you need does not.

"Vegan collagen" — read the label

These contain no collagen. They are blends of vitamin C, glycine, proline, zinc and botanical extracts. That is not a scam in itself — those nutrients do support collagen synthesis — but you can get the same from a decent diet and a cheap vitamin C tablet.

Which alternative suits which diet or allergy?

  • Vegan or vegetarian: turmeric/curcumin, MSM, algal omega-3, vitamin C, lichen-derived vitamin D, corn-fermented glucosamine.
  • Halal or kosher: the same plant and mineral based list — check capsule shells, as gelatin capsules are common. Look for vegetable cellulose (HPMC).
  • Fish allergy: avoid marine collagen and fish oil; use algal omega-3 instead.
  • Shellfish allergy: avoid standard glucosamine; turmeric and MSM are safe choices.
  • On warfarin or other blood thinners: be cautious with turmeric, omega-3 and glucosamine — speak to your pharmacist before starting any of them.

What actually outperforms every supplement?

This is the uncomfortable part of any supplement page. The three things with the strongest evidence in osteoarthritis are free or nearly free:

  • Strength and low-impact exercise. Building the muscle around a joint reduces pain and improves function more reliably than any capsule. Exercise hub.
  • Weight management. Every pound lost takes several pounds of load off the knees and reduces systemic inflammation.
  • An anti-inflammatory eating pattern. Mediterranean-style eating lowers pain and stiffness scores and supports weight control. Diet guide.

UK context: NICE guideline NG226 does not recommend any oral supplement for osteoarthritis, and none of the products on this page are prescribed. Any trial is at your own cost — so run one at a time, for 12 weeks, and stop if nothing changes.

/supplements/glucosamine:
Does glucosamine work for arthritis?

Evidence is mixed, and NICE advises healthcare professionals not to offer glucosamine for osteoarthritis. It is not a cure and should not replace exercise or recommended treatment. Ask a pharmacist before trying it, especially if you take warfarin or other medicines.

What is glucosamine?

Glucosamine is a natural amino sugar that the body uses to build and repair cartilage — the smooth tissue that cushions the ends of bones in a joint. As we age, cartilage breaks down faster than it can be replaced, which is the main driver of osteoarthritis.

Most glucosamine supplements are made from the shells of shellfish (some vegetarian/vegan versions are fermented from corn). They come in three main forms:

  • Glucosamine sulfate — the form used in most positive UK and European trials. This is what to look for on the label.
  • Glucosamine hydrochloride (HCl) — cheaper, but weaker evidence.
  • N-acetyl glucosamine — sometimes added; very little evidence for arthritis.

Sources and safety information

  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
  • NHS: Taking warfarin with other medicines and supplements

What the evidence says

Glucosamine is one of the most-studied joint supplements in the world — and the results are mixed.

  • European trials of glucosamine sulfate (Pavelka 2002, Reginster 2001) found that 1,500 mg/day for 3 years reduced knee OA pain and slowed joint-space narrowing.
  • The US GAIT study (Clegg 2006) found no benefit for mild knee OA, but a subgroup with moderate-to-severe pain did improve when glucosamine was combined with chondroitin.
  • The LEGS trial (Fransen 2015) showed slowed cartilage loss with combined glucosamine + chondroitin over 2 years.
  • The UK's NICE guidelines (NG226) do not recommend glucosamine on the UK healthcare system because the overall effect is small and inconsistent.

Bottom line: it's not a miracle, but it's safe, cheap, and a reasonable 3-month trial if your osteoarthritis pain isn't being controlled by exercise and weight management alone.

Dosage and how to take it

There is no NHS-recommended glucosamine dose for treating arthritis. If you decide to try a product after speaking with a pharmacist:

  • Follow the product label rather than combining several products.
  • Check whether the formulation and source are clearly stated.
  • Agree how and when you will judge benefit.
  • Stop and seek advice if you develop a suspected side effect.

Side effects and safety

Glucosamine is generally well tolerated. The most common side effects are mild and short-lived:

  • Stomach upset, heartburn, nausea
  • Headache, drowsiness
  • Rash or itching

Ask a pharmacist or GP before use if you

  • Have a shellfish or other significant allergy
  • Are pregnant or breastfeeding
  • Take warfarin or another medicine that needs monitoring
  • Are due to have surgery

Always tell your GP or pharmacist about any supplement you start, especially if you take regular medication.

Glucosamine vs chondroitin, MSM and collagen

  • Chondroitin — often combined with glucosamine, but evidence of meaningful benefit is inconsistent.
  • MSM — small studies exist, but the evidence base remains limited.
  • Collagen products — formulations vary and evidence is not strong enough to promise benefit.
  • Turmeric / curcumin — research is ongoing; products vary and interactions are possible.
  • Omega-3 (fish oil) — best evidence is in rheumatoid arthritis, not OA.

Do not replace prescribed treatment with a supplement. A pharmacist can help check interactions and avoid duplicating ingredients across products.

/supplements/msm:
What is MSM and does it help arthritis?

MSM is an organic sulfur compound (methylsulfonylmethane). Small trials at1,500–3,000 mg/day show modest reductions in knee osteoarthritis pain and stiffness over 12 weeks. It is well tolerated and often combined with glucosamine sulfate. Evidence is weaker than for curcumin or glucosamine alone.

What is MSM?

MSM stands for methylsulfonylmethane. It's a natural organic sulfur compound found in small amounts in plants, animals and humans. Sulfur is a building block for collagen and the cartilage that lines our joints.

As a supplement, MSM is sold for joint pain, stiffness, inflammation, exercise recovery, allergies and skin health. In the UK it usually appears either on its own or stacked with glucosamine and chondroitin.

What the evidence says

  • Kim 2006 — 3,000 mg MSM twice daily for 12 weeks improved knee OA pain and physical function vs placebo.
  • Debbi 2011 — 1.125 g MSM three times daily for 12 weeks reduced pain and improved knee OA function vs placebo.
  • 2017 systematic review (Brien et al.) — MSM produced statistically significant but small improvements in pain and function for knee OA.
  • Combined with glucosamine — several trials suggest the combination outperforms either ingredient alone for moderate OA pain.
  • NICE NG226 does not currently recommend MSM on the UK healthcare system.

The honest summary: real but modest effect, decent safety profile, and best used as a 12-week trial alongside exercise and weight management — not as a replacement for them.

Dosage and how to take it

  • Typical dose: 1,500–3,000 mg per day.
  • Split: two or three doses, taken with food.
  • Form: capsule, tablet or unflavoured powder dissolved in water.
  • Trial length: 8–12 weeks before judging the effect.
  • Stack: commonly combined with 1,500 mg glucosamine sulfate.

Side effects and safety

MSM is one of the better-tolerated joint supplements. Mild side effects can include:

  • Bloating, mild diarrhoea or nausea
  • Headache
  • Skin rash or itching
  • Insomnia if taken late in the day

Take care if you

  • Are pregnant or breastfeeding — not enough safety data, avoid
  • Take blood thinners (warfarin, apixaban) — speak to your GP first
  • Have liver or kidney disease

Always tell your GP or pharmacist about any supplement, especially before surgery or if you start a new prescription medicine.

Palestine — rebuilding bodies broken by war

In Gaza, thousands of people are living with crushed joints, amputations, nerve damage and pain that never lets go. Hospitals that survived are overwhelmed, and rehabilitation — the slow, patient work of learning to move again — is one of the first things to disappear.

Without it, a survivable injury becomes a lifetime of immobility. With it, a father learns to walk to the water queue, a child regains the use of a hand, a mother can lift her baby again. This is the work your Zakat and Sadaqah fund.

Zakat is one of the five pillars of Islam — 2.5% of qualifying wealth held for a lunar year, given as worship. At Living With Arthritis, every Zakat contribution is managed with care, integrity and in full alignment with Shariah guidelines, guided by qualified scholars so it reaches those most deserving.

/self-assessment:
What does the arthritis self-assessment do?

The self-assessment asks five short questions: what kind of arthritis you have, your average pain today on a 0–10 scale, how you would describe your mobility, which joints are affected, and which daily activities are limited. It then points you to Living With Arthritis guides that match your answers. Your answers stay in your browser. It is educational and does not diagnose arthritis or replace a clinician.

How to use your results

  • Take your answers to your GP, practice nurse or physiotherapist so the appointment starts from concrete facts: which joints, how much pain, and what you can no longer do.
  • Repeat it every few weeks. A change in pain score or in the activities you find hard is more useful to a clinician than a single reading.
  • If daily tasks are limited, the PIP and benefits guide explains how the DWP looks at daily living and mobility.

When not to wait

Seek same-day help via NHS 111, or call 999 in an emergency, if a joint becomes suddenly hot, red and swollen, especially with fever, or if back pain comes with loss of bladder or bowel control. NICE guidance on rheumatoid arthritis (NG100) advises urgent referral for suspected persistent synovitis, so new swelling in small joints of the hands or feet should be seen by a GP promptly.
